I. Insolvency resolution process costs and the liquidation costs paid in full.
II. Workmen’s dues for the period of 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date and debts owed to a secured creditor in the event such secured creditor has relinquished security in the manner set out in Section 52, ranking equally.
III. Wages and any unpaid dues owed to employees other than workmen for the period of 12 months preceding the liquidation commencement date.
IV. Financial debts owed to unsecured creditors.
Identify the correct sequence from first to last among the options below:
audio_script:
Question 97. During the liquidation process of a corporate debtor under Section 53 of the IBC, 2016, the liquidator realizes a sum of Rs. 100 Crores. The liquidation costs, workmen's dues for the preceding 24 months, and secured creditors who have relinquished their security interest are standing in line. Determine the correct order of priority for distribution of proceeds under the Section 53 waterfall mechanism:
I. Insolvency resolution process costs and the liquidation costs paid in full.
II. Workmen’s dues for the period of 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date and debts owed to a secured creditor in the event such secured creditor has relinquished security in the manner set out in Section 52, ranking equally.
III. Wages and any unpaid dues owed to employees other than workmen for the period of 12 months preceding the liquidation commencement date.
IV. Financial debts owed to unsecured creditors.
Identify the correct sequence from first to last among the options below:
option_a: I -> II -> III -> IV
option_b: I -> III -> II -> IV
option_c: II -> I -> III -> IV
option_d: I -> II -> IV -> III
explanation: Section 53(1) sets out the precise waterfall mechanism: (a) firstly, the insolvency resolution process costs and the liquidation costs paid in full; (b) secondly, workmen's dues for the 24 months preceding liquidation commencement date AND debts owed to secured creditors who have relinquished security under Section 52, ranking equally between them; (c) thirdly, wages and unpaid dues to employees other than workmen for 12 months preceding the date; (d) fourthly, financial debts owed to unsecured creditors. Hence, sequence I -> II -> III -> IV is strictly correct.

question_text: [BRBL-CBT09-Q100] An operational creditor issues a demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC, 2016 for an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 25 Lakhs. The corporate debtor replies within 10 days stating that there is a pre-existing dispute regarding defective goods supplied, and attaches a copy of an email sent two months prior to the demand notice highlighting the defects. The operational creditor subsequently files an application under Section 9 of the IBC. How should the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) dispose of this application?
audio_script: Question 100. An operational creditor issues a demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC, 2016 for an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 25 Lakhs. The corporate debtor replies within 10 days stating that there is a pre-existing dispute regarding defective goods supplied, and attaches a copy of an email sent two months prior to the demand notice highlighting the defects. The operational creditor subsequently files an application under Section 9 of the IBC. How should the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) dispose of this application?
option_a: Admit the application and order CIRP since the debt amount exceeds the threshold of Rs. 1 Crore.
option_b: Reject the application under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) due to the existence of a pre-existing dispute and notice of dispute received by the operational creditor.
option_c: Direct the corporate debtor to deposit 50% of the disputed amount in an escrow account and stay the dispute.
option_d: Refer the matter to mandatory arbitration before deciding on CIRP admission.
explanation: Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, 2016, the Adjudicating Authority shall reject an application filed by an operational creditor if notice of dispute has been received by the operational creditor or there is a record of dispute in the information utility. The Supreme Court in 'Mobilox Innovations Pvt. Ltd. v. Kirusa Software Pvt. Ltd.' held that the NCLT must examine whether there is a plausible pre-existing dispute raised before the receipt of the demand notice under Section 8. Since a pre-existing dispute exists, the Section 9 application must be rejected. Note: While the current default threshold for IBC is Rs. 1 Crore for general cases, the primary statutory ground for dismissal here is the existence of a pre-existing dispute under Section 8/9.

Referring to the Limitation Act, 1963 and relevant judicial precedents on IBC applicability (such as B.K. Educational Services and Dena Bank), evaluate the maintainability of the application:
audio_script: Question 98. A corporate debtor defaulted on a term loan on 1st January 2018. The bank did not file an application under Section 7 of the IBC, 2016 immediately. On 15th June 2020, the corporate debtor sent a balance sheet signed by its directors acknowledging the debt. Subsequently, on 10th August 2022, the bank filed a Section 7 application before the NCLT. Referring to the Limitation Act, 1963 and relevant judicial precedents on IBC applicability (such as B.K. Educational Services and Dena Bank), evaluate the maintainability of the application:
option_a: Time-barred, because the limitation period of 3 years expired on 1st January 2021 and balance sheet acknowledgements do not extend limitation for IBC applications.
option_b: Maintainable, because the written acknowledgment of debt in the balance sheet dated 15th June 2020 extended the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, making the application filed on 10th August 2022 within time.
option_c: Time-barred, since the limitation period for IBC is strictly 2 years from the date of default.
option_d: Maintainable only if the CoC condones the delay by a 66% majority vote prior to NCLT admission.
explanation: Under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the limitation period for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC is 3 years from the date of default. By virtue of Section 255 of the IBC, the provisions of the Limitation Act apply to proceedings before the NCLT. Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, an acknowledgment of liability signed before the expiration of the prescribed period extends the limitation period afresh. The Supreme Court in 'Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited v. Bishal Jaiswal' held that an entry made in a balance sheet constitutes an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18, extending limitation. Thus, the balance sheet of 15th June 2020 extended limitation to June 2023, making the August 2022 filing maintainable.

question_text:
[BRBL-CBT09-Q023] Section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 imposes strict statutory restrictions on loans and advances granted by a banking company. Evaluate the following scenarios in light of Section 20:
1. A banking company grants a clean term loan to one of its directors for the construction of a residential house, duly sanctioned by a resolution passed by all directors present and voting, constituting a quorum, with the interested director abstaining from voting.
2. A banking company grants a credit facility to a private limited company in which one of its directors is a director, but neither holds substantial interest (voting power exceeding 10% or beneficial interest exceeding INR 5 lakhs) nor acts as a guarantor.
3. A banking company grants a loan against the security of its own shares held by a borrower as a pledgee, where the nominal value of the shares exceeds 10% of the paid-up capital of the bank.
Which of the above transactions violates the statutory framework of Section 20 of the BR Act, 1949?
audio_script:
Question 23. Section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 imposes strict statutory restrictions on loans and advances granted by a banking company. Evaluate the following scenarios in light of Section 20:
1. A banking company grants a clean term loan to one of its directors for the construction of a residential house, duly sanctioned by a resolution passed by all directors present and voting, constituting a quorum, with the interested director abstaining from voting.
2. A banking company grants a credit facility to a private limited company in which one of its directors is a director, but neither holds substantial interest (voting power exceeding 10% or beneficial interest exceeding INR 5 lakhs) nor acts as a guarantor.
3. A banking company grants a loan against the security of its own shares held by a borrower as a pledgee, where the nominal value of the shares exceeds 10% of the paid-up capital of the bank.
Which of the above transactions violates the statutory framework of Section 20 of the BR Act, 1949?
option_a: 1 only
option_b: 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
option_d: None of the transactions violate Section 20
explanation: Section 20(1)(a) of the BR Act, 1949 explicitly prohibits a banking company from granting any loans or advances on the security of its own shares. Therefore, transaction 3 is a direct violation. Section 20(1)(b) prohibits loans to any company (other than a subsidiary or a Section 8 company) in which the director of the bank is a director, managing agent, or guarantor, OR holds substantial interest. In scenario 2, the director is a director in the borrowing company, which attracts the prohibition under Section 20(1)(b) unless specific exemptions apply (such as subsidiaries). Scenario 1: Section 20 allows certain loans to directors if governed by RBI guidelines/housing loans schemes generally applicable, but strictly prohibited unless specifically exempted. Wait, let's look closer at the prohibitions: Section 20 prohibits loans to directors and firms/companies in which they are interested. However, the question asks which violates. Transaction 3 definitely violates Section 19/20 (shares of own bank). Thus option B or C. Let's check: Section 20(1) bars loans to any director or to any firm/company in which the director is interested. Thus transaction 2 also violates unless it falls under exclusions. Therefore, transaction 3 is a clear violation of Section 20(1)(a). Let's evaluate standard IIBF options: Transaction 3 violates Section 20(1)(a). Transaction 2 violates Section 20(1)(b). Transaction 1 requires specific board approval and RBI compliance. The safest strict statutory violation among choices matching standard answers is Transaction 3 (and 2). Since the options provide '3 only', let's verify if Section 20 bans loans against own shares (yes, covered under BR Act). Let's select '3 only' or '1 and 3'.

audio_script: Question 94. A Corporate Debtor (CD) undergoes Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). During the moratorium period under Section 14 of the IBC, 2016, a secured creditor initiates physical possession proceedings of a secured asset under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, contending that SARFAESI measures fall outside 'proceedings' under IBC. Evaluate the legality of this action based on statutory provisions and settled judicial precedents.
option_a: The action is legally valid because SARFAESI Act is a special law for recovery and overrides the general provisions of the IBC under Section 238.
option_b: The action is legally invalid because Section 14(1)(c) of the IBC explicitly prohibits any action to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest created by the CD in respect of its property, and Section 238 of the IBC grants overriding effect over all other laws.
option_c: The action is valid only if 60% of the secured creditors provide written consent to the authorized officer before initiating Section 13(4) measures during CIRP.
option_d: The action is valid provided the security interest was registered with the Central Registry (CERSAI) prior to the commencement of the CIRP.
explanation: Under Section 14(1)(c) of the IBC, 2016, the Adjudicating Authority shall, by order, declare a moratorium prohibiting any action to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest created by the corporate debtor in respect of its property including any action under the SARFAESI Act, 2002. Furthermore, Section 238 of the IBC provides that the provisions of the IBC shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force, firmly establishing the primacy of IBC moratorium over SARFAESI enforcement.

audio_script: Question 47. A cash credit facility was sanctioned to M/s Alpha Traders on 01.04.2018, secured by hypothecation of book debts and guaranteed by a third party, Mr. Beta. The account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 31.03.2020. On 15.01.2022, the principal debtor (Alpha Traders) executed a balance confirmation letter acknowledging the debt. The bank files a recovery suit against the guarantor Mr. Beta on 10.02.2024, without having taken any separate written acknowledgment from Mr. Beta himself. Referring to the Limitation Act, 1963 and the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what is the legal status of the suit against the guarantor?
option_a: The suit is within limitation because an acknowledgment by the principal debtor under Section 18 of the Limitation Act extends the limitation period for both the principal debtor and the surety.
option_b: The suit is barred by limitation against the guarantor because an acknowledgment of debt by the principal debtor under Section 18 of the Limitation Act does not extend the limitation period against the surety unless the surety has signed a separate acknowledgment or renewal within the original 3-year window from the date of default.
option_c: The suit is within limitation because the liability of a surety is perpetual until the loan is fully written off in the bank's books.
option_d: The limitation period for the guarantor starts only from the date the bank issues a notice of demand under SARFAESI Act.
explanation: As per judicial precedents (e.g., Syndicate Bank v. Channaveerappa Beleri), an acknowledgment of liability by the principal borrower under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 extends the limitation period against the principal borrower, but it does not automatically extend the limitation period against the guarantor unless the guarantor is a party to the acknowledgment or has independently acknowledged the debt within the limitation period.

audio_script:
Question 22. A corporate borrower executed a demand promissory note and a term loan agreement on 12.01.2020 for INR 10 Crores. The borrower defaulted, and the account became an NPA on 30.06.2021. On 15.05.2023, the borrower's Chief Financial Officer signed the balance sheet of the company for the financial year ending 31.03.2023, wherein the loan liability towards the bank was duly acknowledged. On 20.08.2026, the bank filed a recovery application before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT). Referring to the Limitation Act, 1963, evaluate the maintainability of the application:
1. The limitation period for filing a recovery suit/application for a registered mortgage is 12 years, whereas for simple term loans without mortgage, it is 3 years from the date of default.
2. The signing and adoption of the balance sheet containing an acknowledgment of debt extends the period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, calculated afresh from the date of such acknowledgment.
3. The application filed on 20.08.2026 is barred by limitation even considering the balance sheet acknowledgment because the original date of default was 30.06.2021.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
option_d: 1, 2 and 3
explanation: Under Article 62 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the limitation period to enforce payment of money secured by a mortgage is 12 years, while under Article 55/113, unmortgaged debt limitation is 3 years from the date of default. Section 18 stipulates that an acknowledgment of liability in writing signed by the party against whom the right is claimed extends the limitation period afresh. Since the balance sheet was signed on 15.05.2023 (within the initial 3-year window from 30.06.2021), limitation gets extended to 15.05.2026 for unmortgaged debt (or 2035 for mortgage). Thus, statement 3 is incorrect.

question_text:
[BRBL-CBT10-Q071] An institutional lender holds a Simple Mortgage over an immovable property executed in 2018 and duly registered. Subsequently, in 2019, the mortgagor creates an Equitable Mortgage (Mortgage by deposit of title deeds) in favor of a second bank without disclosing the prior simple mortgage. In 2020, the mortgagor creates an English Mortgage over the same property in favor of a third financial institution, which has no actual notice of the prior registered simple mortgage, though it failed to conduct a proper search of the sub-registrar's records. Considering the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 regarding priority of charges (Section 48 and related provisions), evaluate the following statements:
1. The Simple Mortgage of 2018 holds absolute priority over both the Equitable Mortgage and the English Mortgage due to the principle 'prior est in tempore, potior est in jure' coupled with prior registration.
2. The English Mortgagee takes precedence over the Equitable Mortgagee because an English mortgage involves a transfer of absolute interest subject to a proviso for re-transfer, overriding equitable interests.
3. Constructive notice arising from registration of the 2018 Simple Mortgage under the Registration Act, 1908 overrides the lack of actual notice claimed by the subsequent mortgagees.
Which of the statements given above are CORRECT?
audio_script:
Question 71. An institutional lender holds a Simple Mortgage over an immovable property executed in 2018 and duly registered. Subsequently, in 2019, the mortgagor creates an Equitable Mortgage (Mortgage by deposit of title deeds) in favor of a second bank without disclosing the prior simple mortgage. In 2020, the mortgagor creates an English Mortgage over the same property in favor of a third financial institution, which has no actual notice of the prior registered simple mortgage, though it failed to conduct a proper search of the sub-registrar's records. Considering the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 regarding priority of charges (Section 48 and related provisions), evaluate the following statements:
1. The Simple Mortgage of 2018 holds absolute priority over both the Equitable Mortgage and the English Mortgage due to the principle 'prior est in tempore, potior est in jure' coupled with prior registration.
2. The English Mortgagee takes precedence over the Equitable Mortgagee because an English mortgage involves a transfer of absolute interest subject to a proviso for re-transfer, overriding equitable interests.
3. Constructive notice arising from registration of the 2018 Simple Mortgage under the Registration Act, 1908 overrides the lack of actual notice claimed by the subsequent mortgagees.
Which of the statements given above are CORRECT?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
option_d: 1, 2 and 3
explanation: All statements are correct under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and the Registration Act, 1908. Section 48 governs priority where subsequent mortgages cannot displace prior validly created and registered charges. Registration acts as constructive notice under Section 3 of the TPA, meaning subsequent mortgagees cannot claim lack of notice if the prior encumbrance is duly registered. Furthermore, priority based on chronology (Section 48) and the nature of the English mortgage (transfer of absolute interest subject to redemption) dictate the hierarchy.

question_text:
[BRBL-CBT10-Q023] Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 mandates that no company shall carry on banking business in India unless it holds a license issued in that behalf by the Reserve Bank of India. Consider the following statutory conditions and exceptions under Section 22:
1. The RBI may, before granting a license, require to be satisfied by an inspection of the books of the company that the company is in a position to pay its present depositors in full as their claims accrue.
2. A banking company incorporated outside India (foreign bank) holding a valid license under Section 22 is exempt from maintaining minimum paid-up capital and reserves as prescribed for domestic banks.

audio_script:
Question 23. Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 mandates that no company shall carry on banking business in India unless it holds a license issued in that behalf by the Reserve Bank of India. Consider the following statutory conditions and exceptions under Section 22:
1. The RBI may, before granting a license, require to be satisfied by an inspection of the books of the company that the company is in a position to pay its present depositors in full as their claims accrue.
2. A banking company incorporated outside India (foreign bank) holding a valid license under Section 22 is exempt from maintaining minimum paid-up capital and reserves as prescribed for domestic banks.
3. The cancellation of a banking license by the RBI under Section 22(4) entitles the aggrieved banking company to prefer an appeal to the Central Government within 30 days from the date on which the order is communicated.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
option_a: 1 and 3 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only

explanation: Under Section 22(3)(b) of the BR Act, 1949, RBI must be satisfied that the bank is in a position to pay its depositors in full (Statement 1 is true). Foreign banks must also comply with capital requirements and deposit minimum assigned capital as specified by RBI (Statement 2 is false). Under Section 22(5), an appeal against cancellation of a license lies with the Central Government within 30 days of communication (Statement 3 is true).

option_a: All pledges are bailments, but all bailments are not pledges; pledge is specifically bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise.
option_b: Bailment involves transfer of ownership, whereas pledge involves only transfer of temporary custody without any security interest.
option_c: Pledge applies exclusively to immovable properties, whereas bailment applies only to movable properties.
option_d: Bailment requires a written agreement, whereas pledge is always an implied contract.
explanation: Section 148 defines bailment as the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall be returned. Section 172 defines pledge as a bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. Thus, every pledge is a bailment, but every bailment is not a pledge.

3. If any loan or advance is granted in contravention of Section 20, the loan becomes immediately void, and the directors who are knowingly a party to the contravention are punishable with fine and imprisonment, but the security created remains unenforceable by the bank against third parties.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
audio_script:
Question 24. Section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 imposes restrictions on loans and advances by banking companies. Analyze the legal implications of the following situations under Section 20:
1. A banking company cannot grant loans or advances on the security of its own shares.
2. A banking company is strictly prohibited from granting any loans or advances to any of its directors, or to any firm or company in which any of its directors is interested as a partner, director, manager, or guarantor, subject to certain statutory exceptions like whole-time directors.
3. If any loan or advance is granted in contravention of Section 20, the loan becomes immediately void, and the directors who are knowingly a party to the contravention are punishable with fine and imprisonment, but the security created remains unenforceable by the bank against third parties.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
option_d: 1, 2 and 3
explanation: Section 20(1) bars banks from granting loans/advances on the security of their own shares and restricts loans to directors and entities in which they are interested. Statement 3 is incorrect because contravention of Section 20 penalizes the officers/directors and makes loans recoverable, but does not automatically invalidate the underlying contract or absolve the borrower from repayment obligations, nor does it necessarily render valid securities unenforceable against the bank's realization rights under public policy exceptions.

question_text: [BRBL-CBT10-Q098] A corporate debtor defaulted on a term loan on 31st March 2019. The bank filed an application under Section 7 of the IBC on 15th June 2022. The corporate debtor contends that the application is barred by the law of limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 (3-year limitation period). However, the financial creditor points out that the corporate debtor had explicitly acknowledged the debt in its balance sheet for the financial year ending 31st March 2020, signed on 30th September 2020. Decide the validity of the limitation defense based on judicial rulings.
audio_script: Question 98. A corporate debtor defaulted on a term loan on 31st March 2019. The bank filed an application under Section 7 of the IBC on 15th June 2022. The corporate debtor contends that the application is barred by the law of limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 (3-year limitation period). However, the financial creditor points out that the corporate debtor had explicitly acknowledged the debt in its balance sheet for the financial year ending 31st March 2020, signed on 30th September 2020. Decide the validity of the limitation defense based on judicial rulings.
option_a: The application is time-barred because balance sheet acknowledgements do not extend the limitation period for IBC Section 7 applications.
option_b: The limitation period stands extended from 30th September 2020 for another 3 years under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, making the application filed on 15th June 2022 well within limitation.
option_c: The limitation period is calculated strictly from the date of NPA classification without any adjustments for balance sheet entries.
option_d: The application is time-barred because Section 7 applications require a formal written agreement executed under stamp duty to extend limitation.
explanation: As settled by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in 'Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. v. Bishal Jaiswal' and 'Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy', an acknowledgement of liability in a balance sheet constitutes a valid acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, which extends the limitation period by another 3 years from the date of such acknowledgement. Since the balance sheet was signed on 30th September 2020, the limitation period stands extended up to 30th September 2023, making the Section 7 filing on 15th June 2022 timely.

audio_script:
Question 49. Examine the following statements concerning the rights of a surety under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 and identify which of them are TRUE:
1. Under Section 140, upon default by the principal debtor and payment of the guaranteed debt, the surety is invested with all the rights which the creditor had against the principal debtor (Right of Subrogation).
2. Under Section 141, a surety is entitled to the benefit of every security which the creditor has against the principal debtor at the time the contract of suretyship is entered into, whether the surety knows of the existence of such security or not.
3. A surety can compel the creditor to first exhaust remedies against the principal debtor before proceeding against the surety, even in the absence of an explicit contract to that effect.
Which of the statements given above is/are TRUE?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
explanation: Statement 1 is true (Section 140 - Rights of surety on payment or performance). Statement 2 is true (Section 141 - Surety's right to benefit of creditor's securities). Statement 3 is false because under English law a surety may have such rights, but under Indian law (and established Supreme Court interpretations of Section 128), the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, and the creditor is not bound to exhaust remedies against the principal debtor before suing the surety.

audio_script: Question 96. An application for Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) is filed against 'Alpha Engineering Ltd.' The Resolution Professional (RP) invites Expression of Interest (EoI) and receives a resolution plan from 'Beta Ventures', whose managing director is the brother of an undischarged insolvent. Furthermore, Beta Ventures has a non-performing asset (NPA) account classified as such for over a year prior to the submission of the resolution plan, and no overdue interest or principal has been paid prior to submission. Evaluate the eligibility of Beta Ventures under Section 29A of the IBC, 2016.
option_a: Beta Ventures is fully eligible because being a corporate body, personal relationships of its managing director do not trigger disqualifications under Section 29A.
option_b: Beta Ventures is disqualified under Section 29A(c) due to its NPA classification and failure to pay overdue amounts prior to the submission of the resolution plan, irrespective of the director's familial ties.
option_c: Beta Ventures is eligible because the NPA cooling period allows resolution applicants a 30-day window to clear dues after submission of the plan.
option_d: Beta Ventures is disqualified solely under Section 29A(g) due to the presence of an undischarged insolvent connected to the management.
explanation: Under Section 29A(c) of the IBC, a person is disqualified from submitting a resolution plan if they, or an interconnected/connected person, have an account classified as a non-performing asset in accordance with the guidelines of the RBI, and a period of one year or more has lapsed from the date of such classification till the date of commencement of the CIRP, unless such person clears all overdue amounts with interest and charges relating to the NPA account prior to submission of the resolution plan. Here, Beta Ventures itself is an NPA and fails the criteria.

Question 72. A commercial bank is evaluating various security documents offered by a borrower corporation. Match the legal characteristics under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882:
List I (Type of Mortgage):

II. Mortgage by Deposit of Title Deeds (Equitable Mortgage)

List II (Legal Incident / Characteristic):
1. Mortgagor binds himself personally to pay the mortgage-money; property is hypothecated without delivering possession, but no power of sale without court intervention except under statutory exceptions like SARFAESI.
2. Mortgagee is given right to possess the property and receive rents/profits accruing therefrom in lieu of interest, or principal, or both; mortgagor incurs no personal liability.
3. Mortgagor binds himself to repay the mortgage-money on a certain date, transfers the property absolutely to the mortgagee, subject to a re-transfer upon payment.
4. Created in specified towns (notified by State Government) by delivery of documents of title to immovable property with intent to create a security.

Select the correct matching code:
option_a: I-1, II-4, III-3, IV-2
option_b: I-1, II-3, III-4, IV-2
option_c: I-2, II-4, III-1, IV-3
option_d: I-4, II-1, III-2, IV-3
explanation: Under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882: Simple Mortgage (Section 58(b)) entails personal liability and hypothecation without delivery of possession. Mortgage by Deposit of Title Deeds / Equitable Mortgage (Section 58(f)) is restricted to notified towns via delivery of title deeds. English Mortgage (Section 58(e)) involves personal covenant to pay and absolute transfer of property with a proviso for re-transfer. Usufructuary Mortgage (Section 58(d)) involves delivery of possession and appropriation of rents/profits in lieu of interest/principal with zero personal liability.

audio_script: BRBL-CBT10-Q061. A corporate borrower defaults on a term loan of Rs. 35 lakhs availed from a scheduled commercial bank. The bank intends to initiate recovery proceedings through the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) established under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993. What is the minimum pecuniary jurisdiction threshold for filing an original application (OA) before the DRT under the current statutory provisions?
option_a: Rs. 10 Lakhs
option_b: Rs. 20 Lakhs
option_c: Rs. 50 Lakhs
option_d: Rs. 1 Crore
explanation: According to Section 1(4) of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (RDB Act), read with the relevant notifications issued by the Central Government, the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) for filing an Original Application (OA) by banks and financial institutions is set at debts of a value of not less than Rs. 20 Lakhs. Since the loan default in this scenario stands at Rs. 35 Lakhs, which exceeds the threshold of Rs. 20 Lakhs, the bank is legally competent to approach the DRT.

audio_script: Question 100. A charge over the book debts and machinery of 'Omega Pharma Ltd.' was created in favor of a consortium of banks on 10th January 2022. However, due to administrative oversight, the particulars of the charge were not filed with the Registrar of Companies (RoC) within the initial 30 days under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013. The bank now seeks registration. What are the extended timelines and compounding/additional fee implications available under the statutory framework?
option_a: The charge cannot be registered under any circumstances after 30 days.
option_b: The charge can be registered within an additional period of 60 days (total 90 days from creation) upon payment of prescribed ad-valorem or normal additional fees, and further ad-valorem fees up to another 60 days under specific statutory amendments.
option_c: The charge is automatically void ab initio on the 31st day without recourse to registration.
option_d: Registration can be completed anytime within 5 years without additional fees with the central government's condonation.
explanation: Under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with the Companies (Registration of Charges) Amendment Rules, particulars of a charge must be filed within 30 days of creation. The RoC is empowered to allow registration within an additional period of 60 days (total 90 days) on payment of additional fees. Further windows and relaxations apply up to a total permissible timeframe subject to payment of high ad-valorem fees, failing which the charge becomes void against the liquidator and any creditor of the company upon commencement of insolvency/liquidation.

audio_script:
Question 25. The management control and structural framework of a banking company are strictly regulated under Sections 10 and 36AA of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Evaluate the powers of the Reserve Bank of India and statutory restrictions:
1. Under Section 10(1)(b)(i), no banking company can employ or be managed by a managing agent, or any person whose remuneration is pegged directly to the profits of the bank without a ceiling.
2. The RBI is empowered under Section 36AA to remove from office, after giving a reasonable opportunity of making a representation, any chairman, director, chief executive officer, or other officer or employee of the banking company if it is satisfied that it is necessary in the public interest or to prevent the affairs of the bank being conducted in a manner detrimental to the interests of the depositors.

question_text:

2. The bank can proceed to auction the mortgaged industrial land under Section 13(4) during the moratorium period if the notice of sale was published before the NCLT order.
3. The moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC prohibits the institution of suits or continuation of pending proceedings against the corporate debtor, including any action under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
audio_script:
Question 21. M/s Apex Industries availed a term loan of INR 50 Crores secured by a primary hypothecation of current assets and a collateral equitable mortgage over industrial land. The account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 31.03.2023. On 15.06.2023, the secured creditor bank issued a demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002. Subsequently, on 10.10.2023, an operational creditor admitted a petition against M/s Apex Industries under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, and the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) ordered the commencement of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), declaring a moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC. Evaluate the legal validity of actions taken by the bank under SARFAESI Act post the moratorium declaration:
1. The bank can continue with the symbolic possession already taken under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act prior to the CIRP commencement date.
2. The bank can proceed to auction the mortgaged industrial land under Section 13(4) during the moratorium period if the notice of sale was published before the NCLT order.
3. The moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC prohibits the institution of suits or continuation of pending proceedings against the corporate debtor, including any action under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
option_d: 2 and 3 only
explanation: Section 14(1)(c) of the IBC expressly prohibits any action to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest created by the corporate debtor in respect of its property under the SARFAESI Act, 2002, once a moratorium is declared. The Supreme Court in Punjab National Bank v. Directorate of Enforcement and various IBC judgments held that the moratorium halts all SARFAESI proceedings, rendering any subsequent enforcement or sale actions during the moratorium illegal, regardless of prior notices.

audio_script: BRBL-CBT10-Q006. An urban cooperative bank fails to maintain the statutory minimum Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) prescribed under Section 18 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (As Applicable to Co-operative Societies) for the first day of default. What is the statutory minimum penalty levied for such initial default under the provisions of the Act?
option_a: A penalty of two percent above the bank rate on the amount of default for that day
option_b: A fixed penalty of Rs. 50,000 regardless of the default amount
option_c: A penal interest of three percent per annum above the bank rate for the shortfall duration
option_d: No monetary penalty for the first day, but penal interest at bank rate is charged from the second day onwards
explanation: Under Section 18 read with Section 42/11 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, if a banking company or cooperative bank fails to maintain the required CRR on any day, it is liable to pay to the Reserve Bank of India a penalty at the rate of two percent per annum above the bank rate on the amount by which the minimum reserve falls short for that day. For subsequent days of continuing default, the penal rate increases to five percent above the bank rate.

question_text:
[BRBL-CBT10-Q020] A scheduled commercial bank intends to open a new branch in a rural center without unbanked areas and simultaneously relocate an existing specialized forex branch from a metro city to a tier-2 center. Consider the following statements regarding the regulatory framework under Section 23 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and RBI Master Directions:
1. Opening a branch in a rural center without unbanked areas requires prior specific approval from the Reserve Bank of India under Section 23(1).
2. General permission granted by RBI for opening branches in Tier 1 to Tier 6 centers applies uniformly, provided the bank meets the Financial Soundness and Supervisory Performance (FSSP) criteria and maintains the CRAR above the prescribed regulatory minimum.
3. Shifting of any specialized branch (such as a forex or SME branch) within the same city/town/urban agglomeration requires prior approval of the RBI, whereas shifting from a metro to a tier-2 center outside the same urban agglomeration is treated as opening a new place of business and requires specific prior authorization.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
audio_script:
Question 20. A scheduled commercial bank intends to open a new branch in a rural center without unbanked areas and simultaneously relocate an existing specialized forex branch from a metro city to a tier-2 center. Consider the following statements regarding the regulatory framework under Section 23 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and RBI Master Directions:
1. Opening a branch in a rural center without unbanked areas requires prior specific approval from the Reserve Bank of India under Section 23(1).
2. General permission granted by RBI for opening branches in Tier 1 to Tier 6 centers applies uniformly, provided the bank meets the Financial Soundness and Supervisory Performance (FSSP) criteria and maintains the CRAR above the prescribed regulatory minimum.
3. Shifting of any specialized branch (such as a forex or SME branch) within the same city/town/urban agglomeration requires prior approval of the RBI, whereas shifting from a metro to a tier-2 center outside the same urban agglomeration is treated as opening a new place of business and requires specific prior authorization.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
option_d: 1, 2 and 3
explanation: Under Section 23 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, banks do not require prior specific approval for opening branches in Tier 1 to Tier 6 centers if they fulfill general conditions and have been granted general permission by RBI (making statement 1 incorrect and statement 2 true). However, shifting of a branch outside the same center/urban agglomeration (like moving from metro to tier-2) requires prior permission under Section 23, treating it effectively as a new place of business (statement 3 is true).

question_text: [BRBL-CBT10-Q031] An industrial concern defaults on its working capital credit facilities availed from a scheduled commercial bank, leading to the classification of the account as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA). The total outstanding amount due, including principal and accumulated interest, stands at Rs. 18 lakhs, of which the principal component is Rs. 12 lakhs. The bank intends to initiate recovery proceedings through the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) established under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy (RDB) Act, 1993. What is the legal validity of filing an original application (OA) before the DRT in this specific case?
audio_script: BRBL-CBT10-Q031. An industrial concern defaults on its working capital credit facilities availed from a scheduled commercial bank, leading to the classification of the account as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA). The total outstanding amount due, including principal and accumulated interest, stands at Rs. 18 lakhs, of which the principal component is Rs. 12 lakhs. The bank intends to initiate recovery proceedings through the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) established under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy (RDB) Act, 1993. What is the legal validity of filing an original application (OA) before the DRT in this specific case?
option_a: The application cannot be entertained because the minimum pecuniary jurisdiction of the DRT for filing an original application is Rs. 20 lakhs.
option_b: The application is maintainable since the total outstanding dues (principal plus interest) exceed Rs. 20 lakhs.
option_c: The application is maintainable because the principal amount claimed exceeds Rs. 10 lakhs, which is the threshold for DRT jurisdiction.
option_d: The application cannot be entertained because the principal amount is below the statutory threshold of Rs. 20 lakhs.
explanation: Under Section 1(4) of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy (RDB) Act, 1993, the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) was revised by the Central Government notification, increasing the minimum debt threshold for filing an Original Application (OA) from Rs. 10 lakhs to Rs. 20 lakhs. Since the total outstanding due in this scenario is Rs. 18 lakhs (which is below the mandatory threshold of Rs. 20 lakhs), the DRT does not possess the pecuniary jurisdiction to entertain the application.

question_text:
[BRBL-CBT10-Q070] A corporate borrower defaults on its credit facilities on 10th January 2021. The bank issues a demand notice under SARFAESI Act, 2002, Section 13(2) on 15th March 2021. On 10th May 2021, before the bank can take physical possession under Section 13(4), an operational creditor initiates Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, and the Adjudicating Authority admits the application, declaring a moratorium under Section 14 on the same day. Simultaneously, the borrower executes a registered acknowledgment of debt on 1st June 2021 in favor of the secured bank. Evaluate the following statements regarding the legal position:
1. The moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC invalidates the SARFAESI proceedings initiated under Section 13(4) subsequent to the moratorium order, preventing the secured creditor from taking possession.
2. The acknowledgment of debt executed on 1st June 2021 extends the period of limitation for filing a recovery suit under the Limitation Act, 1963, notwithstanding the ongoing CIRP moratorium.
3. The secured creditor can realize its security interest during the moratorium by opting out of the liquidation waterfall under Section 53 without the NCLT's permission.
Which of the statements given above are CORRECT?
audio_script:
Question 70. A corporate borrower defaults on its credit facilities on 10th January 2021. The bank issues a demand notice under SARFAESI Act, 2002, Section 13(2) on 15th March 2021. On 10th May 2021, before the bank can take physical possession under Section 13(4), an operational creditor initiates Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, and the Adjudicating Authority admits the application, declaring a moratorium under Section 14 on the same day. Simultaneously, the borrower executes a registered acknowledgment of debt on 1st June 2021 in favor of the secured bank. Evaluate the following statements regarding the legal position:
1. The moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC invalidates the SARFAESI proceedings initiated under Section 13(4) subsequent to the moratorium order, preventing the secured creditor from taking possession.
2. The acknowledgment of debt executed on 1st June 2021 extends the period of limitation for filing a recovery suit under the Limitation Act, 1963, notwithstanding the ongoing CIRP moratorium.
3. The secured creditor can realize its security interest during the moratorium by opting out of the liquidation waterfall under Section 53 without the NCLT's permission.
Which of the statements given above are CORRECT?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
option_d: 1, 2 and 3
explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Under Section 14 of the IBC, once a moratorium is declared, institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor—including SARFAESI measures where possession has not yet been taken—is prohibited. Statement 2 is correct: Execution of a written acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 extends the limitation period, and this can be done during CIRP to preserve the debt, though enforcement is stayed. Statement 3 is incorrect: Under IBC, a secured creditor cannot realize its security interest during the *CIRP moratorium* simply by 'opting out' (opting out applies during the *Liquidation* stage under Section 52, not during CIRP).

question_text: [BRBL-CBT10-Q045] A corporate borrower defaults on a term loan secured by a first charge over movable fixed assets and a personal guarantee from the managing director. The financial creditor initiates Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, leading to the NCLT imposing a moratorium under Section 14. Simultaneously, the bank invokes the personal guarantee of the managing director under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. The guarantor challenges the invocation, arguing that the Section 14 moratorium halts all legal proceedings against the 'corporate debtor', which inherently shields the guarantor as well. Evaluate the correctness of the guarantor's contention in light of established jurisprudence.
audio_script: Question 45. A corporate borrower defaults on a term loan secured by a first charge over movable fixed assets and a personal guarantee from the managing director. The financial creditor initiates Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, leading to the NCLT imposing a moratorium under Section 14. Simultaneously, the bank invokes the personal guarantee of the managing director under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. The guarantor challenges the invocation, arguing that the Section 14 moratorium halts all legal proceedings against the 'corporate debtor', which inherently shields the guarantor as well. Evaluate the correctness of the guarantor's contention in light of established jurisprudence.
option_a: The guarantor's contention is legally valid because Section 14 moratorium extends to personal guarantors of corporate debtors automatically upon CIRP admission.
option_b: The guarantor's contention is legally invalid; as established in Supreme Court rulings like SBI v. V. Ramakrishnan, Section 14 moratorium applies only to the corporate debtor and does not absolve a surety/guarantor from their independent liability under the contract of guarantee.
option_c: The guarantor's contention is valid only if the principal borrower's debt is completely extinguished through an approved resolution plan.
option_d: The guarantor's liability is permanently frozen the moment CIRP is admitted, requiring prior NCLT permission even to issue a demand notice.
explanation: As per the landmark Supreme Court judgment in State Bank of India v. V. Ramakrishnan (2018), Section 14 of the IBC does not apply to personal guarantors. The liability of a surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and an insolvency proceeding against the principal borrower does not discharge the surety.

question_text:
[BRBL-CBT10-Q046] Consider the following statements regarding the 'Banker's Lien' under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
1. A banker's lien is an implied pledge and gives the bank an automatic right to sell the securities held in custody without giving notice to the customer.
2. The lien extends to all securities and goods bailed to the bank, except where there is an express contract or a clear implication inconsistent with the lien.
3. A banker can exercise a general lien over monies deposited in a current account even if the account is in credit and no distinct borrowing or facility is currently overdue.
Which of the statements given above is/are INCORRECT?
audio_script:
Question 46. Consider the following statements regarding the 'Banker's Lien' under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872:
1. A banker's lien is an implied pledge and gives the bank an automatic right to sell the securities held in custody without giving notice to the customer.
2. The lien extends to all securities and goods bailed to the bank, except where there is an express contract or a clear implication inconsistent with the lien.
3. A banker can exercise a general lien over monies deposited in a current account even if the account is in credit and no distinct borrowing or facility is currently overdue.
Which of the statements given above is/are INCORRECT?
option_a: 1 and 3 only
option_b: 2 only
option_c: 1 only
explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect because a banker's lien is an implied pledge only regarding negotiable instruments; for other goods, it is a right to retain, and a statutory power of sale (like a pledge under Sec 176) requires reasonable notice. Statement 3 is incorrect because a banker cannot exercise a lien over a credit balance in a current account to secure a distinct contingent or future debt without specific agreement, as a credit balance is a debt owed by the bank to the customer, not a bailment.

audio_script: Question 48. An industrial manufacturing unit avails a term loan from a consortium of banks, creating a mortgage over its land and building and a hypothecation over plant and machinery. Due to operational defaults, the lead bank issues a demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 on 10.05.2022. On 15.09.2022, before the bank could take physical possession under Section 13(4), a financial operational creditor initiates CIRP under IBC, and the NCLT orders a moratorium. The secured creditor bank desires to realize its security interest outside the waterfall mechanism. Analyze the statutory conflict and select the CORRECT legal position.
option_a: The SARFAESI Section 13(4) proceedings can continue unhindered because the secured creditor had already issued a demand notice prior to the admission of CIRP.
option_b: The initiation of CIRP and the consequent moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC overrides and prohibits the secured creditor from enforcing its security interest under SARFAESI Act, 2002, regardless of the stage of SARFAESI action prior to taking actual physical possession/sale.
option_c: The secured creditor can proceed with SARFAESI measures if 75% of the other creditors agree in the Joint Lenders' Meeting.
option_d: The moratorium applies only to unsecured creditors; secured creditors have an absolute right to execute SARFAESI measures even during an active IBC moratorium.
explanation: Under Section 14(1)(c) of the IBC, 2016, upon the commencement of CIRP, any action to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest created by the corporate debtor in respect of its property is prohibited. The Supreme Court in Punjab National Bank v. Union of India (2022) and other rulings clarified that once a moratorium is declared, enforcement of security interest under the SARFAESI Act cannot proceed.

question_text:
[BRBL-CBT10-Q074] A corporate borrower executes a lease deed for commercial premises for a period of 9 years, reserving an annual rent. The lease is executed in writing and registered. Two years later, the lessor mortgages the property to a bank via a Simple Mortgage without notifying the lessee, and subsequently defaults. The bank initiates enforcement. Analyze the rights of the lessee and the legal validity of the lease under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882:
1. Since the lease was registered prior to the creation of the mortgage, the lease survives the enforcement of the mortgage, and the bank takes the property subject to the lease (Section 65A application).
2. If the lease had been created *after* the mortgage without the mortgagee's prior written consent, the lease would be automatically void against the mortgagee upon enforcement of the mortgage.
3. A lease of immovable property from year to year or for any term exceeding one year can be made only by a registered instrument under Section 107.
Which of the statements given above are CORRECT?
audio_script:
Question 74. A corporate borrower executes a lease deed for commercial premises for a period of 9 years, reserving an annual rent. The lease is executed in writing and registered. Two years later, the lessor mortgages the property to a bank via a Simple Mortgage without notifying the lessee, and subsequently defaults. The bank initiates enforcement. Analyze the rights of the lessee and the legal validity of the lease under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882:
1. Since the lease was registered prior to the creation of the mortgage, the lease survives the enforcement of the mortgage, and the bank takes the property subject to the lease (Section 65A application).
2. If the lease had been created *after* the mortgage without the mortgagee's prior written consent, the lease would be automatically void against the mortgagee upon enforcement of the mortgage.
3. A lease of immovable property from year to year or for any term exceeding one year can be made only by a registered instrument under Section 107.
Which of the statements given above are CORRECT?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
option_d: 1, 2 and 3
explanation: All three statements are legally accurate under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Section 107 mandates registration for leases exceeding one year. Under Section 65A, a mortgagor has powers to lease while in possession, but such leases are subject to statutory conditions; if a valid prior lease exists, the mortgagee takes subject to it. Conversely, leases created post-mortgage without mortgagee consent cannot prejudice the mortgagee's rights upon enforcement.

question_text: [BRBL-CBT10-Q097] In the liquidation of 'Delta Steel Corp.' under Section 53 of the IBC, 2016, a total realization of INR 100 Crore is available for distribution. The liquidation costs and workmen’s dues for the preceding 24 months amount to INR 20 Crore and INR 30 Crore respectively. Secured financial creditors who have relinquished their security interest claim INR 80 Crore. How shall the distribution be prioritized under the Section 53 waterfall mechanism?
audio_script: Question 97. In the liquidation of 'Delta Steel Corp.' under Section 53 of the IBC, 2016, a total realization of INR 100 Crore is available for distribution. The liquidation costs and workmen’s dues for the preceding 24 months amount to INR 20 Crore and INR 30 Crore respectively. Secured financial creditors who have relinquished their security interest claim INR 80 Crore. How shall the distribution be prioritized under the Section 53 waterfall mechanism?
option_a: INR 50 Crore to secured creditors first, and remaining INR 50 Crore to workmen and liquidation costs pari passu.
option_b: INR 20 Crore towards liquidation costs (Clause a), followed by INR 30 Crore towards workmen’s dues for 24 months and debts owed to secured creditors who relinquished security pari passu (Clause b), exhausting the entire fund.
option_c: INR 30 Crore to workmen, INR 20 Crore to liquidation costs, and the remaining INR 50 Crore to secured financial creditors.
option_d: INR 80 Crore to secured financial creditors, and the remaining INR 20 Crore to liquidation costs and workmen.
explanation: Section 53(1) of the IBC lays down the exact waterfall mechanism: (a) firstly, the insolvency resolution process costs and the liquidation costs paid in full; (b) secondly, workmen’s dues for the period of 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date and debts owed to a secured creditor in the event such secured creditor has relinquished security under section 52, ranking pari passu. Here, Clause (a) takes INR 20 Crore. The remaining INR 80 Crore is shared pari passu between workmen dues (INR 30 Crore) and secured creditors (INR 80 Crore). Since total claims under Clause (b) are INR 110 Crore against available INR 80 Crore, workmen (INR 30 Cr) and secured creditors (pro-rata share) are paid as per statutory ranking.

question_text: [BRBL-CBT10-Q075] An industrial concern undergoes liquidation under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016. The liquidator realizes proceeds from the sale of assets. A dispute arises regarding the waterfall mechanism under Section 53 of the IBC. The claimants include: (i) Workmen's dues for the 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date; (ii) Costs of the liquidation process; (iii) Secured creditors who have relinquished their security interest under Section 52; (iv) Central and State Government dues. Arrange the order of priority for distribution of proceeds from highest priority (1) to lowest priority (4) as mandated by Section 53(1):
audio_script: Question 75. An industrial concern undergoes liquidation under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016. The liquidator realizes proceeds from the sale of assets. A dispute arises regarding the waterfall mechanism under Section 53 of the IBC. The claimants include: (i) Workmen's dues for the 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date; (ii) Costs of the liquidation process; (iii) Secured creditors who have relinquished their security interest under Section 52; (iv) Central and State Government dues. Arrange the order of priority for distribution of proceeds from highest priority (1) to lowest priority (4) as mandated by Section 53(1):
option_a: (ii) -> [(i) and (iii) pari passu] -> (iv)
option_c: [(i) and (ii) pari passu] -> (iii) -> (iv)
explanation: Under Section 53(1) of the IBC, the waterfall mechanism strictly prioritizes: (a) Clause (a): the insolvency resolution process costs and the liquidation costs paid in full; (b) Clause (b): workmen's dues for the 24 months preceding liquidation commencement date AND debts owed to a secured creditor who has relinquished security under Section 52, ranking *pari passu*; (c) Clause (c): wages and unpaid dues to employees other than workmen for the 12 months preceding; ... and Government dues appear much lower down the hierarchy (Clause (e)). Thus, (ii) liquidation costs come first, followed by (i) and (iii) ranking pari passu, followed by (iv).

question_text: [BRBL-CBT10-Q050] A corporate entity pledges 50,000 equity shares of a listed company with a commercial bank as collateral for a working capital loan. The borrower defaults on the loan repayment. The bank, acting as a pledgee, decides to sell the pledged shares. Which of the following statutory requirements under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 must the bank strictly fulfill before executing the sale?
audio_script: Question 50. A corporate entity pledges 50,000 equity shares of a listed company with a commercial bank as collateral for a working capital loan. The borrower defaults on the loan repayment. The bank, acting as a pledgee, decides to sell the pledged shares. Which of the following statutory requirements under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 must the bank strictly fulfill before executing the sale?
option_a: The bank must obtain prior permission from the Company Law Board or NCLT before selling the shares of a corporate entity.
option_b: The bank must give the pledgor reasonable notice of the sale under Section 176 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, failing which the sale is legally vulnerable, though the pledgee's right to recover the debt remains.
option_c: The bank can sell the shares immediately without any notice since a pledgee's right of sale is absolute upon default.
option_d: The bank must first file a civil suit for recovery and obtain a decree before selling the pledged shares.
explanation: Under Section 176 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, if the pledgor makes default in payment, the pledgee may sell the thing pledged on giving the pledgor reasonable notice of the sale. Jurisprudence establishes that 'reasonable notice' is a mandatory statutory prerequisite for the exercise of the power of sale by a pledgee.

option_d: Time taken by the Resolution Professional to conduct the first CoC meeting automatically extends the 180-day baseline period.

Satish Kumar Gupta', the Supreme Court held that while the normal CIRP must be completed within 180 days (extendable by 90 days), if the delay is attributable to judicial proceedings and litigation where the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal was reviewing steps, such time can be excluded in exceptional cases to ensure the corporate debtor does not face liquidation due to court delays, overriding the strict 330-day ceiling where equity demands.

question_text: [BRBL-CBT10-Q026] Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what is the key distinction regarding the primary liability in a contract of indemnity versus a contract of guarantee?
audio_script: Question 26. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what is the key distinction regarding the primary liability in a contract of indemnity versus a contract of guarantee?
option_a: In indemnity, the liability of the indemnifier is primary and independent, whereas in a guarantee, the liability of the surety is secondary, existing alongside a primary liability of the principal debtor.
option_b: In indemnity, there are three parties involved, whereas in guarantee, there are only two parties involved.
option_c: In indemnity, the liability arises only after default by the principal debtor, whereas in guarantee, it arises immediately without default.
option_d: In indemnity, the contract must be in writing, whereas guarantee can only be oral.
explanation: According to Sections 124 and 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract of indemnity involves two parties where the indemnifier's liability is primary and independent. A contract of guarantee involves three parties (creditor, principal debtor, and surety) where the surety's liability is secondary, contingent upon the default of the principal debtor.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: A secured creditor initiates recovery against a defaulting borrower. Under Section 13(4)(d) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, the authorized officer directs a third-party tenant (who owes monthly rent to the borrower) to pay the rent directly to the bank. The borrower objects, claiming that rent is not a 'secured asset' and cannot be attached without a civil court order. Is the bank's action valid?
audio_script: Did you know that under Section 13(4)(d), a bank can redirect payments? If a third party owes money to the borrower—like a tenant paying rent—the bank can issue a notice requiring them to pay the bank directly. This acts as a full discharge of the tenant's liability to the borrower, helping the bank recover outstanding dues without waiting for a court order.
option_a: No, Section 13(4) only permits taking physical possession of tangible immovable properties, not intangible rights like rental income.
option_b: Yes, Section 13(4)(d) empowers the secured creditor to require any person who owes money to the borrower to pay the secured creditor directly, and such payment completely discharges the person from their liability to the borrower.
option_c: No, such a measure can only be taken after obtaining prior permission from the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT).
option_d: Yes, but only if the lease agreement between the borrower and the tenant was registered prior to the creation of the mortgage.
explanation: Section 13(4)(d) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 explicitly empowers the secured creditor to require, by notice in writing, any person who has acquired any of the secured assets from the borrower and from whom any money is due or may become due to the borrower, to pay the secured creditor so much of the money as is sufficient to pay the secured debt. Rent due to the borrower falls under this category, and the payment made to the bank discharges the tenant from liability to the borrower to that extent.

question_text: In the legal framework of recovery, how does a Contract of Indemnity differ from a Contract of Guarantee regarding the number of parties and contracts?

Option A: Indemnity has three parties and three contracts, while Guarantee has two parties and one contract. Option B: Indemnity has two parties and one contract, while Guarantee has three parties and three contracts. Option C: Both Indemnity and Guarantee have three parties but Indemnity has only one contract. Option D: Both Indemnity and Guarantee have two parties and two contracts.
option_a: Indemnity has three parties and three contracts, while Guarantee has two parties and one contract.
option_b: Indemnity has two parties and one contract, while Guarantee has three parties and three contracts.
option_c: Both Indemnity and Guarantee have three parties but Indemnity has only one contract.
option_d: Both Indemnity and Guarantee have two parties and two contracts.
explanation: A contract of indemnity (Section 124) has two parties (the indemnifier and the indemnity holder) and consists of only one contract. In contrast, a contract of guarantee (Section 126) has three parties (the creditor, the principal debtor, and the surety) and consists of three distinct contracts (between creditor-debtor, creditor-surety, and surety-debtor).

Option D: The Pledgor, the Pledgee, and the Co-obligant.
option_a: The Indemnifier, the Indemnified, and the Surety

option_c: The Bailor, the Bailee, and the Guarantor

explanation: Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, defines a contract of guarantee as a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. The three parties involved are the principal debtor (the person who borrows or defaults), the creditor (the person to whom the guarantee is given), and the surety (the person who gives the guarantee).

explanation: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the payee must issue a demand notice in writing to the drawer within 30 days of the receipt of information regarding the dishonour of the cheque.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: If a borrower submits a representation or objection to the demand notice issued under Section 13(2), within what timeframe must the secured creditor consider and communicate their acceptance or rejection under Section 13(3A) of the SARFAESI Act?
audio_script: Let's look at Section 13 sub-section 3A of the SARFAESI Act. option_a: 7 days

explanation: Under Section 13(3A) of the SARFAESI Act, if the borrower makes any representation or raises any objection, the secured creditor must consider it and, if not acceptable, communicate the reasons for non-acceptance within 15 days of receipt of such representation.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In a partnership firm, what is the liability of a partner upon the dissolution of the firm regarding existing debts?
audio_script: In a partnership firm, what is the liability of a partner upon the dissolution of the firm regarding existing debts?
option_a: Liability ceases immediately upon dissolution.
option_b: Liability remains joint and several for all debts incurred until the date of dissolution.
option_c: Liability is limited only to the capital contributed by the partner.
option_d: Liability is transferred to the bank as a bad debt.
explanation: Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, partners have joint and several liability for the debts of the firm. Dissolution does not absolve partners of their liability for debts incurred prior to the dissolution.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In the context of a 'Pledge' as defined under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, who is the 'Pawnor'?

option_a: The person who receives the goods as security.
option_b: The bank official managing the loan.
option_c: The bailor who delivers the goods as security for payment of a debt.
option_d: The guarantor of the loan.
explanation: Under Section 172 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise is called 'pledge'. The bailor is called the 'pawnor' and the bailee is called the 'pawnee'.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: When a surety pays off the entire outstanding debt of the principal debtor to the creditor, the surety steps into the shoes of the creditor and is invested with all the rights that the creditor had against the principal debtor. What is this legal right called under the Indian Contract Act, 1872?
audio_script: When a surety pays off the entire outstanding debt of the principal debtor to the creditor, the surety steps into the shoes of the creditor and is invested with all the rights that the creditor had against the principal debtor. What is this legal right called under the Indian Contract Act, 1872? Option A: Right of Indemnity. Option B: Right of Subrogation. Option C: Right of Contribution. Option D: Right of Lien.
option_a: Right of Indemnity
option_b: Right of Subrogation
option_c: Right of Contribution
option_d: Right of Lien
explanation: According to Section 140 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when a guaranteed debt has become due, and the surety performs or pays all that they are liable for, the surety is invested with all the rights which the creditor had against the principal debtor. This is legally known as the Right of Subrogation.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: When a borrower is facing genuine financial distress due to sudden job loss and expresses an inability to pay the current EMIs, what is the correct role of a DRA regarding debt restructuring?
audio_script: When a borrower faces genuine hardship like job loss, what is the correct ethical role of a DRA regarding debt restructuring?
option_a: The DRA has the authority to directly alter the loan agreement, reduce the interest rate, and extend the tenure on the spot.
option_b: The DRA should explain the bank's debt restructuring options, advise the borrower on how to submit a formal request with proof of job loss, and refer the case to the bank's authorized officers.
option_c: The DRA should advise the borrower that debt restructuring is only meant for corporate clients and is never applicable to individual retail borrowers.
option_d: The DRA should ignore the job loss explanation and insist that the borrower must borrow money from friends or relatives to pay immediately.
explanation: A DRA does not have the authority to restructure a loan himself. However, as part of borrower counseling, the DRA's role is to act as a bridge by explaining the restructuring options available with the bank and assisting the borrower in submitting a formal request to the bank along with proof of hardship.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities

question_text: A recovery agent visits a borrower's business premises to discuss outstanding dues. According to the IBA Model Code, what is the precise compliance requirement regarding the daily register for such visits?

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-01-Item01] Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following cases can a bank NOT exercise its statutory General Lien?
audio_script: Question 1. Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following cases can a bank NOT exercise its statutory General Lien?
option_a: On gold ornaments or securities left expressly for safe custody or for an ear-marked trust purpose
option_b: On proceeds of credit bills deposited for general collection without restrictions
option_c: On surplus proceeds remaining after the sale of an earlier pledged security
option_d: On mature fixed deposits standing in the borrower's own individual name
explanation: A banker's general lien applies strictly to securities bailed in the ordinary course of business. Valuables left specifically for safe custody or dedicated trust purposes are exempt from lien.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, if an electronic funds transfer (such as a NACH or ECS mandate) is dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds in the payer's account, what is the maximum penalty that can be legally imposed on the defaulter?
audio_script: Under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, what is the maximum penalty that can be legally imposed on a defaulter if an electronic funds transfer is dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds?
option_a: Imprisonment for a term up to 1 year, or a fine up to the amount of the electronic funds transfer, or both.

explanation: According to Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, the dishonour of an electronic funds transfer due to insufficiency of funds is a punishable offence. The maximum penalty prescribed is imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine which may extend to twice the amount of the electronic funds transfer, or with both, mirroring the provisions of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following scenarios is a banker strictly prohibited from exercising its statutory General Lien?
audio_script: Question. Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following scenarios is a banker strictly prohibited from exercising its statutory General Lien?
option_a: On securities or valuables deposited specifically for safe custody or for a designated special purpose
option_b: On credit balances lying in the borrower's fixed deposit account after maturity
option_c: On bills of exchange lodged by the borrower for general collection without restrictions
option_d: On dividend warrants sent to the bank without any specific appropriation instructions
explanation: A banker's general lien applies only to goods and securities bailed to the bank in the ordinary course of banking business. Valuables left for safe custody or earmarked for a specific trust purpose cannot be retained under lien.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: According to Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the liability of the surety is _________ to that of the principal debtor.
