audio_script: Applying Clayton's Rule to a running current account with fluctuating debit and credit balances, how are subsequent deposits appropriated when a debtor makes payments without specifying which debt they are to be applied against?
option_a: Deposits are appropriated proportionately across all existing debts, both old and new.
option_b: The earliest debit item in the account is matched and discharged by the earliest credit item, following the chronological 'first-in, first-out' principle.
option_c: The latest credit payment is always applied to the most recently incurred debit balance.
option_d: The bank holds the payments in a suspense account until the customer explicitly provides written appropriation instructions.
explanation: Clayton's Rule establishes that in a running current account, every payment made into the account is presumed to be applied to discharge the earliest debt item on the debit side of the account ('first-in, first-out'). This rule applies automatically in the absence of specific appropriation by the debtor or creditor.

option_c: On surplus proceeds remaining after the sale of an earlier pledged security
option_d: On mature fixed deposits standing in the borrower's own individual name
explanation: A banker's general lien applies strictly to securities bailed in the ordinary course of business. Valuables left specifically for safe custody or dedicated trust purposes are exempt from lien.

question_text: [CBT-15-Item12] What legal principle governs the Right of Set-off exercisable by a lending institution against a customer's deposit accounts?
audio_script: Question 12. What legal principle governs the Right of Set-off exercisable by a lending institution against a customer's deposit accounts?

option_b: A compulsory prior clearance certificate obtained from the local Debt Recovery Tribunal

explanation: Set-off requires mutuality of debts—the debts must be between the same parties in the same legal right and capacity (e.g., individual credit cannot be set off against partnership dues).

option_d: All independent accounts belonging to the customer's immediate blood relatives
explanation: A Garnishee Order Nisi attaches only the debts due or accruing due at the time of service. It does not attach future credits or uncleared cheques.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: A term loan account became a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 15th January 2020. The standard limitation period of 3 years to file a recovery suit under the Limitation Act would normally expire on 14th January 2023. However, on 10th January 2023, the borrower makes a written and signed acknowledgement of debt. Furthermore, on 5th January 2025, the borrower makes a part-payment of principal through an account transfer, evidenced by a writing signed by them. What is the fresh limitation period expiration date calculated from the last valid statutory trigger under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963?
audio_script: A term loan account became an NPA on 15th January 2020. An acknowledgement of debt was given in writing on 10th January 2023, and a part payment was made on 5th January 2025. Calculate the fresh limitation expiration date.
option_a: 14th January 2026
option_b: 5th January 2028
option_c: 10th January 2026
option_d: 15th January 2026
explanation: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, a fresh period of limitation starts from the time the acknowledgement was signed (10th January 2023), extending the limitation to 9th January 2026. Before this new expiry, under Section 19, a part-payment was made and signed on 5th January 2025. This creates a fresh period of limitation of 3 years starting from 5th January 2025, thereby extending the final limitation expiration date to 5th January 2028.

audio_script: During a recovery negotiation under RBI Fair Practices Code guidelines, a borrower trapped in acute debt denial repeatedly refuses to acknowledge the default, displaying aggressive hostility. Threatening legal action prematurely violates the Fair Practices Code regarding harassment, and agents do not have unilateral waiver authority.

explanation: Under Section 133 of the Indian Contract Act, any variance made without the surety's consent, in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor, discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: M/s Apex Traders maintains a current account with a credit balance of Rs. 4,50,000 and jointly holds a term deposit of Rs. 3,00,000 with a third party, Mr. Sen, styled 'Either or Survivor'. The sole proprietorship firm defaults on a cash credit facility of Rs. 5,00,000. Considering the legal prerequisites of the banker's right of set-off regarding 'mutuality', can the bank exercise set-off against the term deposit account?
audio_script: A sole proprietorship firm defaults on a cash credit facility. Can the bank exercise set-off against a joint term deposit held by the proprietor with a third party? Evaluate based on the mutuality of debts.
option_a: Yes, because the sole proprietor is fully liable for the firm's debts and has an equal beneficial interest in the joint account.
option_b: No, because the required element of mutuality is absent as the debts are not due in the same right and capacity (one is single proprietorship, the other is joint ownership).
option_c: Yes, provided a 14-day statutory notice is served to both account holders prior to the debit entry.
option_d: No, unless a specific hypothecation deed was executed exclusively over the term deposit at the time of opening the current account.
explanation: For the banker's right of set-off to apply, the debts must be mutual, meaning they must be due to and from the same persons in the same right and capacity. A debt due from a sole proprietorship cannot be set off against a joint account holding because the capacity of the debtor (sole owner) differs from the joint owners of the term deposit.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: When a Sole Proprietorship firm defaults on a bank credit facility, how is the legal identity of the proprietor treated in relation to recovery proceedings?
audio_script: When a Sole Proprietorship firm defaults on a bank credit facility, how is the legal identity of the proprietor treated?
option_a: The sole proprietorship has a separate legal entity distinct from the proprietor, limiting recovery to business assets only.
option_b: The sole proprietorship and the proprietor are legally one and the same; thus, the proprietor bears unlimited personal liability for all business debts.
option_c: The proprietor is liable only up to the value of the movable assets registered under the trade license.
option_d: Recovery proceedings can only be initiated against the firm's commercial bank accounts and not against personal assets.
explanation: A sole proprietorship does not have a separate legal identity independent of its owner. Therefore, under law, the business debts are the personal debts of the sole proprietor, making both business and personal assets liable for attachment and recovery.

option_a: No, the creditor must exhaust all remedies against the principal debtor's property first.
option_b: Yes, because the surety's liability is co-extensive and the surety can be sued without suing the principal debtor first.
option_c: No, the surety must be given a fresh notice of 90 days before execution.

explanation: Since the surety's liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, the surety is immediately liable when default occurs. The creditor is not bound to exhaust remedies against the principal debtor before suing or executing against the surety.

question_text: Under Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016, a moratorium is declared upon the admission of a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). audio_script: Under Section 14 of the IBC, 2016, a moratorium is declared upon the admission of CIRP. Which of the following accurately describes the legal position regarding the invocation of a personal guarantee given by a director for the corporate debtor's debt during this moratorium period?
option_a: The moratorium under Section 14 strictly applies to the corporate debtor and automatically extends to stay any recovery proceedings or invocation of personal guarantees against the personal guarantor.
option_b: The moratorium under Section 14 applies only to the corporate debtor and does not bar the creditor from initiating or continuing recovery actions or invoking a personal guarantee against the personal guarantor.
option_c: Creditors can initiate recovery against the personal guarantor only after obtaining explicit permission from the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) bench handling the corporate debtor's CIRP.

It does not bar the initiation or continuation of legal proceedings or recovery actions, including the invocation of personal guarantees, against personal guarantors of the corporate debtor.

option_c: The debt automatically binds the trust corpus via the doctrine of necessity.

explanation: Trustees have no inherent or implied power to borrow money or mortgage trust property unless specifically authorized by the Trust Deed. If borrowing powers are absent, the loan does not bind the trust estate, and the lender's remedy is restricted to the personal liability of the trustees who contracted the debt.

question_text: Mr. Sharma deposited a sealed envelope containing gold ornaments explicitly for 'Safe Custody' at Bank of Baroda, receiving a safe custody receipt. Simultaneously, Mr. Sharma defaulted on an unsecured personal loan availed from the same branch. Can the bank exercise its banker's lien under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, over the gold ornaments in safe custody to recover the personal loan default?
audio_script: Mr. Sharma deposited a sealed envelope containing gold ornaments explicitly for Safe Custody at Bank of Baroda. Simultaneously, he defaulted on an unsecured personal loan at the same branch. Can the bank exercise its banker's lien under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act over the gold ornaments?
option_a: Yes, because Section 171 grants a general lien to bankers over all goods bailed to them by a customer.
option_b: No, because goods received for safe custody create a trust or special contract that excludes the operation of the general banker's lien.
option_c: Yes, provided the bank gives a 14-day prior statutory notice to the borrower before exercising the lien.
option_d: No, unless the customer executes a separate hypothecation deed specifically covering safe custody items.
explanation: Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the banker's general lien does not apply to goods or valuables left with the bank for a specific purpose, such as safe custody, where the bank acts as a bailee under a special contract or trust. Therefore, a banker's lien cannot be exercised over safe custody deposits.

question_text: A registered partnership firm takes a credit facility from a bank, with Partner A executing the loan documents purportedly on behalf of the firm. Subsequently, Partner B retires from the firm without issuing a public notice as mandated by Section 45 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The firm defaults on the debt, and the bank initiates recovery proceedings before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT). Partner B contends that he was not a partner when the default occurred and had formally assigned his share. What is the legal liability of Partner B under the Act?
audio_script: A registered partnership firm takes a bank loan, and partner B retires without giving a public notice under Section 45. The firm defaults, and Partner B claims he is not liable because he retired before the default. What is his legal liability?
option_a: Partner B is completely absolved of liability because the default occurred after his retirement.
option_b: Partner B remains liable to the bank for the debt because no public notice of his retirement was given as required by Section 45, making him liable to third parties who deal with the firm without knowing of his retirement.
option_c: Partner B is liable only if the bank proves that he personally utilized the disbursed loan funds.
option_d: Partner B's liability is restricted strictly to the capital he held in the firm on the exact date of his retirement notice to his co-partners inter se.
explanation: Under Section 45 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, partners continue to be liable to third parties for any act done by any of them which would have been an act of the firm if done prior to the retirement, until public notice is given of the retirement. Since Partner B failed to issue a public notice, he remains liable to the bank for the credit facility.

option_c: Personal assets can only be attached if a specific guarantee was executed distinct from the proprietorship loan agreement.

explanation: A sole proprietorship has no separate legal existence apart from its owner. Therefore, the proprietor has unlimited personal liability, meaning business debts can be recovered by attaching both business assets and personal properties of the proprietor.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Which of the following retail loan products is generally classified as an 'unsecured loan' where no specific tangible asset is hypothecated or mortgaged to the lending bank?
audio_script: Which of the following retail loan products is generally classified as an unsecured loan where no specific tangible asset is hypothecated or mortgaged to the lending bank?
option_a: Home Loan
option_b: Car Loan
option_c: Personal Loan
option_d: Loan against Fixed Deposit
explanation: A personal loan is typically an unsecured retail loan granted by banks based on the borrower's credit history and income, without requiring any tangible collateral, unlike home loans, car loans, or loans against fixed deposits.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under the provisions of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, if a borrower's account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) and the secured creditor issues a demand notice under Section 13(2), within what statutory timeframe must the borrower make the representation or raise objections to the notice, and within how many days must the authorized officer reply to such representation from the date of receipt?
audio_script: Under the SARFAESI Act, 2002, after a Section 13(2) demand notice is issued for an NPA account, what is the statutory timeframe for the borrower to raise objections, and within how many days must the authorized officer reply to it?
option_a: Within 30 days for representation by the borrower; within 15 days for the reply by the authorized officer.
option_b: Within 60 days for representation by the borrower; within 30 days for the reply by the authorized officer.
option_c: Within 15 days for representation by the borrower; within 7 days for the reply by the authorized officer.
option_d: Within 45 days for representation by the borrower; within 15 days for the reply by the authorized officer.
explanation: According to Section 13(3A) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, if the borrower makes any representation or raises any objection upon receipt of the demand notice under Section 13(2), the secured creditor shall consider such representation or objection within 30 days from the date of receipt of such representation or objection and communicate the reasons for non-acceptance to the borrower. Although the general notice period under Section 13(2) to discharge the liability is 60 days, the specific window to make a representation and the corresponding reply timeline are governed by Section 13(3A).

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: As per RBI guidelines on Digital Lending, what is the mandated look-up period or cooling-off window during which a borrower can repay the principal and proportionate APR without incurring any penalty, and does this apply to loans of all tenures?
audio_script: As per RBI guidelines on Digital Lending, what is the mandated cooling-off window during which a borrower can repay the principal and proportionate APR without penalty, and does this apply to all loan tenures?
option_a: 3 days; applicable only to loans with a tenure of 1 year or more
option_b: Not less than 1 day for digital loans up to 7 days, and not less than 3 days for digital loans with a tenure of more than 7 days
option_c: 7 days uniformly for all digital loans regardless of tenure
option_d: 14 days; applicable only to microfinance loans regulated by RBI
explanation: According to RBI guidelines on digital lending, Regulated Entities (REs) must provide a cooling-off/look-up period during which borrowers can exit digital loans without penalty. This is stipulated as not less than 1 day for digital loans having a tenure of up to 7 days, and not less than 3 days for digital loans having a tenure of more than 7 days.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Which specific section of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016 mandates the declaration of a moratorium prohibiting the institution of suits or continuation of pending proceedings against the corporate debtor upon the admission of a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP)?
audio_script: Which specific section of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 mandates the declaration of a moratorium upon admission of CIRP?
option_a: Section 12
option_b: Section 14
option_c: Section 16
option_d: Section 9
explanation: Section 14 of the IBC, 2016 provides for the declaration of a moratorium by the Adjudicating Authority prohibiting institution or continuation of suits, execution of judgments, and recovery of any property by an owner/lessor once CIRP is admitted.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Which entities are legally permitted to directly disburse and collect digital loans under the RBI framework, ensuring that funds flow directly between the bank account of the Regulated Entity and the borrower?
audio_script: Which entities are legally permitted to directly disburse and collect digital loans under the RBI framework, ensuring that funds flow directly between the bank account of the Regulated Entity and the borrower?
option_a: Lending Service Providers (LSPs) directly
option_b: Digital Lending Apps (DLAs) through escrow accounts
option_c: Regulated Entities (REs) directly, bypassing pass-through accounts of third parties
option_d: Recovery agents appointed by the LSP
explanation: RBI guidelines mandate that all loan disbursments and repayments must be executed directly between the bank account of the Regulated Entity (RE) and the borrower without any pass-through or pool account of the LSP or any third party.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: What is the legal consequence for a Debt Recovery Agent who breaches client data confidentiality by selling borrower contact lists to third-party marketing agencies?
audio_script: What is the legal consequence for a Debt Recovery Agent who breaches client data confidentiality by selling borrower contact lists to third-party marketing agencies?
option_a: Only a verbal warning from the lending bank
option_b: Immediate termination of agency contract, blacklisting by IBA/RBI, and potential penal action under the IT Act
option_c: A mandatory 7-day community service order
option_d: Conversion of the loan into an unsecured grant
explanation: Data breach and unauthorized sharing of customer PII (Personally Identifiable Information) attracts severe penal consequences under the IT Act, contractual termination, and blacklisting.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 deals with the effect of acknowledgement of liability in writing. For such an acknowledgement to successfully extend the limitation period for a debt, what are the mandatory statutory prerequisites under this section?
audio_script: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 deals with the effect of acknowledgement of liability in writing. For such an acknowledgement to successfully extend the limitation period for a debt, what are the mandatory statutory prerequisites under this section?
option_a: It must be made orally before two independent witnesses after the expiry of the original limitation period.
option_b: It must be signed only by a court-appointed receiver before the expiration of the prescribed period and registered mandatorily.
option_c: It must be in writing, signed by the party against whom the property or right is claimed, and made before the expiration of the prescribed limitation period.
option_d: It can be unsigned, provided it is sent via registered post after the limitation period has already expired.
explanation: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 states that a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when an acknowledgement of liability has been made in writing and signed by the party against whom such property or right is claimed, provided the acknowledgement is made before the expiration of the prescribed limitation period.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In working capital assessment under the traditional lending norms, the 'Drawing Power' (DP) of a borrower is calculated based on which of the following?
audio_script: In working capital assessment under the traditional lending norms, the Drawing Power of a borrower is calculated based on which of the following?
option_a: Sanctioned limit minus total term loan liabilities.
option_b: Eligible current assets (stocks and book debts) minus statutory/other margins prescribed by the bank.
option_c: Total fixed assets less accumulated depreciation.
option_d: Paid-up capital plus free reserves of the borrowing company.
explanation: Drawing Power (DP) is the limit up to which a firm can draw funds against the security of current assets (stocks and debtors) after deducting the applicable margins stipulated by the bank.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under the RBI Digital Lending Guidelines (DLGs), regarding the direct account disbursal mandate, all loan disbursals and repayments must be executed strictly through which of the following channels, with limited regulatory exceptions?
audio_script: Under the RBI Digital Lending Guidelines, regarding direct account disbursal, how must all loan disbursals and repayments be executed?
option_a: Through the pooled account of the Lending Service Provider (LSP) maintained with a scheduled commercial bank.
option_b: Directly between the bank account of the Regulated Entity (RE) and the bank account of the borrower without any pass-through or pool account of third parties.
option_c: Via digital wallets or prepaid payment instruments managed by the LSP, subject to prior borrower consent.
option_d: Through cash or bearer cheques if the loan amount is below Rupees 50,000.
explanation: RBI Digital Lending Guidelines mandate that all loan disbursals and repayments shall be executed only between the bank accounts of the Regulated Entity (RE) and the borrower directly, without any pass-through or pool account of the Lending Service Provider (LSP) or any third party.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: In the context of NACH and ECS mandate dishonour penalties under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, a complaint can be filed by the aggrieved party within how many days of the cause of action arising, typically following the statutory notice period?
audio_script: In the context of NACH and ECS mandate dishonour penalties under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, a complaint can be filed by the aggrieved party within how many days of the cause of action arising, typically following the statutory notice period?
option_a: 15 days
option_b: 30 days
option_c: 45 days
option_d: 90 days
explanation: Similar to provisions under the Negotiable Instruments Act made applicable via Section 25, the payee must make a demand for payment by issuing a notice in writing within 30 days of receiving information about the dishonour, and the complaint must be filed within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities

option_a: Home Loan

explanation: Personal loans are unsecured retail credit products granted by banks based on the borrower's credit history and income without requiring any tangible collateral or security.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: As per Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, how many days does the drawer of the dishonoured NACH/ECS mandate have to make payment of the demanded amount after the receipt of the written notice from the payee, to avoid criminal prosecution?
audio_script: As per Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, how many days does the drawer have to make payment after receiving the notice to avoid prosecution?
option_a: 7 days

option_d: 45 days
explanation: Under Section 25(1)(c) of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, the drawer of the electronic funds transfer instruction fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice, thereby completing the ingredients of the offence.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Which RBI guideline-backed concept ensures that banks do not put all their funds into a single sector or borrower, thereby mitigating credit risk?
audio_script: Which RBI guideline-backed concept ensures that banks do not put all their funds into a single sector or borrower, thereby mitigating credit risk?
option_a: Principle of Diversification of Risks
option_b: Principle of Instant Liquidation
option_c: Statutory Liquidity Monopoly
option_d: Unsecured Lending Mandate
explanation: Diversification of risk is a core lending principle backed by RBI exposure norms, stating that banks should distribute credit across various industries, sectors, and borrowers to avoid concentration risk.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-16-Item01] Under Article 55 of the Limitation Act, 1963, what is the limitation period for initiating legal action for breach of contract on an unsecured promissory note?
audio_script: Question 1. Under Article 55 of the Limitation Act, 1963, what is the limitation period for initiating legal action for breach of contract on an unsecured promissory note?
option_a: 3 Years from the date when the contract is broken or default occurs
option_b: 12 Years in accordance with mortgage debt recovery norms
option_c: 1 Year from the date the recall notice is dispatched
option_d: 6 Months under the Summary Suit provisions of Order XXXVII CPC
explanation: For breach of simple contract or recovery of money on an unsecured basis / demand promissory note, the limitation period is 3 years under Article 55.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under the provisions governing Permanent Lok Adalats established under Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the maximum value of property or debt disputes involving public utility services that can be adjudicated if the parties fail to reach a settlement?
audio_script: What is the maximum value of property or debt disputes for Permanent Lok Adalats under Section 22B of the LSA Act, 1987?
option_a: Up to Rs. 10 Lakhs
option_b: Up to Rs. 20 Lakhs
option_c: Up to Rs. 1 Crore
option_d: Up to Rs. 5 Crores
explanation: As per amendments to the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, Permanent Lok Adalats have jurisdiction up to Rs. 1 Crore in disputes relating to public utility services when a settlement fails, though this ceiling can be notified by the Central Government.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under Customer Due Diligence (CDD) measures, if a customer is permitted to open an account based on a Simplified Due Diligence (SDD) process, within what maximum timeframe must the bank obtain formal Officially Valid Documents for full KYC compliance if the balance or transaction limits exceed prescribed thresholds?
audio_script: Under CDD measures, if a customer opens an account via simplified due diligence, within what maximum timeframe must the bank obtain formal OVDs if limits are exceeded?
option_a: 12 months
option_b: 6 months
option_c: 18 months
option_d: 24 months
explanation: As per RBI instructions on small accounts and simplified procedures, if the bank permits operation of accounts based on simplified measures, documents for full KYC must be obtained within a stipulated period, typically within 6 months, extendable by another 6 months in certain conditions.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-16-Item02] Under Section 21 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the legal nature and finality of an Award passed by a Lok Adalat in a debt settlement?
audio_script: Question 2. Under Section 21 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the legal nature and finality of an Award passed by a Lok Adalat in a debt settlement?
option_a: It is deemed to be a decree of a Civil Court, final and binding on all parties, and strictly non-appealable
option_b: It is an advisory recommendation that must be confirmed by the High Court within 30 days
option_c: It can be challenged before the District Sessions Court within 60 days of communication
option_d: It has no binding effect unless the borrower ratifies it through an affidavit
explanation: A Lok Adalat award is deemed to be a decree of a Civil Court under Section 21 of the LSA Act. Because it is founded on mutual consent, no appeal lies against it.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Which retail loan product typically carries a higher rate of interest due to its unsecured nature and lack of collateral?

option_a: Housing Loan
option_b: Personal Loan
option_c: Vehicle Loan
option_d: Loan against Fixed Deposit
explanation: Personal loans are unsecured credit lines, carrying higher default risks for lenders, which results in significantly higher interest rates compared to secured loans like housing or vehicle loans.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In the context of Anti-Money Laundering (AML) guidelines, which of the following scenarios is considered a classic transaction red flag indicating potential laundering or structuring?
audio_script: In the context of AML guidelines, which scenario is considered a classic transaction red flag indicating potential structuring?
option_a: A salaried individual receiving their monthly salary via direct credit.
option_b: Multiple cash deposits made just below the reporting threshold in various branches within a short timeframe.
option_c: A retired person receiving regular pension transfers from a government treasury.
option_d: An established corporate entity transferring funds to its verified overseas vendor.
explanation: Structuring (often called smurfing) involves conducting financial transactions in a specific pattern calculated to avoid the creation of certain records or reports required under AML laws, such as making multiple cash deposits just below the regulatory threshold limit.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: If a borrower files a formal grievance regarding abusive language used during a recovery call, what primary piece of evidence must the bank or DRA produce to the Banking Ombudsman or regulator?
audio_script: If a borrower files a formal grievance regarding abusive language used during a recovery call, what primary piece of evidence must the bank or DRA produce to the Banking Ombudsman or regulator?
option_a: The borrower's bank statement for the last three years
option_b: The mandatory preserved call recording of the interaction
option_c: The original loan agreement signed with a physical stamp
option_d: The CIBIL credit report of the borrower
explanation: Preserving call recordings for a minimum of 6 months serves as critical audit evidence to resolve disputes and verify complaints regarding DRA conduct during recovery calls.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In the context of lending principles, which of the following best defines the 'margin requirement' stipulated by banks against securities pledged?
audio_script: In the context of lending principles, which of the following best defines the margin requirement stipulated by banks against securities pledged?
option_a: The exact loan amount disbursed to the borrower as a percentage of the asset value.
option_b: The difference between the market value of the security and the maximum loan amount granted against it.
option_c: The interest rate charged by the bank over and above the repo rate.
option_d: The mandatory cash reserve ratio maintained by the bank with the RBI.
explanation: Margin is the percentage of the market value of security that is not funded by the bank. It represents the safety buffer maintained by the bank to cover potential declines in asset value.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under a contract of guarantee, if the principal debtor makes a default in payment, can the creditor sue the surety directly without first suing the principal debtor?
audio_script: Under a contract of guarantee, if the principal debtor makes a default in payment, can the creditor sue the surety directly without first suing the principal debtor?
option_a: No, the creditor must always exhaust legal remedies against the principal debtor first.
option_b: Yes, because the surety's liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor under Section 128.
option_c: No, unless written permission is obtained from the Reserve Bank of India.
option_d: Yes, but only if the loan amount is less than one lakh rupees.
explanation: Since the surety's liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor under Section 128, the creditor can proceed directly against the surety upon default without needing to sue the principal debtor first.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-16-Item03] Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, what is the statutory time window within which the complainant must issue the legal demand notice after receiving the cheque return memo?
audio_script: Question 3. Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, what is the statutory time window within which the complainant must issue the legal demand notice after receiving the cheque return memo?
option_a: Within 30 days of the receipt of information from the bank regarding the dishonour
option_b: Within 15 days of the date stamped on the return memo
option_c: Within 60 days in alignment with statutory default notices
option_d: Within 7 days of dishonour to preserve summary trial rights
explanation: Section 138 proviso (b) requires the payee to give a notice in writing to the drawer within 30 days of receiving information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, what is the maximum financial penalty (fine) that can be imposed by the court upon conviction for electronic fund transfer / NACH mandate dishonour?
audio_script: Under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, what is the maximum financial penalty (fine) that can be imposed by the court upon conviction for electronic fund transfer / NACH mandate dishonour?
option_a: Equal to the mandate amount
option_b: Up to twice the amount of the electronic funds transfer
option_c: A fixed statutory fine of Rs. 50,000
option_d: Up to three times the amount of the electronic funds transfer
explanation: Section 25(1) outlines that the punishment can be imprisonment up to 2 years, or with a fine which may extend to twice the amount of the electronic funds transfer, or with both.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: A non-deposit-taking NBFC categorized under the Base Layer (NBFC-BL) pursuant to RBI Scale Based Regulation fails to meet its asset size threshold and transitions into the Middle Layer. module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: In the context of Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, electronic funds transfer includes transactions carried out through systems like NACH or ECS. For penal provisions to apply, what primary condition regarding the account must be fulfilled?
audio_script: In the context of Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, electronic funds transfer includes transactions carried out through systems like NACH or ECS. For penal provisions to apply, what primary condition regarding the account must be fulfilled?
option_a: The account must be a corporate current account only

option_c: The transaction value must exceed one lakh rupees
option_d: The account must be dormant for at least 6 months
explanation: Section 25(1) clearly specifies that the electronic funds transfer must have been initiated from an account maintained by the drawer for discharging, wholly or in part, any debt or other liability, for the penal provisions to attract upon dishonour due to insufficiency of funds.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Which designated authority in India acts as the central national agency responsible for receiving, processing, analyzing, and disseminating information relating to suspect financial transactions under the PMLA, 2002?

option_a: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)

option_c: Financial Intelligence Unit - India (FIU-IND)
option_d: Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-16-Item04] Under Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, what is the maximum percentage of the cheque amount that a Court can direct the drawer to pay as Interim Compensation?

explanation: Section 143A empowers the Court trying a Section 138 complaint to order the drawer to pay interim compensation up to a maximum of 20% of the cheque amount.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Within how many days of receiving information about the return of the electronic funds transfer unpaid must the payee make a demand for payment in writing to the drawer under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007?
audio_script: Within how many days of receiving information about the return of the electronic funds transfer unpaid must the payee make a demand for payment in writing to the drawer under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007?

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: When a borrower in default exhibits debt denial by refusing to acknowledge the outstanding dues, how should a certified Debt Recovery Agent respond as per ethical collection standards?

option_a: Threaten immediate coercive legal action to break the denial

option_c: Calmly present transparent statement of accounts and maintain a professional, non-confrontational tone

explanation: Ethical debt collection under RBI and IBA guidelines requires agents to maintain composure, avoid threats, and rely on transparent documentation like statements of accounts to address denial professionally.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the person in respect of whose default the guarantee is given is known as the:

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: What is the statutory payment window provided to the drawer under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, to make the payment after the receipt of the demand notice for a dishonoured NACH/ECS mandate?
audio_script: What is the statutory payment window provided to the drawer under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, to make the payment after the receipt of the demand notice for a dishonoured NACH/ECS mandate?

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, if a partnership firm is not registered, what specific legal disability does Section 69 impose on the firm or its partners regarding the recovery of debts from borrowers/third parties through civil courts?
audio_script: Under the Indian Partnership Act, what legal disability does Section 69 impose on unregistered firms regarding debt recovery?
option_a: Partners cannot file a criminal suit for cheque bounce under Section 138 of the NI Act.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-16-Item05] What is the statutory timeline for filing an appeal before the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) against an order of the DRT under Section 20 of the RDB Act, 1993?
audio_script: Question 5. What is the statutory timeline for filing an appeal before the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) against an order of the DRT under Section 20 of the RDB Act, 1993?

option_d: Within 90 days following the publication of the final recovery certificate
explanation: Section 20 of the RDB Act prescribes a 30-day timeline to file an appeal before the DRAT, subject to mandatory pre-deposit of 50% (relaxable to not less than 25%).

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: What is the primary objective of the RBI Fair Practices Code regarding loan recovery and interactions with customers?
audio_script: What is the primary objective of the RBI Fair Practices Code regarding loan recovery and interactions with customers?
option_a: To ensure absolute recovery of dues regardless of methods used
option_b: To promote fair, transparent, and respectful dealing with borrowers while prohibiting harassment
option_c: To penalize banks for issuing unsecured loans
option_d: To exempt borrowers from repayment obligations
explanation: The Fair Practices Code aims to build transparent and ethical relationships between financial institutions/agents and borrowers, ensuring recovery is conducted without resorting to intimidation or harassment.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: In structuring a legitimate repayment plan during a negotiation where the borrower denies capacity to pay due to multi-creditor debt traps, how should a trained DRA apply active listening and objective problem-solving in accordance with RBI Fair Practices Code?
audio_script: In structuring a legitimate repayment plan during a negotiation where the borrower denies capacity to pay due to multi-creditor debt traps, how should a trained DRA apply active listening and objective problem-solving in accordance with RBI Fair Practices Code?
option_a: Demand priority repayment to your specific bank by threatening legal notices before other creditors.
option_b: Listen actively to the cash-flow constraints, avoid intrusive or public shaming tactics, and guide the borrower toward formal debt restructuring or bank-approved settlement options.
option_c: Advise the borrower to default on other competing lenders to pay off the current bank's dues fully.
option_d: Ignore the cash-flow analysis and insist on weekly cash collections outside standard banking hours.
explanation: DRAs must adhere to strict ethical codes, avoiding public shaming, coercion, or interference with other liabilities. Active listening helps identify genuine constraints, allowing agents to direct borrowers to formal restructuring mechanisms.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: A corporate borrower maintains a current account with a credit balance of INR 5,00,000 and has a defaulted term loan facility of INR 8,00,000 which is currently due and payable. The bank wishes to exercise its banker's lien and right of set-off without issuing any prior notice to the borrower, citing urgent recovery protocols. Under settled banking law and principles governing the right of set-off, which of the following prerequisites is legally critical regarding notice before exercising set-off in the absence of a specific contractual waiver?
audio_script: A corporate borrower maintains a current account with a credit balance of 5 lakh rupees and has a defaulted term loan of 8 lakh rupees due and payable. The bank wants to exercise its right of set-off without prior notice. Which legal prerequisite regarding notice applies in the absence of a contractual waiver?
option_a: Prior notice is strictly mandatory in all circumstances to provide the borrower an opportunity to dispute the balance before set-off can be executed.
option_b: No notice is required if the debts are mutual, due, and payable, though giving notice is a prudent banking practice to prevent disputes.
option_c: A mandatory 14-day statutory notice under the SARFAESI Act must be served prior to exercising the common law right of set-off.
option_d: Notice is required only if the account is held in joint names, but not for sole proprietorships or corporate accounts.
explanation: Under the common law right of banker's set-off, if the debts are mutual and both are due and payable, the bank can exercise set-off without prior notice, provided there is no contrary contract. However, notice is frequently given as a matter of prudence to avoid disputes regarding the exact computation of balances.

option_c: Threaten immediate escalation to third-party recovery agencies to compel the borrower to stop shouting and listen.
option_d: Disconnect the call or leave the premises instantly without providing any alternative contact mechanism.
explanation: Under RBI guidelines and DRA Code of Conduct, agents must handle distressed borrowers with professionalism, empathy, and dignity. Employing empathetic mirroring and a calm tone de-escalates hostility, complying with the mandate against harassment and abusive behavior.

option_d: Maintaining a visit log is optional if the DRA is carrying a body-worn camera or recording the audio on a smartphone.

explanation: RBI guidelines mandate that recovery agents must respect the borrower's privacy and dignity, restricting visit timings and prohibiting public shaming or harassment.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Regarding the operational duties of a Debt Recovery Agent (DRA), which of the following statements correctly defines the regulatory rule on the non-delegation of recovery duties?
audio_script: Regarding the operational duties of a Debt Recovery Agent, which of the following statements correctly defines the regulatory rule on the non-delegation of recovery duties?
option_a: A DRA can sub-contract recovery tasks to local independent collection agencies if the workload exceeds operational capacity.
option_b: A DRA can delegate field visits to unregistered freelance agents provided they carry an authorization letter from the principal DRA.
option_c: Recovery functions entrusted to a certified DRA are non-delegable, meaning the certified individual or agency must execute the duties directly through their own certified and empaneled personnel without sub-contracting.
option_d: A DRA may outsource tele-calling recovery operations to foreign call centers without prior bank approval.
explanation: Under IIBF and RBI framework, recovery work assigned to a DRA involves fiduciary responsibility and strict regulatory compliance. The principle of non-delegation dictates that the certified DRA cannot sub-contract or assign recovery mandates to uncertified third parties or external agencies not empaneled by the bank.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

option_a: Only the principal loan amount

option_c: The recovery agent's contact details

explanation: The Key Fact Statement (KFS) must provide a standardized format encompassing all-inclusive cost of digital loans, including the Annual Percentage Rate (APR), recovery charges, and all hidden or explicit fees.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: During a field visit for a defaulted cash-credit account with an outstanding balance of Rs. 8,50,000, the borrower offers Rs. 3,00,000 in cash as full and final settlement, claiming he has to leave for abroad immediately. The DRA agent accepts the cash, issues a handwritten plain paper receipt signed by himself, and promises to deposit it by the next working day. Which of the following regulatory breaches has the DRA committed under the IIBF Code of Conduct and RBI guidelines?
audio_script: During a field visit, a DRA accepts cash for a settlement and issues a handwritten receipt. What is the regulatory breach?
option_a: Accepting cash payment without issuing an official pre-printed instant receipt generated through a secure banking device or immediate bank channel, and failing to secure prior written bank approval for the OTS compromise.
option_b: Violating Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act by accepting cash instead of a cheque for an overdue amount exceeding Rs. 5,00,000.
option_c: Failing to deposit the cash within 2 hours of collection into the DRA's personal designated escrow account maintained for recovery operations.
option_d: Breaching the SARFAESI Act, 2002 timeline by not issuing a 60-day demand notice prior to accepting part-payment in cash.
explanation: DRAs are strictly prohibited from accepting cash collections without issuing an official, system-generated instant receipt authorized by the bank. Furthermore, any One-Time Settlement (OTS) or compromise offer must be formally evaluated and approved by the competent authority of the lending institution before acceptance. Accepting cash and issuing unauthorized receipts constitutes gross professional misconduct and potential fraud.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: As per the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) guidelines on Digital Lending, all digital lending disbursements must be made strictly through which of the following routes, bypassing pass-through accounts?

option_a: Directly from the bank account of the Lending Service Provider (LSP) to the borrower's loan account
option_b: Directly from the bank account of the Regulated Entity (RE) to the bank account of the borrower
option_c: Through a designated escrow account managed by third-party payment aggregators
option_d: In cash or via bearer cheques issued by the non-banking financial company
explanation: According to the RBI Digital Lending Guidelines, loan disbursements must be executed directly from the bank account of the Regulated Entity (RE, such as a bank or NBFC) to the bank account of the borrower without any passthrough or pooling account of the Lending Service Provider (LSP) or any third party.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities

explanation: According to RBI KYC Master Directions, periodic updation of KYC shall be carried out at least once in every two years for high-risk customers, once in every eight years for medium-risk customers, and once in every ten years for low-risk customers.

option_a: Challenge the borrower's claim of distress and continue pressing for immediate asset seizure on the spot.
option_b: Immediately disengage from coercive communication, ensure physical safety, use calming de-escalation language, and promptly report the incident to the lender's nodal officer.
option_c: Record the interaction on personal social media to expose the borrower's uncooperative behavior.
option_d: Increase the volume of demands to assert authority and compel compliance despite the threats.
explanation: RBI and DRA guidelines strictly prohibit harassment, intimidation, or aggressive tactics. When extreme distress or threats occur, agents must prioritize safety, de-escalate without coercion, and report matters to the financial institution.

audio_script: In a win-win settlement negotiation scenario under RBI’s framework for Compromise Settlements and Technical Write-offs, a borrower repeatedly denies the total outstanding amount including penal interest, citing severe business losses. option_a: Refuse to bifurcate the principal and penal interest, insisting on an upfront lump-sum payment of the entire disputed ledger balance.

option_c: Offer an unauthorized waiver of the entire principal amount to close the account within the same business day.
option_d: Warn the borrower that debt denial automatically invalidates their eligibility for any legal settlement scheme.
explanation: Effective win-win negotiations require active listening to validate genuine financial hardships, followed by exploring structured settlements like compromise settlements permitted under RBI guidelines, ensuring the lender's recovery while offering feasible relief.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: When extending credit facilities to a Public Limited Company, what critical statutory verification must a bank or debt recovery agent perform regarding borrowing powers under Section 180 of the Companies Act, 2013?
audio_script: When extending credit to a Public Limited Company, what verification is required under Section 180 of the Companies Act?
option_a: Board resolution is sufficient for borrowing any amount exceeding paid-up capital.
option_b: Ordinary resolution passed in a general meeting if borrowings exceed aggregate paid-up share capital and free reserves.
option_c: Special resolution passed in a general meeting if borrowings exceed aggregate paid-up share capital and free reserves.
option_d: Prior written approval from the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for all term loans.
explanation: As per Section 180(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Board of Directors of a public company cannot borrow money exceeding the aggregate of its paid-up share capital, free reserves, and securities premium (apart from temporary loans obtained in the ordinary course of business) without obtaining approval of the company by a special resolution in a general meeting.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics

explanation: RBI guidelines on engaging recovery agents explicitly mandate that recovery duties, including location verification and borrower contact, cannot be sub-contracted or delegated by the authorized DRA to any unauthorized third-party agencies or individuals, ensuring direct accountability to the lender bank.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, what is the primary consequence if an electronic funds transfer instruction (such as an ECS or NACH mandate) is dishonoured by the bank on which it is drawn due to insufficient funds?
audio_script: Under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, what is the primary consequence if an electronic funds transfer instruction such as an ECS or NACH mandate is dishonoured by the bank on which it is drawn due to insufficient funds?

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 31 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, which of the following categories of security interest is explicitly exempted from the application of the Act, specifically regarding the threshold limit of principal and interest due?
audio_script: Under Section 31 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, which of the following categories of security interest is explicitly exempted from the application of the Act, specifically regarding the threshold limit of principal and interest due?

option_b: Any secured debt where the amount due is less than one lakh rupees.
option_c: Any security interest created on agricultural land.
option_d: All of the above.
explanation: Section 31 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 outlines exemptions where the provisions of the Act shall not apply. These include a security interest created in agricultural land (Section 31(i)), any case in which the amount due is less than 20% of the principal amount and interest thereon (Section 31(o)), and any case in which the amount due is less than one lakh rupees (Section 31(enacted via notification/amendment provisions matching lower thresholds), thus all listed options are correct exemptions under Section 31).

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: If an NBFC meets the criteria of Rs. 100 Crore asset size and Rs. 20 Lakhs minimum default, what is the mandatory statutory notice period that must be provided to the borrower under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act before taking enforcement actions?

option_d: 14 days
explanation: Under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, the secured creditor must issue a 60-day notice to the borrower to discharge their liabilities in full, failing which the creditor can exercise enforcement rights under Section 13(4).

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Which of the following actions by a Debt Recovery Agent would constitute a direct breach of data privacy and confidentiality codes?

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under the current statutory provisions, what is the minimum default claim amount required for a notified NBFC with the requisite asset size to initiate recovery proceedings under the SARFAESI Act, 2002?

explanation: Notified NBFCs with an asset size of Rs. 100 Crore or more can invoke the SARFAESI Act provisions only when the borrower's default amount is Rs. 20 Lakhs or more.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Regarding the 'cooling-off' or look-up period mandated by RBI for digital loans issued by Regulated Entities and their LSPs, which of the following statements is legally accurate?
audio_script: Regarding the cooling-off period mandated by RBI for digital loans, which of the following statements is legally accurate?
option_a: Borrowers must be given a cooling-off period of at least 14 days during which they can exit the loan by paying the principal and proportionate APR without penalty.
option_b: Borrowers are allowed a standardized cooling-off period determined by the RE, during which they can exit the digital loan by paying only the principal and proportionate APR, without any prepayment penalty.
option_c: A mandatory 7-day cooling-off period applies exclusively to microfinance digital loans, during which recovery calls are strictly prohibited.
option_d: The cooling-off period is optional and can be waived if the borrower provides a digital waiver during the onboarding process.
explanation: RBI guidelines require REs to provide a cooling-off/look-up period during which the borrower can exit the digital loan by paying the principal and proportionate APR without any penalty. The exact period is determined by the board-approved policy of the RE, subject to regulatory expectations.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: What is the primary structural distinction between a Term Loan and a Working Capital facility regarding their repayment source and purpose?
audio_script: What is the primary structural distinction between a Term Loan and a Working Capital facility regarding their repayment source and purpose?
option_a: Term loans are unsecured facilities repaid from daily sales, whereas working capital loans require immovable property mortgages.
option_b: Term loans are meant for acquiring capital assets and are repaid from future operational cash flows, whereas working capital loans finance day-to-day operating cycles and are repaid from the realization of current assets.
option_c: Term loans have a maximum maturity of 12 months, whereas working capital loans are extended for periods exceeding 5 years.
option_d: Working capital loans are governed strictly by the SARFAESI Act, whereas term loans fall outside debt recovery legislation.
explanation: Term loans are structured for capital expenditure (machinery, building) and repaid over a longer duration from projected cash generation. Working capital loans fund short-term operational assets like inventory and receivables and are rolled over or adjusted through the conversion cycle of current assets.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under the RBI AML (Anti-Money Laundering) guidelines, how is a Politically Exposed Person (PEP) generally classified in terms of risk categorization by regulated entities?
audio_script: Under the RBI AML guidelines, how is a Politically Exposed Person, or PEP, generally classified in terms of risk categorization by regulated entities?
option_a: Low Risk
option_b: Medium Risk
option_c: High Risk
option_d: Zero Risk
explanation: RBI guidelines mandate that Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) entrusted with prominent public functions by foreign or domestic countries—such as heads of states, senior politicians, and judicial officials—must invariably be subjected to High-Risk customer categorization and enhanced due diligence (EDD).

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: During a recovery visit for a defaulted retail loan, a borrower disputes the outstanding principal amount, claiming an uncredited cash deposit made at the bank's branch, and demands an immediate resolution. According to the regulatory framework and the Code of Conduct governing Debt Recovery Agents (DRAs), what is the precise mandatory timeline and procedure for the DRA regarding this customer grievance?
audio_script: During a recovery visit, a borrower disputes the outstanding amount due to an uncredited deposit. Within what timeframe must the DRA report this grievance to the bank's nodal officer?
option_a: Resolve the grievance at the borrower's doorstep within 12 hours and adjust the ledger accordingly.
option_b: Report the customer grievance to the bank's designated nodal officer within 24 hours for formal logging and escalation.
option_c: Wait for the end of the monthly reconciliation cycle before notifying the bank about disputed accounts.
option_d: Inform the borrower to directly approach the banking ombudsman without involving the bank's recovery channel.
explanation: As per the regulatory guidelines and Code of Conduct for Debt Recovery Agents, any formal dispute or grievance raised by a borrower regarding the loan account must be reported by the DRA to the bank's nodal officer within 24 hours to ensure immediate tracking, stoppage of coercive recovery actions during investigation, and compliance with fair practices.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: When a recovery agent visits a borrower's residence, what must they do with their authorization letter issued by the bank?

option_c: Mail it to the borrower's employer after the visit
option_d: Submit it permanently to the borrower during the first interaction
explanation: Recovery agents must display or produce their authorization letters issued by the bank whenever requested by the borrower to establish their official locus standi.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, once a notice is issued by the secured creditor to the borrower specifying the default and demanding repayment, what is the mandatory statutory time period within which the borrower must discharge their liabilities in full?
audio_script: Under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, once a notice is issued by the secured creditor to the borrower specifying the default and demanding repayment, what is the mandatory statutory time period within which the borrower must discharge their liabilities in full?
option_a: 30 days from the date of notice
option_b: 60 days from the date of notice
option_c: 90 days from the date of notice
option_d: 15 days from the date of notice
explanation: According to Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, the secured creditor must give a notice in writing to the borrower requiring them to discharge their liabilities in full within 60 days from the date of the notice, failing which the secured creditor is entitled to exercise measures under Section 13(4).

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: According to the IBA Model Code of Conduct for Debt Recovery Agents, when a DRA visits a borrower's residence or workplace, what specific document(s) along with their DRA identity badge must they mandatorily carry and exhibit to the borrower upon request?
audio_script: According to the IBA Model Code of Conduct for Debt Recovery Agents, when a DRA visits a borrower's residence or workplace, what specific document along with their DRA identity badge must they mandatorily carry and exhibit to the borrower upon request?
option_a: Only a copy of the loan agreement and statement of account
option_b: A formal authorization letter issued by the bank along with a copy of the consumer grievance redressal procedure
option_c: An Aadhaar verification certificate and police clearance certificate
option_d: A court warrant issued under the SARFAESI Act
explanation: Under the IBA Model Code of Conduct, Debt Recovery Agents must carry their DRA identity card and an official authorization letter from the bank. They are required to produce these documents for inspection upon demand by the borrower to establish their genuine identity and authority.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

explanation: The Upper Layer (NBFC-UL) consists of NBFCs specifically singled out by the RBI based on a scoring methodology encompassing size, leverage, interconnectedness, etc., warranting tighter regulation.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: What is the mandatory statutory period given to the drawer of a dishonoured cheque to make payment of the cheque amount after the receipt of the formal demand notice issued under Section 138(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881?

option_a: 7 days

explanation: According to proviso (c) to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the offence is committed only if the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: [CBT-17-Item01] Under RBI's Master Directions on Digital Lending, what is the mandatory requirement regarding the Key Fact Statement (KFS)?

option_d: KFS is only mandatory for corporate entity borrowers with turnover exceeding Rs 100 Crore
explanation: Under RBI Digital Lending Directions, a standardized KFS with full disclosure of APR and cooling-off terms must be provided to the borrower prior to agreement execution.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Which regulatory body's guidelines form the foundation for the Model Code of Conduct adopted by the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) for recovery agents?

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: In the context of the RBI guidelines on Digital Lending, who bears the ultimate regulatory and legal responsibility for any compliance failures or coercive recovery practices deployed by a Lending Service Provider (LSP) engaged by the institution?
audio_script: In the context of RBI digital lending guidelines, who bears ultimate regulatory responsibility for compliance failures or coercive recovery practices by an LSP?
option_a: The Lending Service Provider (LSP) exclusively, as they directly interface with the borrowers.

option_d: Jointly and severally by the Chief Executive Officer of the LSP and the Director of the RE.
explanation: RBI guidelines explicitly state that Regulated Entities (REs) cannot abdicate their regulatory responsibilities. REs remain fully accountable for compliance, customer grievance redressal, and ethical recovery practices, even when utilizing outsourced LSPs and digital channels.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: An aggrieved party wishes to file an appeal against the order of the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) to the Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) under Section 20 of the RDB Act, 1993. What is the statutory limitation period for filing such an appeal?

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Section 139 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 stipulates that if the creditor does any act which is inconsistent with the rights of the surety, or omits to do any act which his duty to the surety requires him to do, and the eventual remedy of the surety against the principal debtor is impaired, what is the effect on the surety?
audio_script: Under Section 139 of the Indian Contract Act, what is the effect on the surety if the creditor's omission impairs the surety's eventual remedy against the principal debtor?
option_a: The surety is partially discharged up to the value of the impaired security.
option_b: The surety is discharged completely from their liability.
option_c: The surety can only sue the creditor for damages but remains liable to pay the debt.
option_d: The surety's liability is suspended until the remedy is restored by the court.
explanation: Section 139 states that if the creditor does any act that impairs the surety's eventual remedy against the principal debtor, the surety is discharged. Any major impairment of the surety's rights and remedies due to the creditor's default releases the surety entirely.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: In the context of the RDB Act, 1993, which of the following modes of recovery is NOT typically exercised by the Recovery Officer for executing a recovery certificate?

option_a: Attachment and sale of the movable or immovable property of the defendant

option_c: Appointment of a receiver for the management of the defendant's properties
option_d: Direct criminal prosecution and imprisonment of the borrower for default
explanation: The Recovery Officer executes recovery certificates through civil measures like attachment and sale of property, arrest and detention, and appointment of receivers, but does not conduct criminal prosecution for mere debt default under this Act.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: According to Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, the dishonour of an electronic funds transfer instruction due to insufficient funds is deemed to be an offence similar to the dishonour of a cheque under which section of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881?

option_d: Section 148
explanation: Section 25(1) of the PSS Act stipulates that where an electronic funds transfer instruction is dishonoured due to insufficient funds in the account, it shall be deemed to constitute an offence and shall be punishable in like manner as under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

option_a: Base Layer
option_b: Middle Layer
option_c: Upper Layer
option_d: Bottom Layer
explanation: The Upper Layer (UL) of NBFCs under the SBR framework is populated by identifying them through a comprehensive scoring methodology based on parameters like size, interconnectedness, complexity, and supervisory inputs, warranting stricter regulation than the Middle Layer.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Which of the following describes the 'Cash Budget Method' of assessing working capital, which is typically recommended for seasonal industries like sugar mills or tea gardens?
audio_script: Which of the following describes the Cash Budget Method of assessing working capital, which is typically recommended for seasonal industries like sugar mills or tea gardens?
option_a: Assessment based on peak inventory levels minus trade creditors over a 12-month period.
option_b: Assessment based on month-by-month projection of cash inflows and cash outflows to determine the peak deficit funding requirement.
option_c: Assessment based on fixed percentage of annual gross sales turnover without inventory breakdown.
option_d: Assessment based on the net worth of the promoters plus unsecured market loans.
explanation: For seasonal industries, cash flows are erratic. The Cash Budget Method evaluates projected monthly receipts and payments to find the exact peak cash deficit, ensuring precise working capital financing rather than standard operating cycle formulas.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: [CBT-17-Item03] Under RBI Master Directions, what are the statutory eligibility thresholds for an NBFC to enforce security interests under the SARFAESI Act, 2002?

option_a: Asset size of Rs 100 Crore and above, with a minimum default claim threshold of Rs 20 Lakh
option_b: Asset size of Rs 500 Crore and above, with a minimum default claim threshold of Rs 1 Crore
option_c: Asset size of Rs 50 Crore and above, with a minimum default claim threshold of Rs 5 Lakh
option_d: Asset size of Rs 1,000 Crore with zero net Non-Performing Assets
explanation: NBFCs with an asset size of Rs 100 Crore and above are notified as financial institutions under the SARFAESI Act with a minimum debt enforcement threshold of Rs 20 Lakh.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, what is the legal consequence on existing debts of a registered partnership firm when a partner retires without giving public notice of retirement under Section 45?
audio_script: Under the Indian Partnership Act 1932, what is the legal consequence on existing debts of a registered partnership firm when a partner retires without giving public notice of retirement under Section 45?
option_a: The retired partner remains liable for all debts incurred even after retirement
option_b: The retired partner continues to be liable to third parties for acts done before retirement until public notice is given
option_c: The retired partner is absolved of all past and future liabilities immediately upon signing the retirement deed
option_d: The firm is automatically dissolved and recovery proceedings are stayed
explanation: According to Section 45 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, partners continue to be liable as such to third parties for any act done by any of them which would have been an act of the firm if done before the public notice, until public notice is given of the retirement.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under Section 84 of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies (MSCS) Act, 2002, if a dispute touching the constitution, management, or business of a multi-state co-operative society is referred to arbitration, what is the statutory status and execution mechanism of the arbitral award when it is filed with the concerned Civil Court?
audio_script: Under Section 84 of the MSCS Act 2002, how is an arbitral award executed when filed with the Civil Court?
option_a: It is treated as a decree of the Civil Court and shall be executed in the same manner as a decree of that Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
option_b: It must be re-adjudicated by the Civil Court through a summary suit before execution can commence.
option_c: It can only be executed by the Central Registrar directly without intervention of any Civil Court.
option_d: It is merely a recommendation and requires approval from the State Government where the assets are situated.
explanation: According to Section 84 of the MSCS Act, 2002, an award made under the arbitration provisions shall be deemed to be a decree of the Civil Court and shall be executed in the same manner as a decree of such court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, once filed before the court having jurisdiction.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: In the Scale Based Regulation framework, when does an NBFC transition from the Upper Layer (NBFC-UL) to the Top Layer (NBFC-TL)?
audio_script: In the Scale Based Regulation framework, when does an NBFC transition from the Upper Layer to the Top Layer?
option_a: Automatically when asset size crosses Rs. 5,000 crore
option_b: When the RBI determines that there is a substantial increase in systemic risk from the specific NBFC
option_c: Every three years mandatorily
option_d: When the NBFC decides to convert into a commercial bank
explanation: The Top Layer (NBFC-TL) is ideally expected to be empty and is populated only if the RBI sees substantial systemic risk emanating from specific NBFCs in the Upper Layer.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-17-Item04] Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following cases can a bank NOT exercise its statutory General Lien?
audio_script: Question 4. Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following cases can a bank NOT exercise its statutory General Lien?
option_a: On gold ornaments or securities left expressly for safe custody or for an ear-marked trust purpose
option_b: On proceeds of credit bills deposited for general collection without restrictions
