explanation: Hypothecation is a charge created over movable property for securing a debt without the transfer of either ownership or possession to the lender, typically executed via a hypothecation deed.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In the context of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) debt liability, under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, and relevant provisions of Hindu Law, what is the legal extent of liability of a coparcener (other than the Karta) when a bank initiates recovery proceedings against a business loan availed by the Karta for family business purposes?
audio_script: In the context of a Hindu Undivided Family debt liability, under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Amendment Act, 2005, and relevant provisions of Hindu Law, what is the legal extent of liability of a coparcener other than the Karta when a bank initiates recovery proceedings against a business loan availed by the Karta for family business purposes?
option_a: Coparceners have unlimited personal liability extending to their separate and self-acquired properties for all debts contracted by the Karta.
option_b: Coparceners have liability that is strictly limited to the extent of their respective coparcenary share/interest in the joint family property.
option_c: Coparceners hold absolute immunity from any debt recovery actions, and only the Karta's personal assets can be attached by the bank.
option_d: Coparceners are jointly and severally liable with their entire personal assets, identical to partners in a general partnership.
explanation: Under Hindu Law, while the Karta has the authority to contract debts for legal necessity or benefit of the estate incurring unlimited personal liability, the other coparceners (including daughters who became coparceners post-2005 amendment) are not personally liable beyond their share in the ancestral/joint family property, unless they have explicitly executed personal guarantees.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-17-Item15] Under Section 21 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the legal nature and finality of an Award passed by a Lok Adalat in a debt settlement?
audio_script: Question 15. Under Section 21 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the legal nature and finality of an Award passed by a Lok Adalat in a debt settlement?
option_a: It is deemed to be a decree of a Civil Court, final and binding on all parties, and strictly non-appealable
option_b: It is an advisory recommendation that must be confirmed by the High Court within 30 days
option_c: It can be challenged before the District Sessions Court within 60 days of communication
option_d: It has no binding effect unless the borrower ratifies it through an affidavit
explanation: A Lok Adalat award is deemed to be a decree of a Civil Court under Section 21 of the LSA Act. Because it is founded on mutual consent, no appeal lies against it.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: When initiating recovery against a Company registered under the Companies Act, 2013, which statutory charge must be registered with the Registrar of Companies (RoC) under Section 77 to ensure priority during liquidation?
audio_script: When initiating recovery against a Company registered under the Companies Act 2013, which statutory charge must be registered with the Registrar of Companies under Section 77 to ensure priority during liquidation?
option_a: Charge on movable property only
option_b: Charge on book debts only
option_c: Charge created on the property or assets or any of its undertakings, whether tangible or otherwise
option_d: Floating charge on intangible assets exclusively
explanation: Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates that every company creating a charge on its property or assets or any of its undertakings (tangible or otherwise) must register the particulars of the charge with the RoC, failing which the charge is void against the liquidator and creditors upon winding up.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Can loan repayments under RBI Digital Lending Guidelines be routed through a third-party pool account maintained by an LSP?
audio_script: Can loan repayments under RBI Digital Lending Guidelines be routed through a third-party pool account maintained by an LSP?
option_a: Yes, if the borrower consents
option_b: Yes, for ease of collection
option_c: No, repayments must be executed directly between the borrower's bank account and the RE's bank account
option_d: Yes, provided the LSP is registered with NPCI
explanation: RBI guidelines strictly prohibit any third-party pool accounts. Loan repayments must also flow directly from the borrower's bank account to the RE's bank account without passing through an LSP's pool account.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Under the RBI Code of Conduct, within what permissible timeframe are Debt Recovery Agents permitted to contact borrowers for recovery discussions?
audio_script: Under the RBI Code of Conduct, within what permissible timeframe are Debt Recovery Agents permitted to contact borrowers for recovery discussions?
option_a: Anytime 24 hours a day, 7 days a week
option_b: Only between 8:00 AM and 7:00 PM
option_c: Between 7:00 AM and 9:00 PM, avoiding odd hours
option_d: Only on weekends between 10:00 AM and 4:00 PM
explanation: RBI guidelines stipulate that recovery calls and visits must be restricted to reasonable hours, typically between 7:00 AM and 9:00 PM, to prevent harassment and respect privacy.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: As per the provisions of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the primary distinction regarding the pecuniary jurisdiction of a Permanent Lok Adalat compared to a regular Lok Adalat in public utility services disputes?
audio_script: As per the provisions of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the primary distinction regarding the pecuniary jurisdiction of a Permanent Lok Adalat compared to a regular Lok Adalat in public utility services disputes?
option_a: Permanent Lok Adalats have a lower pecuniary ceiling of Rs. 10 Lakhs.
option_b: Permanent Lok Adalats have jurisdiction up to Rs. 1 Crore in public utility disputes, which can be further modified by the Central Government.
option_c: Permanent Lok Adalats do not have any pecuniary limit for disputes relating to public utility services.
option_d: Permanent Lok Adalats can only handle cases up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.
explanation: Under Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, Permanent Lok Adalats have jurisdiction in respect of public utility services up to an amount of Rs. 1 Crore, which the Central Government may increase from time to time by notification.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: What is the primary asset size threshold for non-deposit-taking Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFC-ND) to be mandatorily categorized under the Middle Layer of the Scale Based Regulation (SBR) framework?
audio_script: What is the primary asset size threshold for non-deposit-taking NBFCs to be categorized under the Middle Layer of the SBR framework?
option_a: INR 500 crore and above
option_b: INR 1,000 crore and above
option_c: INR 5,000 crore and above
option_d: INR 10,000 crore and above
explanation: According to the RBI's Scale Based Regulation (SBR) guidelines, non-deposit-taking NBFCs with an asset size of INR 1,000 crore and above fall under the Middle Layer.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: What is the mandatory statutory timeline under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Security Interest and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI) and CERSAI rules for registering the creation, modification, or satisfaction of a security interest with the Central Registry?
audio_script: What is the mandatory statutory timeline under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Security Interest and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI) and CERSAI rules for registering the creation, modification, or satisfaction of a security interest with the Central Registry?
option_a: Within 15 days from the date of execution of the security agreement.
option_b: Within 30 days from the date of creation, modification, or satisfaction of the security interest, with a provision for condonation of delay by the Central Registrar.
option_c: Within 60 days from the date of issuing the demand notice under Section 13(2).
option_d: Within 90 days from the date of classification of the account as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA).
explanation: Under Chapter IV-A of the SARFAESI Act and the CERSAI rules, particulars of the creation, modification, or satisfaction of a security interest must be filed with the Central Registry within 30 days from the date of such creation, modification, or satisfaction, subject to provisions allowing the Central Registrar to condone delays.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: If an NBFC with an asset size of Rs. 80 Crores initiates recovery proceedings by issuing a notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act for a default amounting to Rs. 30 Lakhs, what is the legal validity of such action?
audio_script: If an NBFC with an asset size of Rs. 80 Crores initiates recovery proceedings by issuing a notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act for a default amounting to Rs. 30 Lakhs, what is the legal validity of such action?
option_a: Valid, because the default amount exceeds the Rs. 20 Lakhs threshold.
option_b: Invalid, because the NBFC fails to meet the mandatory minimum asset size threshold of Rs. 100 Crores, despite the default amount being above Rs. 20 Lakhs.
option_c: Valid, provided the State Government grants a special exemption.
option_d: Invalid, because NBFCs cannot use SARFAESI under any circumstances without prior RBI clearance.
explanation: To exercise powers under the SARFAESI Act, an NBFC must satisfy BOTH conditions: a minimum asset size of Rs. 100 Crore AND a minimum default claim of Rs. 20 Lakhs. Since the asset size is only Rs. 80 Crores, the action is legally invalid.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: According to the provisions of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, security interest creation in respect of property must be registered with CERSAI within how many days of the transaction?
audio_script: According to the provisions of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, security interest creation in respect of property must be registered with CERSAI within how many days of the transaction?
option_a: 15 days
option_b: 30 days
option_c: 60 days
option_d: 90 days
explanation: As per the rules under the SARFAESI Act, particulars of creation, modification, or satisfaction of security interest must be registered with CERSAI within 30 days of such transaction.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under credit card operations regulatory framework, when must a credit card account be reported as overdue or defaulted to Credit Information Companies (CICs) to prevent multi-month accumulation?
audio_script: Under credit card operations regulatory framework, when must a credit card account be reported as overdue or defaulted to Credit Information Companies (CICs) to prevent multi-month accumulation?
option_a: Within 7 days of the payment due date
option_b: Upon the completion of 30 days from the payment due date
option_c: Only after the account is classified as NPA at 90 days
option_d: Before the expiry of 30 days from the date of classification as 'stagnant' or 'overdue'
explanation: As per RBI guidelines on Credit Card and Debit Card - Issuance and Conduct Directions, banks/NBFCs shall report a credit card account as overdue to CICs only after the card has been outstanding for more than 30 days past the due date, ensuring correct timeline reporting.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: According to the IBA Model Code of Conduct for Debt Recovery Agents, when is a recovery agent permitted to visit the borrower's or guarantor's residence or workplace?
audio_script: According to the IBA Model Code of Conduct for Debt Recovery Agents, when is a recovery agent permitted to visit the borrower's or guarantor's residence or workplace?
option_a: At any time of the day or night provided the borrower is in default for more than 90 days.
option_b: Only between 07:00 AM and 07:00 PM, unless special permission is obtained from the local police.
option_c: During normal business hours, or as otherwise agreed upon through direct contact with the borrower, ensuring privacy and dignity are maintained.
option_d: Strictly between 09:00 AM and 05:00 PM on weekdays, excluding public holidays.
explanation: Under the IBA Model Code of Conduct, debt recovery agents are expected to visit the borrower's residence or workplace only during normal business hours or as mutually agreed through direct contact, ensuring that the borrower's privacy and dignity are respected at all times.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: In accordance with the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) principles and standard debt collection guidelines, a DRA contacts a borrower's employer to verify employment status. During the call, the DRA discloses the specific outstanding loan amount and the number of days the account is past due (DPD) to the HR manager to pressure the borrower. What is the regulatory status of this action under privacy guidelines?
audio_script: A DRA discloses a borrower's exact loan amount and overdue status to the employer's HR manager to pressure payment. Is this action permissible under data privacy guidelines?
option_a: Permissible, as employers have a legal right to know the financial liabilities of their employees.
option_b: Permissible, provided the borrower gave implied consent by listing the employer in the loan application.
option_c: Impermissible, because sharing specific financial profile details and DPD status with third parties like employers violates non-disclosure and data minimization principles.
option_d: Permissible only if the loan is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) for more than 90 days.
explanation: Under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) principles and RBI's fair practices code, a borrower's financial profile, exact debt amount, and repayment status are sensitive personal data. Disclosing this to employers or relatives to coerce payment constitutes a severe breach of privacy and confidentiality, as collection efforts must be directed solely at the principal borrower without causing public embarrassment.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under the provisions of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, what is the minimum asset size threshold and the minimum default claim amount required for a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) to enforce security interest without the intervention of a court or tribunal?
audio_script: Under the provisions of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, what is the minimum asset size threshold and the minimum default claim amount required for a Non-Banking Financial Company to enforce security interest without the intervention of a court or tribunal?
option_a: Asset size of Rs. 500 Crore and default claim of Rs. 50 Lakhs
option_b: Asset size of Rs. 100 Crore and default claim of Rs. 20 Lakhs
option_c: Asset size of Rs. 100 Crore and default claim of Rs. 50 Lakhs
option_d: Asset size of Rs. 500 Crore and default claim of Rs. 20 Lakhs
explanation: As per the notifications issued under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 by the Central Government, Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) with an asset size of Rs. 100 Crore and above are notified as 'financial institutions', and they are eligible to enforce security interests for a minimum default claim amount of Rs. 20 Lakhs and above.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, when an application is filed by a secured creditor before the District Magistrate (DM) or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM), the application must be supported by an affidavit sworn by the authorized officer containing a specific declaration comprising how many distinct points/parameters as mandated by the statute?
audio_script: Under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, how many points must the authorized officer's affidavit contain when applying to the DM or CMM?
option_a: 5 points
option_b: 7 points
option_c: 9 points
option_d: 11 points
explanation: As per Section 14(1) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, the application by the secured creditor to the DM/CMM must be accompanied by an affidavit duly affirmed by the authorized officer declaring 9 specific points/parameters relating to the due categorization of the account as NPA, service of demand notice, non-compliance by the borrower, aggregate dues, details of secured assets, etc., to ensure proper statutory compliance before taking physical possession.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005 (CICRA) and RBI guidelines on Credit Card operations, what is the mandatory cooling-off period or timeline within which a scheduled commercial bank must update the credit information status of a settled credit card default account to a Credit Information Company (CICI) like CIBIL, post full and final settlement?
audio_script: Under CICRA and RBI guidelines, what is the mandatory timeline for a bank to update a settled credit card default to a Credit Information Company?
option_a: Within 7 working days from the date of settlement
option_b: Within 30 days from the end of the relevant reporting fortnight
option_c: Within 15 days from the date of settlement
option_d: Within 90 days matching the NPA upgrade cycle
explanation: As per RBI Master Circular on Credit Card and Debit Card - Operations and Services, banks must submit updated credit data to Credit Information Companies at least fortnightly (every 15 days or monthly as per updated CICRA frameworks, typically mandated within 30 days of the reporting cycle closing to reflect 'settled' or 'closed' status).

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: When a borrower demonstrates genuine hardship resulting from medical emergencies or involuntary job loss, what is the primary objective of the debt restructuring framework mandated for Debt Recovery Agents and lenders under RBI directives?
audio_script: When a borrower demonstrates genuine hardship resulting from medical emergencies or involuntary job loss, what is the primary objective of the debt restructuring framework mandated for Debt Recovery Agents and lenders under RBI directives?
option_a: To initiate immediate legal proceedings under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 to protect the lender's capital.
option_b: To rehabilitate the borrower by recalibrating repayment terms, thereby avoiding immediate asset classification downgrade.
option_c: To permanently waive the principal outstanding while recovering only the cumulative interest component.
option_d: To transfer the distressed loan portfolio directly to an Asset Reconstruction Company (ARC) without review.
explanation: Debt restructuring for genuine hardship aims to rehabilitate viable borrowers experiencing temporary cash flow mismatches by modifying terms like tenure extension or interest rate reduction, preventing immediate default and NPA classification.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: With respect to digital lending apps, RBI regulations explicitly prohibit Regulated Entities and their LSPs from accessing which of the following from the borrower's mobile device?
audio_script: With respect to digital lending apps, RBI regulations explicitly prohibit Regulated Entities and their LSPs from accessing which of the following from the borrower's mobile device?
option_a: Device storage location data
option_b: Mobile data such as media files, contact lists, and call logs
option_c: Installed applications list for security audits
option_d: Network connectivity status
explanation: RBI explicitly prohibits digital lending apps from accessing mobile data like contact lists, media files, call logs, and external storage, permitting only need-based access.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: What is the statutory time frame provided under Section 25 of the PSS Act, 2007 for the drawer of the dishonoured electronic funds transfer mandate to make the payment of the demanded amount to the payee after the receipt of the written demand notice?
audio_script: What is the statutory time frame provided under Section 25 of the PSS Act, 2007 for the drawer of the dishonoured electronic funds transfer mandate to make the payment of the demanded amount to the payee after the receipt of the written demand notice?
option_a: 7 days
option_b: 14 days
option_c: 15 days
option_d: 30 days
explanation: Section 25(1)(c) of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 mandates that the drawer of the electronic funds transfer instruction fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-18-Item01] Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, what is the statutory time window within which the complainant must issue the legal demand notice after receiving the cheque return memo?
audio_script: Question 1. Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, what is the statutory time window within which the complainant must issue the legal demand notice after receiving the cheque return memo?
option_a: Within 30 days of the receipt of information from the bank regarding the dishonour
option_b: Within 15 days of the date stamped on the return memo
option_c: Within 60 days in alignment with statutory default notices
option_d: Within 7 days of dishonour to preserve summary trial rights
explanation: Section 138 proviso (b) requires the payee to give a notice in writing to the drawer within 30 days of receiving information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: In adherence to the IBA Model Code of Conduct, what specific time restriction and prior notice protocol apply when a Debt Recovery Agent intends to conduct a home visit to a defaulting borrower?
audio_script: In adherence to the IBA Model Code of Conduct, what specific time restriction and prior notice protocol apply when a Debt Recovery Agent intends to conduct a home visit to a defaulting borrower?
option_a: Visits can be made anytime between 6:00 AM and 10:00 PM without prior notice if the account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA).
option_b: Visits are restricted to normal business hours (8:00 AM to 7:00 PM), and prior notice must be given unless specific authorization for surprise checks exists under exceptional fraud cases.
option_c: Visits must strictly respect borrower privacy, generally restricted between 7:00 AM and 7:00 PM, and adequate notice must be provided, avoiding unannounced surprise visits that harass the debtor.
option_d: No prior notice is required if the recovery agent is accompanied by a bank official, provided the visit occurs before sunset.
explanation: IBA guidelines dictate that visits should be made at an appropriate time (typically between 7:00 AM and 7:00 PM) with adequate prior notice to respect the borrower's privacy and avoid harassment.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: According to the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the maximum pecuniary jurisdiction limit for filing and settling debt recovery cases before a regular Lok Adalat?
audio_script: According to the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the maximum pecuniary jurisdiction limit for filing and settling debt recovery cases before a regular Lok Adalat?
option_a: Rs. 10 Lakhs
option_b: Rs. 20 Lakhs
option_c: Rs. 50 Lakhs
option_d: No monetary ceiling exists for regular Lok Adalats
explanation: Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, regular Lok Adalats have jurisdiction over cases involving compounding of offenses and civil cases including recovery suits where the claim amount does not exceed Rs. 20 Lakhs.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: According to the RBI guidelines and the Code of Conduct for Debt Recovery Agents, what is the permissible time window during which agents are generally allowed to make telephone calls or visit a borrower's residence for recovery purposes?
audio_script: According to the RBI guidelines and the Code of Conduct for Debt Recovery Agents, what is the permissible time window during which agents are generally allowed to make telephone calls or visit a borrower's residence for recovery purposes?
option_a: 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM
option_b: 7:00 AM to 7:00 PM
option_c: 8:00 AM to 7:00 PM
option_d: 9:00 AM to 9:00 PM
explanation: As per the RBI guidelines and standard Code of Conduct for Recovery Agents, agents must respect the privacy of borrowers and are permitted to contact them only between 7:00 AM and 7:00 PM to avoid harassment and inappropriate intrusion.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) principles and RBI guidelines on recovery agents, a DRA contacts a borrower's employer to ascertain their whereabouts after failing to reach the borrower for 48 hours. The employer enquires about the exact default amount and overdue loan tenure. What is the legally compliant course of action for the agent under privacy norms?
audio_script: Under the DPDP principles and RBI guidelines, a DRA contacts a borrower's employer after failing to reach the borrower for 48 hours. The employer asks for the exact default amount and overdue loan tenure. What is the legally compliant course of action?
option_a: Disclose the exact default amount and overdue tenure since the employer has a right to know for workplace conduct.
option_b: Refuse to disclose any financial particulars or loan details, restricting the communication strictly to obtaining contact coordinates as permitted.
option_c: Disclose the overdue tenure but keep the exact default amount confidential to balance privacy and recovery.
option_d: Share the complete financial profile only if the employer provides a written undertaking of non-disclosure.
explanation: Under privacy guidelines and data minimization principles, financial profiles, default amounts, and loan specifics of a borrower cannot be disclosed to third parties including employers, relatives, or neighbors. Agents are restricted solely to verifying contact details without breaching the borrower's right to privacy.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Under the RBI prudential framework for resolution of stressed assets, which of the following correctly identifies a hallmark indicator used by banks to classify a default as a 'willful default' rather than a consequence of genuine macroeconomic hardship?
audio_script: Under the RBI prudential framework for resolution of stressed assets, which of the following correctly identifies a hallmark indicator used by banks to classify a default as a willful default rather than a consequence of genuine macroeconomic hardship?
option_a: Diverting funds from the specific sanctioned purpose for which credit was originally extended.
option_b: Experiencing a drop in monthly salary due to widespread corporate downsizing and sector-wide recession.
option_c: Failing to service the debt due to catastrophic medical hospitalization expenses of an immediate dependent.
option_d: Requesting a moratorium on loan repayments due to seasonal fluctuations in agricultural output.
explanation: Diversion of funds is a textbook criterion under RBI guidelines for declaring a borrower as a willful defaulter, distinguishing it from unavoidable genuine hardship situations like illness or job loss.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: What is the typical regulatory stipulation regarding the unsecured component of retail credit, such as personal loans and credit cards, in terms of risk weightings under RBI norms?
audio_script: What is the typical regulatory stipulation regarding the unsecured component of retail credit, such as personal loans and credit cards, in terms of risk weightings under RBI norms?
option_a: Risk weights on consumer credit are reduced to encourage retail lending.
option_b: Risk weights on consumer credit (excluding housing, education, and microfinance) are increased by 25 percentage points.
option_c: Risk weights remain unchanged at 100% for all unsecured lending.
option_d: Unsecured personal loans are exempted from capital adequacy requirements.
explanation: To check overheating in unsecured retail credit, the RBI increased the risk weights on consumer credit exposure of commercial banks and NBFCs (including personal loans and credit cards, but excluding housing, education, vehicle loans, and microfinance loans) by 25 percentage points to 125%.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: As per the guidelines governing Debt Recovery Agents, what primary documents must a recovery agent display and carry during a visit to a borrower?
audio_script: As per the guidelines governing Debt Recovery Agents, what primary documents must a recovery agent display and carry during a visit to a borrower?
option_a: Only a copy of the loan agreement and a demand promissory note.
option_b: Official photo identity card issued by the bank or agency and an authorization letter from the bank.
option_c: A certificate from the local police station and a copy of the SARFAESI notice.
option_d: A PAN card and an Aadhaar card for personal verification.
explanation: To ensure transparency and prevent harassment, recovery agents must prominently display their official photo identity card issued by the bank/agency and carry an explicit authorization letter from the bank when visiting borrowers.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: In the context of recovery proceedings, how many parties are fundamentally involved in a contract of indemnity defined under Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as opposed to a contract of guarantee?
audio_script: In the context of recovery proceedings, how many parties are fundamentally involved in a contract of indemnity defined under Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as opposed to a contract of guarantee?
option_a: One party
option_b: Two parties
option_c: Three parties
option_d: Four parties
explanation: A contract of indemnity involves only two parties (the indemnifier and the indemnified/promisee), whereas a contract of guarantee involves three parties (the principal debtor, the creditor, and the surety).

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Which of the following is considered an effective de-escalation tactic when a borrower becomes verbally abusive or extremely agitated during a recovery call?
audio_script: Which of the following is considered an effective de-escalation tactic when a borrower becomes verbally abusive or extremely agitated during a recovery call?
option_a: Matching the borrower's aggressive tone to assert dominance
option_b: Disconnecting the phone immediately without warning
option_c: Speaking in a calm, measured, and low-pitched voice to defuse tension
option_d: Threatening to notify local law enforcement for verbal abuse
explanation: De-escalation tactics require the DRA to keep their voice calm, steady, and low-pitched to help lower the emotional intensity of an agitated borrower.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under Section 101 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, what specific document is issued by the Registrar to enable direct execution and recovery of dues as arrears of land revenue without approaching a civil court?
audio_script: Under Section 101 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, what specific document is issued by the Registrar to enable direct execution and recovery of dues as arrears of land revenue without approaching a civil court?
option_a: Arbitration Award
option_b: Recovery Certificate
option_c: Liquidator Order
option_d: Attachment Warrant
explanation: Section 101 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act allows co-operative banks to obtain a Recovery Certificate directly from the Registrar upon application, which has the force of a decree and can be executed for recovery as arrears of land revenue.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Under the RBI Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets, when evaluating a borrower's default status for debt restructuring, which specific classification parameter legally distinguishes a 'willful default' from 'genuine hardship' caused by temporary cash flow mismatches?
audio_script: Under the RBI Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets, when evaluating a borrower's default status for debt restructuring, which specific classification parameter legally distinguishes a willful default from genuine hardship caused by temporary cash flow mismatches?
option_a: Intentional non-payment despite having adequate cash flows and liquid assets, versus inability to pay due to verifiable external economic shocks or job loss.
option_b: A default exceeding a continuous period of 90 days without prior written intimation to the lending institution.
option_c: The failure to execute a tripartite escrow agreement within 30 days of classification as a Special Mention Account (SMA-2).
option_d: The total aggregate credit facilities crossing the threshold limit of Rs. 50 crores without adequate collateral backing.
explanation: RBI Master Directions on Willful Defaulters define a willful default fundamentally by the presence of intent, where the borrower has the capacity to pay but deliberately withholds payment, as opposed to genuine hardship characterized by involuntary financial distress like verified job loss or sudden illness.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Why is the 'Principle of Purpose' considered a critical pillar of sound credit management by banks?
audio_script: Why is the 'Principle of Purpose' considered a critical pillar of sound credit management by banks?
option_a: It ensures that funds are utilized for productive, legal, and economically viable activities
option_b: It allows the borrower to divert funds for speculative stock market trading
option_c: It exempts the borrower from providing any collateral security
option_d: It permits banks to charge arbitrary interest rates without RBI oversight
explanation: The principle of purpose dictates that credit must be sanctioned for genuine, productive, and legitimate commercial needs, ensuring automatic repayment generation and preventing fund diversion.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-18-Item02] Under Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, what is the maximum percentage of the cheque amount that a Court can direct the drawer to pay as Interim Compensation?
audio_script: Question 2. Under Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, what is the maximum percentage of the cheque amount that a Court can direct the drawer to pay as Interim Compensation?
option_a: Not exceeding 20% of the amount of the dishonoured cheque
option_b: Not exceeding 50% of the total claim value
option_c: Not exceeding 10% subject to approval by the Sessions Court
option_d: Not exceeding 100% of the unpaid loan principal
explanation: Section 143A empowers the Court trying a Section 138 complaint to order the drawer to pay interim compensation up to a maximum of 20% of the cheque amount.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: As per RBI guidelines on Digital Lending, what is the mandatory cooling-off period during which a borrower can repay the principal and proportionate APR without any penalty, and how should interest for the days the money was held be treated?
audio_script: As per RBI guidelines on Digital Lending, what is the mandatory cooling-off period during which a borrower can repay the principal and proportionate APR without any penalty, and how should interest for the days the money was held be treated?
option_a: 3 days; interest is completely waived for the entire duration.
option_b: 7 to 14 days depending on the loan tenor; interest for the exact period the money was held is charged at the APR.
option_c: 5 days; only administrative charges are recovered.
option_d: 15 days; a flat 2% penalty is levied on the principal.
explanation: RBI digital lending guidelines mandate a cooling-off/look-up period ranging from 7 to 14 days (depending on the tenor of the loan) during which borrowers can exit the digital loan by paying the principal and proportionate APR without penalty. Interest for the exact period the funds were held must be charged proportionally.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-18-Item03] What is the statutory timeline for filing an appeal before the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) against an order of the DRT under Section 20 of the RDB Act, 1993?
audio_script: Question 3. What is the statutory timeline for filing an appeal before the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) against an order of the DRT under Section 20 of the RDB Act, 1993?
option_a: Within 30 days from the date of receipt of the DRT order, accompanied by mandatory pre-deposit
option_b: Within 60 days with no requirement of pre-deposit for individual debtors
option_c: Within 45 days upon obtaining leave from the High Court
option_d: Within 90 days following the publication of the final recovery certificate
explanation: Section 20 of the RDB Act prescribes a 30-day timeline to file an appeal before the DRAT, subject to mandatory pre-deposit of 50% (relaxable to not less than 25%).

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: [CBT-18-Item04] Under RBI guidelines on Fair Practices Code, what is the strict restriction regarding visiting or contacting borrowers at their place of employment/workplace?
audio_script: Question 4. Under RBI guidelines on Fair Practices Code, what is the strict restriction regarding visiting or contacting borrowers at their place of employment/workplace?
option_a: Agents must not visit or call borrowers at work unless specifically requested or consented to by the borrower
option_b: Agents are free to visit workplaces during normal corporate working hours without prior intimation
option_c: Agents may discuss the borrower's default with coworkers to apply peer recovery pressure
option_d: Agents can request the employer to withhold 50% of the borrower's monthly remuneration directly
explanation: RBI guidelines explicitly prohibit agents from visiting or contacting a borrower at their workplace without prior consent, and strictly prohibit disclosing debt details to colleagues.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: For an electronic funds transfer system like NACH regulated by RBI under the PSS Act, 2007, when does a presumption in favour of the holder (similar to Section 139 of the NI Act) apply regarding the receipt of the electronic fund transfer instruction for discharge of debt?
audio_script: For an electronic funds transfer system like NACH regulated by RBI under the PSS Act, 2007, when does a presumption in favour of the holder (similar to Section 139 of the NI Act) apply regarding the receipt of the electronic fund transfer instruction for discharge of debt?
option_a: It is presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the electronic fund transfer instruction was received by the holder for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability
option_b: No statutory presumption exists under the PSS Act and the burden of proof is entirely on the bank
option_c: Presumption applies only if registered with the Central Registry (CERSAI)
option_d: Presumption applies only after criminal trial concludes
explanation: Section 25(3) of the PSS Act, 2007 incorporates provisions akin to Section 139 of the NI Act, establishing a legal presumption that the electronic fund transfer instruction was issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In the context of bank lending principles, which of the following best describes the principle of 'Liquidity'?
audio_script: In the context of bank lending principles, which of the following best describes the principle of 'Liquidity'?
option_a: The ability of the borrower to convert fixed assets into cash immediately during default.
option_b: The capacity of the bank to ensure that funds lent are recoverable within a reasonable timeframe or on demand to meet depositor obligations.
option_c: The maintenance of a mandatory cash reserve ratio with the Reserve Bank of India.
option_d: The requirement that all loans must be sanctioned only against liquid securities such as gold or government bonds.
explanation: According to the principles of sound lending, liquidity ensures that the borrower's enterprise generates sufficient cash flow or the security can be easily realized so that the bank's funds do not get locked up indefinitely, enabling the bank to meet unexpected demands from depositors.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, a complaint for the dishonour of an ECS or NACH mandate can be filed up to a fine extending to how many times the amount of the electronic funds transfer instruction?
audio_script: Under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, a complaint for the dishonour of an ECS or NACH mandate can be filed up to a fine extending to how many times the amount of the electronic funds transfer instruction?
option_a: One time
option_b: Twice
option_c: Three times
option_d: Five times
explanation: Section 25 of the PSS Act stipulates that punishment can include a fine which may extend to twice the amount of the electronic funds transfer instruction, or imprisonment up to 2 years, or both.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: In the context of electronic fund transfers and NACH mandates governed under Section 25 of the PSS Act, 2007, what presumption does the court make regarding the dishonour, unless the contrary is proved?
audio_script: In the context of electronic fund transfers and NACH mandates governed under Section 25 of the PSS Act, 2007, what presumption does the court make regarding the dishonour, unless the contrary is proved?
option_a: Presumption of fraud by the collecting bank
option_b: Presumption that the electronic funds transfer instruction was issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability
option_c: Presumption of insolvency of the drawer
option_d: Presumption of technical failure by the payment gateway
explanation: Section 25(2) establishes that the Court shall presume, unless the contrary is proved, that the electronic funds transfer instruction was received by the holder for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, mirroring the statutory presumption found in Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: According to the IBA Code of Conduct, what time window is generally considered acceptable for making personal visits or telephone calls to borrowers, barring exceptional circumstances?
audio_script: According to the IBA Code of Conduct, what time window is generally considered acceptable for making personal visits or telephone calls to borrowers, barring exceptional circumstances?
option_a: 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM
option_b: 7:00 AM to 7:00 PM
option_c: 8:00 AM to 7:00 PM
option_d: 9:00 AM to 9:00 PM
explanation: The IBA guidelines specify that customer interactions, including visits and calls, should be restricted to reasonable hours, typically between 7:00 AM and 7:00 PM, to avoid undue harassment.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under the RBI guidelines on digital lending, what is the term used for agents engaged by Regulated Entities to carry out customer acquisition, underwriting support, pricing, or recovery?
audio_script: Under the RBI guidelines on digital lending, what is the term used for agents engaged by Regulated Entities to carry out customer acquisition, underwriting support, pricing, or recovery?
option_a: Lending Service Providers (LSPs)
option_b: Core Investment Companies (CICs)
option_c: Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs)
option_d: Merchant Banking Partners
explanation: Lending Service Providers (LSPs) are agents of Regulated Entities who carry out customer acquisition, pricing support, underwriting support, disbursement, servicing, monitoring, and recovery of specific loan or loan portfolio on behalf of REs.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Which legal provision under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, establishes the banker's general lien over goods and securities bailed to them?
audio_script: Which legal provision under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, establishes the banker's general lien over goods and securities bailed to them?
option_a: Section 165
option_b: Section 171
option_c: Section 172
option_d: Section 180
explanation: Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, grants bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court, and policy-brokers a general lien, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, upon any goods bailed to them as security for a general balance of account.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: A customer deposits a sealed box containing gold ornaments explicitly for 'safe custody' while traveling abroad, and simultaneously maintains a savings account with a delinquent overdraft balance of Rs. 2,005,400. Can the bank exercise a banker's lien on this sealed box under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872?
audio_script: A customer deposits a sealed box for safe custody while maintaining a delinquent overdraft balance. Can the bank exercise a banker's lien on the sealed box?
option_a: Yes, because Section 171 grants a general lien on all securities received in the course of banking business.
option_b: No, because goods deposited for safe custody constitute a special contract that excludes the operation of a general banker's lien.
option_c: Yes, provided the bank gives a 14-day statutory notice before seizing the safe custody deposit.
option_d: No, unless the customer has signed a specific hypothecation deed assigning the contents of the safe custody box to the loan account.
explanation: Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a banker's general lien does not apply to goods or valuables left with the bank for a specific purpose, such as 'safe custody', as this creates a bailment with a specific contract that overrides the general lien.

The bank wishes to exercise its banker's right of set-off to recover the personal debt from the proprietorship account. Considering the legal principle of mutuality of debts, which of the following statements is correct regarding the bank's right of set-off in this scenario?
audio_script: A sole proprietorship firm maintains a current account with a credit balance of Rs. 4,50,000. The same individual also maintains a personal savings account which is overdrawn by Rs. 1,50,000. Can the bank exercise its right of set-off? Choose the correct legal position.
option_a: The bank can exercise set-off immediately without notice because a sole proprietor and the proprietorship firm are legally the same entity, satisfying the condition of mutuality.
option_b: The bank cannot exercise set-off because debts due in different capacities (one in personal capacity and another in business capacity) lack the essential requirement of mutuality.
option_c: The bank can exercise set-off only after serving a mandatory 30-day prior written notice to the account holder under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
option_d: The bank can exercise set-off only if the proprietorship account also has a running overdraft facility.
explanation: In Indian law, a sole proprietorship is not a separate legal entity distinct from its proprietor. Therefore, debts owed by the proprietor personally and funds held in the name of the sole proprietorship satisfy the requirement of mutuality, as they belong to and are owed by the exact same natural person. The bank can exercise the right of set-off, subject to prior notice where required by contract or practice.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: [CBT-18-Item08] Under RBI Master Directions, what are the statutory eligibility thresholds for an NBFC to enforce security interests under the SARFAESI Act, 2002?
audio_script: Question 8. Under RBI Master Directions, what are the statutory eligibility thresholds for an NBFC to enforce security interests under the SARFAESI Act, 2002?
option_a: Asset size of Rs 100 Crore and above, with a minimum default claim threshold of Rs 20 Lakh
option_b: Asset size of Rs 500 Crore and above, with a minimum default claim threshold of Rs 1 Crore
option_c: Asset size of Rs 50 Crore and above, with a minimum default claim threshold of Rs 5 Lakh
option_d: Asset size of Rs 1,000 Crore with zero net Non-Performing Assets
explanation: NBFCs with an asset size of Rs 100 Crore and above are notified as financial institutions under the SARFAESI Act with a minimum debt enforcement threshold of Rs 20 Lakh.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: As per RBI digital lending regulations, borrowers must be provided a look-up period (cool-off period) during which they can exit digital loans without penalty. What is the mandatory minimum look-up period for loans with a tenor of more than 7 days?
audio_script: As per RBI digital lending regulations, borrowers must be provided a look-up period cool off period during which they can exit digital loans without penalty. What is the mandatory minimum look up period for loans with a tenor of more than 7 days?
option_a: 1 day
option_b: 3 days
option_c: 7 days
option_d: 14 days
explanation: RBI mandates that Regulated Entities shall provide a cool-off/look-up period during which the borrowers can exit the digital loan by paying the principal and proportionate APR without any penalty, which must be at least 3 days for loans having a tenor of 7 days or more.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities

option_a: Acquisition of land and heavy machinery
option_b: Day-to-day operational expenses like inventory and receivables
option_c: Construction of a new factory building
option_d: Long-term expansion into international markets
explanation: Working capital loans are short-term credit facilities extended to finance day-to-day operational requirements such as the purchase of raw materials, maintenance of inventory, and funding of trade receivables.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Under the operational guidelines for Debt Recovery Agents, which official document must be mandatorily displayed or carried and produced upon demand during a home visit?
audio_script: Under the operational guidelines for Debt Recovery Agents, which official document must be mandatorily displayed or carried and produced upon demand during a home visit?
option_a: Only a valid driving license issued by the transport authority
option_b: A copy of the borrower's loan sanction letter
option_c: An identity card issued by the bank/agency and an authorization letter
option_d: A clearance certificate from the local police station
explanation: Recovery agents are required to carry and display their identity card issued by the bank or agency along with an explicit authorization letter from the bank, which must be produced upon demand.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In retail credit card default management, revolving credit behavior often triggers the Fair Practices Code for Lenders. According to RBI guidelines on credit card dues, what is the maximum permissible period after the payment due date before an issuer can report a credit card account as overdue or past due to a Credit Information Company, and what constitutes the precise trigger for NPA classification of credit cards?
audio_script: According to RBI guidelines on credit card dues, what is the maximum permissible period before reporting past due, and what is the NPA trigger for credit cards?
option_a: Reported immediately on Day 1; NPA if minimum amount due is unpaid for 90 days continuously
option_b: Reported within 3 days; NPA if the credit card account remains 'overdue' continuously for more than 90 days as per IRAC norms
option_c: Reported after 30 days; NPA if statement balance is unpaid for 180 days
option_d: No reporting required if settled within 60 days; NPA does not apply to credit cards
explanation: As per RBI's prudential norms on IRAC and credit card operations, a credit card account is treated as NPA if the minimum amount due is not paid continuously for more than 90 days. Reporting to CIBICs follows specific timelines post the payment due date, typically recognizing a grace period before tagging as 'past due'.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-18-Item09] Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following cases can a bank NOT exercise its statutory General Lien?
audio_script: Question 9. Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following cases can a bank NOT exercise its statutory General Lien?
option_a: On gold ornaments or securities left expressly for safe custody or for an ear-marked trust purpose
option_b: On proceeds of credit bills deposited for general collection without restrictions
option_c: On surplus proceeds remaining after the sale of an earlier pledged security
option_d: On mature fixed deposits standing in the borrower's own individual name
explanation: A banker's general lien applies strictly to securities bailed in the ordinary course of business. Valuables left specifically for safe custody or dedicated trust purposes are exempt from lien.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics

option_a: Blacklisting the borrower's PAN and Aadhaar across all Credit Information Companies (CICs) instantly.
option_b: Offering an opportunity for comprehensive financial counseling and exploring viable restructuring options under RBI guidelines.
option_c: Serving a mandatory 7-day statutory notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act with doubled penal charges.
option_d: Seizing all movable personal assets of the borrower's immediate family members.
explanation: RBI code of conduct mandates that recovery agents must offer empathetic counseling and assess restructuring feasibility for genuine hardship cases before resorting to aggressive recovery measures.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: When a borrower exhibits debt denial by repeatedly avoiding calls or refusing to acknowledge genuine loan defaults, what is the recommended initial approach for a DRA under ethical recovery standards?
audio_script: When a borrower exhibits debt denial by repeatedly avoiding calls or refusing to acknowledge genuine loan defaults, what is the recommended initial approach for a DRA under ethical recovery standards?
option_a: Threatening immediate legal seizure of household assets
option_b: Maintaining calm, empathetic, and professional communication to re-establish trust
option_c: Visiting the borrower's workplace unannounced to create social pressure
option_d: Blocking the borrower's account permanently
explanation: Ethical recovery standards mandate maintaining a calm, empathetic, and professional demeanor to address debt denial constructively rather than resorting to intimidation or harassment.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-18-Item10] What legal principle governs the Right of Set-off exercisable by a lending institution against a customer's deposit accounts?
audio_script: Question 10. What legal principle governs the Right of Set-off exercisable by a lending institution against a customer's deposit accounts?
option_a: Mutuality of debts where claims are due to and from the same parties in the exact same legal capacity
option_b: A compulsory prior clearance certificate obtained from the local Debt Recovery Tribunal
option_c: An irrevocable court warrant issued by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate
option_d: The requirement that the customer must be declared an insolvent by a civil court
explanation: Set-off requires mutuality of debts—the debts must be between the same parties in the same legal right and capacity (e.g., individual credit cannot be set off against partnership dues).

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-18-Item11] When a bank branch receives a Garnishee Order Nisi issued under Order XXI Rule 46 of the Civil Procedure Code, what specific funds are attached?
audio_script: Question 11. When a bank branch receives a Garnishee Order Nisi issued under Order XXI Rule 46 of the Civil Procedure Code, what specific funds are attached?
option_a: Only the cleared credit balance due or accruing due at the exact moment the order is served on the bank
option_b: All future salary credits and remittances credited to the account over the subsequent 6 months
option_c: Uncleared cheques and bills deposited for collection that have not yet been realized
option_d: All independent accounts belonging to the customer's immediate blood relatives
explanation: A Garnishee Order Nisi attaches only the debts due or accruing due at the time of service. It does not attach future credits or uncleared cheques.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-18-Item12] Under RBI Master Directions on KYC, which among the following is categorized as an Officially Valid Document (OVD) for Proof of Identity and Address?

option_a: Job Card issued by NREGA duly signed by an authorized officer of the State Government
option_b: Ration Card issued by the Food and Civil Supplies Department
option_c: Identity Card issued by a registered private limited company
option_d: Utility electric bill not older than two calendar months
explanation: Officially Valid Documents (OVDs) under RBI KYC Directions include Passport, Driving Licence, Proof of Aadhaar, Voter ID, NREGA Job Card, and NPR Letter.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: As per the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, what is the status of a registered partnership firm's liability towards recovery of bank dues if one of the partners retires without giving public notice?
audio_script: As per the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, what is the status of a registered partnership firm's liability towards recovery of bank dues if one of the partners retires without giving public notice?
option_a: The retired partner continues to be liable as a partner to third parties for acts done before public notice is given.
option_b: The retired partner is absolved of all past and future liabilities instantly upon signing the internal retirement deed.
option_c: Only the remaining active partners are liable for pre-retirement debts.
option_d: The firm gets automatically dissolved, freezing all recovery proceedings.
explanation: Under Section 32(3) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, a retiring partner remains liable to third parties for any acts/debts until a public notice of the retirement is given.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: In the context of the Scale Based Regulation (SBR) framework, if an NBFC is classified into the 'Upper Layer' (UL) by the Reserve Bank of India based on a scoring methodology, within what timeframe must the NBFC put in place a board-approved policy and comply with enhanced regulatory requirements?
audio_script: Under the SBR framework, if an NBFC is classified into the Upper Layer by the RBI, within what timeframe must it comply with enhanced regulatory requirements?
option_a: 3 months from the date of classification
option_b: 6 months from the date of classification
option_c: 12 months from the date of classification
option_d: 24 months from the date of classification
explanation: Once an NBFC is populated in the Upper Layer (UL) based on the parametric scoring methodology, it is required to put in place a board-approved policy for implementation and comply with the enhanced regulatory requirements within 12 months from the date of such classification.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Can a creditor file a recovery suit directly against the surety without suing the principal debtor first, keeping Section 128 in view?
audio_script: Can a creditor file a recovery suit directly against the surety without suing the principal debtor first, keeping Section 128 in view?
option_a: No, the creditor must exhaust all legal remedies against the principal debtor first.
option_b: Yes, because the surety's liability is co-extensive, the creditor can sue the surety directly.
option_c: No, RBI guidelines strictly prohibit approaching the guarantor before 180 days of default.
option_d: Yes, but only if the principal debtor has filed for bankruptcy.
explanation: Because the surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor under Section 128, the surety is liable on default. The creditor is not bound to exhaust their remedies against the principal debtor before suing the surety.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: According to Section 19 of the Limitation Act 1963, what effect does a part payment of the principal debt or payment of interest have on the limitation period, provided such payment is made before the expiry of the original period?
audio_script: According to Section 19 of the Limitation Act 1963, what effect does a part payment of the principal debt or payment of interest have on the limitation period, provided such payment is made before the expiry of the original period?
option_a: It shortens the limitation period by half.
option_b: A fresh period of limitation computes from the time when the payment was made.
option_c: It has no legal effect on the limitation period.
option_d: It converts a secured loan into an unsecured loan.
explanation: Section 19 of the Limitation Act 1963 provides that where payment on account of a debt or of interest on a legacy is made before the expiration of the prescribed period by the person liable, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the payment was made.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-18-Item13] As per RBI Master Directions on KYC, what is the mandatory periodic updation (re-KYC) requirement for accounts categorized under 'High Risk'?

option_a: At least once every 2 years
option_b: At least once every 5 years
option_c: At least once every 8 years
option_d: At least once every 10 years
explanation: Periodic re-KYC must be conducted at least once every 2 years for high risk, 8 years for medium risk, and 10 years for low risk accounts.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-18-Item14] In the case of a contract entered into with a Minor for a recovery loan, what is the fundamental legal status under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Mohori Bibee precedent)?
audio_script: Question 14. In the case of a contract entered into with a Minor for a recovery loan, what is the fundamental legal status under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Mohori Bibee precedent)?
option_a: The contract is void ab initio (void from the very beginning) and unenforceable
option_b: The contract is voidable strictly at the option of the lending bank
option_c: The contract becomes legally binding as soon as the minor attains majority
option_d: The minor's natural parents are automatically liable to liquidate the debt
explanation: As established in Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, an agreement with a minor is void ab initio and no contractual liability or debt recovery suit can arise against a minor.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-18-Item15] Under the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, what is the legal position regarding daughters as coparceners in a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)?
audio_script: Question 15. Under the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, what is the legal position regarding daughters as coparceners in a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)?
option_a: A daughter is a coparcener by birth in her own right with the same rights and liabilities as a son
option_b: A daughter only acquires coparcenary status after the demise of the Karta
option_c: A daughter cannot be a coparcener and cannot be allotted ancestral partition shares
option_d: A daughter's coparcenary rights are limited strictly to self-acquired movable assets
explanation: Under the 2005 amendment to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, daughters have the exact same coparcenary rights and liabilities by birth as sons.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: When a banking institution extends credit facilities to a Private Limited Company, which legal document primarily establishes the company's borrowing powers and limits?
audio_script: When a banking institution extends credit facilities to a Private Limited Company, which legal document primarily establishes the company's borrowing powers and limits?
option_a: Certificate of Incorporation
option_b: Memorandum of Association (MoA) and Articles of Association (AoA)
option_c: Board Resolution passed in an Annual General Meeting
option_d: Director Identification Number (DIN) registry
explanation: The Memorandum of Association (MoA) defines the objects and powers of a company (including borrowing powers), while the Articles of Association (AoA) govern the internal management and procedures for exercising those powers.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Which statutory framework governs the legal validity and penal consequences of dishonour of electronic clearing service (ECS) or National Automated Clearing House (NACH) payment instructions due to insufficient funds?
audio_script: Which statutory framework governs the legal validity and penal consequences of dishonour of electronic clearing service (ECS) or National Automated Clearing House (NACH) payment instructions due to insufficient funds?
option_a: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

option_c: The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007

explanation: Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 specifically provides for the penal provisions regarding the dishonour of electronic funds transfer instructions, including ECS and NACH mandates.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

option_b: Must maintain a minimum specified investment grade rating from at least two SEBI-registered credit rating agencies
option_c: Credit rating is not mandatory for NBFC-Ds if their Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio is above 20%
option_d: Must hold an AAA rating exclusively from CRISIL or ICRA
explanation: An NBFC-D must have a minimum investment grade credit rating from at least one of the approved credit rating agencies to be eligible to accept or renew public deposits, as per the RBI Master Directions on NBFC Acceptance of Public Deposits.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: The principle of liquidity in lending requires that:
audio_script: The principle of liquidity in lending requires that:
option_a: The bank must hold 100% cash reserves for all loans disbursed
option_b: The borrower must be able to convert assets into cash quickly to meet loan repayment schedules
option_c: The loan must be disbursed exclusively in liquid cash rather than through account transfers
option_d: The borrower's factory must be located near a seaport
explanation: The principle of liquidity ensures that the borrower's enterprise generates sufficient cash flows matching the repayment schedule, allowing timely discharge of debt obligations.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-18-Item16] Under Section 26D of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, what is the statutory restriction on a secured creditor if it fails to register its security interest on the CERSAI portal?
audio_script: Question 16. Under Section 26D of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, what is the statutory restriction on a secured creditor if it fails to register its security interest on the CERSAI portal?
option_a: The secured creditor cannot exercise any enforcement rights of taking possession or sale under Chapter III of the Act
option_b: The underlying loan contract automatically gets converted into an unsecured promissory grant
option_c: The borrower is granted a 12-month statutory moratorium on all interest payments
option_d: The presiding officer of the DRT is mandated to dismiss the recovery certificate with costs
explanation: Section 26D explicitly debars secured creditors from exercising any SARFAESI enforcement powers unless the security interest is duly registered with CERSAI.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: During the cool-off or look-up period provided to a borrower for a digital loan, if the borrower decides to exit the loan, what charges is the borrower required to pay?
audio_script: During the cool-off period provided to a borrower for a digital loan, if the borrower decides to exit the loan, what charges is the borrower required to pay?
option_a: Full tenure interest and heavy prepayment penalties
option_b: Only the principal amount and proportionate APR without any penalty
option_c: Processing fees along with a 5 percent cancellation fee
option_d: No payments whatsoever, even the principal is waived
explanation: During the look-up period, borrowers shall be allowed to exit the digital loan upon payment of the principal and the proportionate APR without any penalty being charged for early repayment.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under the RBI Digital Lending Guidelines, direct disbursal of digital loans must be executed strictly through which of the following channels?
audio_script: Under the RBI Digital Lending Guidelines, direct disbursal of digital loans must be executed strictly through which of the following channels?
option_a: Through the pooled escrow account managed by the Lending Service Provider
option_b: Directly from the bank account of the Regulated Entity to the bank account of the borrower
option_c: Via a digital wallet operated by an unregulated third-party fintech partner
option_d: Through cash handling agents authorized by the digital platform
explanation: RBI Digital Lending Guidelines mandate that all loan disbursals and repayments must be executed directly between the bank accounts of the Regulated Entity (RE) and the borrower without any pass-through or pooling account of the Lending Service Provider (LSP) or any third party.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: What is the statutory time limit mandated for registering security interest transactions with CERSAI from the date of creation of such security interest?

option_a: 15 days
