module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: According to the IBA Model Code for Debt Recovery Agents, when a DRA approaches a borrower for collection, which of the following combination of documents must the agent mandatorily carry and exhibit unasked to the borrower?
audio_script: According to the IBA Model Code for Debt Recovery Agents, when a DRA approaches a borrower for collection, which of the following combination of documents must the agent mandatorily carry and exhibit unasked to the borrower?
option_a: Only the Agency Identity Card issued by the collection agency and a copy of the loan agreement.
option_b: The Identity Card issued by the bank or a certified copy of the authorization letter from the bank, along with identity proof of the DRA.
option_c: A verbal authorization from the bank branch manager and an official visiting card.
option_d: Only the PAN card and the certification certificate issued by IIBF.
explanation: As per the IBA Model Code of Conduct, DRAs must carry their identity card (issued by the bank or the agency) and specifically an authorization letter from the bank, displaying the same to the customer unasked to establish their genuine locus standi.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Which of the following describes the appropriate handling of call recordings containing borrower interactions under RBI's stringent data privacy norms for recovery operations?
audio_script: Which of the following describes the appropriate handling of call recordings containing borrower interactions under RBI's stringent data privacy norms for recovery operations?
option_a: Recordings must be deleted immediately after the call ends to save storage
option_b: Recordings must be archived securely and restricted from unauthorized access for at least 6 months
option_c: Recordings can be shared publicly on social media to deter other defaulters
option_d: Recordings must be handed over physically to the borrower every week
explanation: Data privacy norms dictate that all borrower communications recorded by collection agencies must be stored securely, encrypted where necessary, restricted from unauthorized access, and retained for the mandatory 6-month period.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-21-Item06] Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following cases can a bank NOT exercise its statutory General Lien?
audio_script: Question 6. Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following cases can a bank NOT exercise its statutory General Lien?
option_a: On gold ornaments or securities left expressly for safe custody or for an ear-marked trust purpose
option_b: On proceeds of credit bills deposited for general collection without restrictions
option_c: On surplus proceeds remaining after the sale of an earlier pledged security
option_d: On mature fixed deposits standing in the borrower's own individual name
explanation: A banker's general lien applies strictly to securities bailed in the ordinary course of business. Valuables left specifically for safe custody or dedicated trust purposes are exempt from lien.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: According to Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, within what timeframe must the payee or the holder in due course make a demand for payment in writing after receiving information about the dishonour of the electronic funds transfer?
audio_script: According to Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, within what timeframe must the payee or the holder in due course make a demand for payment in writing after receiving information about the dishonour of the electronic funds transfer?
option_a: Within 15 days
option_b: Within 30 days
option_c: Within 60 days
option_d: Within 90 days
explanation: Under Section 25(1)(b) of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, the payee or the holder in due course of the electronic funds transfer must make a demand for the payment of the said amount by giving a notice in writing to the drawer within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the electronic funds transfer as unpaid.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under the RBI regulatory framework for digital lending, Regulated Entities must ensure that a cool-off or look-up period is provided to borrowers during which they can exit the digital loan without any penalty. What is the standard mandate regarding access to mobile phone data?
audio_script: Under the RBI regulatory framework for digital lending, Regulated Entities must ensure that a cool-off or look-up period is provided to borrowers during which they can exit the digital loan without any penalty. What is the standard mandate regarding access to mobile phone data?
option_a: Lending apps are allowed to access mobile phone media with prior user consent.
option_b: Lending apps are strictly prohibited from accessing mobile phone data like media, contact lists, and files.
option_c: Lending apps can access call logs for credit scoring purposes only.
option_d: Lending apps may access device storage only after loan default occurs.
explanation: RBI digital lending guidelines mandate that Regulated Entities must ensure that digital lending apps do not access mobile phone resources such as file and media, contact lists, call logs, etc., ensuring strict customer privacy.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-21-Item07] What legal principle governs the Right of Set-off exercisable by a lending institution against a customer's deposit accounts?
audio_script: Question 7. What legal principle governs the Right of Set-off exercisable by a lending institution against a customer's deposit accounts?
option_a: Mutuality of debts where claims are due to and from the same parties in the exact same legal capacity
option_b: A compulsory prior clearance certificate obtained from the local Debt Recovery Tribunal
option_c: An irrevocable court warrant issued by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate
option_d: The requirement that the customer must be declared an insolvent by a civil court
explanation: Set-off requires mutuality of debts—the debts must be between the same parties in the same legal right and capacity (e.g., individual credit cannot be set off against partnership dues).

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) governed by Mitakshara law, the Karta executes a mortgage of ancestral property to secure a business loan without the consent of minor coparceners and without demonstrating 'legal necessity' (Aghama). Subsequently, a total partition of the HUF takes place under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005. As a Debt Recovery Agent examining the asset's enforceability, what is the legal status of the mortgage and the extent of the coparceners' liability post-partition?
audio_script: In a Hindu Undivided Family governed by Mitakshara law, the Karta mortgages ancestral property without legal necessity or minor consent. A total partition then occurs. What is the status of the mortgage and coparceners' liability?
option_a: The mortgage is entirely void ab initio, and coparceners bear zero personal or ancestral liability post-partition.
option_b: The mortgage binds only the Karta's undivided share at the time of alienation; post-partition, the coparceners receive their shares free of encumbrance unless the bank proves legal necessity or benefit of the estate.
option_c: The mortgage automatically converts into a joint personal debt of all adult coparceners under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act.
option_d: The partition invalidates the bank's right to SARFAESI action, restricting recovery exclusively to unsecured personal assets of the Karta.
explanation: Under Mitakshara law, a Karta's alienation of ancestral property without legal necessity or consent of coparceners is not void ab initio, but is voidable to the extent of the coparceners' shares. Post-partition, the alienee (bank) can only proceed against the share allotted to the Karta in the partition, unless the bank successfully discharges the burden of proof establishing that the loan was taken for legal necessity (Aghama) or benefit of the estate.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under the SBR framework, how does the RBI determine which NBFCs fall into the Upper Layer (NBFC-UL) for enhanced regulatory and supervisory requirements?
audio_script: Under the SBR framework, how does RBI determine which NBFCs fall into the Upper Layer for enhanced regulatory requirements?
option_a: Through a quantitative scoring methodology based on parameters like size, leverage, interconnectedness, and complexity.
option_b: Based solely on the voluntary application submitted by the Board of Directors of the respective NBFC.
option_c: Through a public bidding process conducted annually.
option_d: By selecting the top 10 oldest NBFCs operating in India.
explanation: The Upper Layer (NBFC-UL) is populated based on a comprehensive scoring methodology evaluated by the RBI using specific parameters such as asset size, leverage, interconnectedness, complexity, and current market footprint.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: An NBFC-Investment and Credit Company (NBFC-ICC) categorized under the 'Base Layer' (NBFC-BL) pursuant to RBI Scale Based Regulations has failed to raise its net owned funds (NOF) to the threshold requirement of Rs. 10 crore by the ultimate transition timeline prescribed by the RBI. What is the immediate regulatory consequence regarding its operations?
audio_script: An NBFC Investment and Credit Company categorized under the Base Layer pursuant to RBI Scale Based Regulations has failed to raise its net owned funds to the threshold requirement of Rs 10 crore by the ultimate transition timeline prescribed by the RBI. What is the immediate regulatory consequence regarding its operations?
option_a: It is automatically upgraded to the Middle Layer without penal action
option_b: Its Certificate of Registration (CoR) is liable to be cancelled by the RBI for failing to meet the minimum NOF statutory requirement
option_c: It is permitted a further 3-year grace period upon paying a compounding penalty
option_d: It can continue operations indefinitely provided its leverage ratio does not exceed 2x
explanation: Under the RBI SBR guidelines, the baseline NOF for NBFC-BL was progressively raised to Rs. 10 crore. Failure to achieve the mandated NOF within the stipulated glide path timeline results in the RBI cancelling the Certificate of Registration (CoR) under the provisions of the RBI Act, 1934.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the maximum pecuniary jurisdiction threshold specified for Permanent Lok Adalats in respect of public utility services before the amendment, and how does it contrast with regular Lok Adalats?
audio_script: Under Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the maximum pecuniary jurisdiction threshold specified for Permanent Lok Adalats in respect of public utility services before the amendment, and how does it contrast with regular Lok Adalats?
option_a: Up to Rs 10 Lakhs, whereas regular Lok Adalats have no monetary limit
option_b: Up to Rs 1 Crore, whereas regular Lok Adalats deal with disputes irrespective of any upper limit
option_c: Up to Rs 50 Lakhs, whereas regular Lok Adalats are restricted to cases below Rs 10 Lakhs
option_d: Up to Rs 5 Crores, whereas regular Lok Adalats can only handle pre-litigation matters
explanation: Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 states that Permanent Lok Adalats have jurisdiction in respect of public utility services for disputes involving a value up to Rs 1 Crore (which was later amended to remove or enhance the limit via notifications/amendments up to Rs 5 Crores in certain contexts), whereas regular Lok Adalats can take up cases regardless of the quantum involved provided both parties consent.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: During a field visit for a delinquent account with an outstanding balance of Rs. 4,50,000, the borrower offers to pay Rs. 2,00,000 in cash as full and final settlement, claiming he has verbal consent from the bank manager. As per the strict IIBF Code of Conduct and DRA guidelines regarding cash collection and OTS (One Time Settlement) protocols, what is the mandatory course of action for the Debt Recovery Agent?
audio_script: During a field visit for a delinquent account with an outstanding balance of Rs. 4,50,000, the borrower offers to pay Rs. 2,00,000 in cash as full and final settlement, claiming he has verbal consent from the bank manager. As per the strict IIBF Code of Conduct and DRA guidelines regarding cash collection and OTS protocols, what is the mandatory course of action for the Debt Recovery Agent?
option_a: Accept the cash, issue a handwritten temporary receipt, and deposit the amount in the bank within 24 hours.
option_b: Refuse cash collection entirely, decline the OTS proposal as verbal consent is invalid, and direct the borrower to deposit funds directly into the loan account or obtain a formal written OTS approval letter along with an official instant digital receipt.
option_c: Accept the cash provided the borrower signs an indemnity bond and gives a written confession of the settlement terms.
option_d: Keep the cash in safe custody and obtain post-facto written approval from the branch manager within 7 business days.
explanation: DRA guidelines strictly prohibit cash collection without issuing an official instant machine-generated/digital receipt from the bank. Furthermore, an OTS (One-Time Settlement) cannot be executed based on verbal assurances and requires explicit, formal written approval from the competent authority/bank branch. DRAs are not authorized to negotiate or finalize OTS terms or accept cash settlements on the spot.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: During debt denial management, a borrower repeatedly insists that their credit card dues are waived due to a supposed government scheme that does not exist. How should an ethically compliant DRA handle this misinformation under standard regulatory training protocols?
audio_script: During debt denial management, a borrower repeatedly insists that their credit card dues are waived due to a supposed government scheme that does not exist. How should an ethically compliant DRA handle this misinformation under standard regulatory training protocols?
option_a: Agree with the borrower to avoid conflict and close the file falsely.
option_b: Gently correct the misconception by referring to the legally binding terms of the Cardmember Agreement and provide factual clarity without being confrontational.
option_c: Threaten immediate police action for attempting fraud.
option_d: Ignore the borrower's claim and threaten to seize their property the same day.
explanation: An ethical DRA must address misinformation with factual transparency, referencing loan agreements and official guidelines while maintaining politeness, ensuring the borrower understands their contractual liability without resorting to intimidation.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: If a drawer makes payment of the cheque amount within the stipulated 15-day period following the receipt of the statutory notice under Section 138, what is the legal consequence regarding penal action?
audio_script: If a drawer pays the cheque amount within the 15-day notice window under Section 138, what is the legal consequence?
option_a: The drawer is still liable for criminal prosecution and a fine.
option_b: The drawer commits no offense, and no criminal complaint can be filed against them under Section 138.
option_c: The bank is penalized for issuing a wrongful return memo.
option_d: The debt is written off automatically by the financial institution.
explanation: Under proviso (c) to Section 138, the offense is complete only if the drawer fails to make the payment within 15 days of receiving the notice. If payment is made within this 15-day window, no offense is committed, and no criminal action can be pursued under this section.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: According to Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, an electronic fund transfer instruction (such as NACH/ECS) is treated as dishonoured when it is returned unpaid by the bank due to which primary reason?
audio_script: According to Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, an electronic fund transfer instruction such as NACH or ECS is treated as dishonoured when it is returned unpaid by the bank due to which primary reason?
option_a: Mismatch in account holder's signature
option_b: Insufficient funds in the drawer's account
option_c: Account being frozen by a court order
option_d: Closure of the bank branch
explanation: Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act explicitly applies when an electronic funds transfer instruction is returned unpaid primarily because the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the instruction.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: When a co-operative bank initiates recovery proceedings via a Registrar's award or Section 101 certificate, what is the primary advantage over filing a regular suit in a Civil Court?
audio_script: What is the primary advantage of a Section 101 certificate over a regular civil suit for a co-op bank?
option_a: It bypasses the lengthy trial process of civil courts and permits direct execution of recovery.
option_b: It automatically waives the principal amount, recovering only the interest.
option_c: It shifts the liability of the loan to the State Government treasury.
option_d: It prevents the borrower from filing any appeal or legal challenge.
explanation: The primary objective of provisions like Section 101 is to provide a summary procedure for speedy recovery of dues without the protracted delays associated with ordinary civil court litigation.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: In the context of transparent Annual Percentage Rate (APR) calculation for digital loans mandated by the RBI, which of the following components must compulsorily be included in the APR computation, and who bears the cost of execution of recovery mechanisms?
audio_script: In the context of transparent Annual Percentage Rate calculation for digital loans mandated by the RBI, which of the following components must compulsorily be included in the APR computation, and who bears the cost of execution of recovery mechanisms?
option_a: Only principal and nominal interest rate; Borrower bears all hidden costs.
option_b: All-inclusive cost of digital loans including interest, processing fees, insurance charges, and any other charges levied upfront, while the cost cannot be recovered from the borrower if not explicitly stated in the KFS.
option_c: Interest rate plus penal charges levied on default; Lender bears all processing costs.
option_d: APR excludes third-party fees like insurance if paid directly to the service provider.
explanation: RBI mandates that APR must capture all-inclusive cost of digital loans, including interest and all other charges such as processing fees, insurance, etc. All fees and charges must be explicitly stated in the KFS upfront, and any charge not mentioned cannot be levied on the borrower.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: According to Section 21 of the RDB Act, 1993, what is the mandatory pre-deposit requirement for the Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) to entertain an appeal filed by a person from whom debt is due to the bank?
audio_script: According to Section 21 of the RDB Act, 1993, what is the mandatory pre-deposit requirement for the DRAT to entertain an appeal filed by a person from whom debt is due to the bank?
option_a: 25% of the debt amount due under the order
option_b: 30% of the debt amount due under the order
option_c: 50% of the debt amount due under the order, which can be reduced to 25% by the appellate tribunal for reasons to be recorded
option_d: 75% of the debt amount due under the order
explanation: Section 21 mandates a deposit of 50% of the amount of debt due as determined by the DRT before the DRAT can entertain an appeal. However, the DRAT has the discretion to reduce it to not less than 25% for recorded reasons.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: What does CERSAI stand for in the context of the regulatory framework governing asset reconstruction and security interest in India?
audio_script: What does CERSAI stand for in the context of the regulatory framework governing asset reconstruction and security interest in India?
option_a: Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India
option_b: Credit Evaluation and Recovery Statistics Authority of India
option_c: Central Enforcement and Recovery Security Asset Institution
option_d: Credit Exchange and Registry for Security Assets of India
explanation: CERSAI stands for Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India, established under Section 20 of the SARFAESI Act.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: According to RBI guidelines on Fair Practices Code for Lenders and Debt Recovery Agents, for how many minimum months must banks and their recovery agents preserve the call recordings of conversations made to borrowers for recovery purposes?
audio_script: According to RBI guidelines on Fair Practices Code for Lenders and Debt Recovery Agents, for how many minimum months must banks and their recovery agents preserve the call recordings of conversations made to borrowers for recovery purposes?
option_a: 1 month
option_b: 3 months
option_c: 6 months
option_d: 12 months
explanation: RBI directives mandate that banks and their engaged recovery agents must preserve call recordings of conversations with borrowers for a minimum period of 6 months to address any grievances or complaints regarding coercive recovery practices.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: In the context of digital lending operations involving an LSP and an RE, if a default occurs in a portfolio covered under an FLDG arrangement, within how many days must the RE invoke the guarantee, and who holds the ultimate responsibility for continuous credit underwriting and monitoring?
audio_script: In the context of digital lending operations involving an LSP and an RE, if a default occurs in a portfolio covered under an FLDG arrangement, within how many days must the RE invoke the guarantee, and who holds the ultimate responsibility for continuous credit underwriting and monitoring?
option_a: Within 30 days of default; the responsibility lies solely with the LSP's automated credit algorithms
option_b: Within 60 days of default; the responsibility is shared equally between the RE and LSP
option_c: Within 120 days of default; the Regulated Entity (RE) retains the ultimate responsibility for continuous credit underwriting and monitoring
option_d: Within 90 days of default; the Regulated Entity (RE) retains the ultimate responsibility for continuous credit underwriting and monitoring
explanation: RBI digital lending guidelines mandate that invocation of the FLDG must be made by the RE within a maximum of 90 days of default of any loan in the portfolio. Despite outsourcing tech or sourcing to LSPs, the RE cannot abdicate its responsibility for continuous credit underwriting, risk assessment, and monitoring of the loan portfolio.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Can a secured creditor take possession of a secured asset under Section 13(4) if the borrower has submitted a representation under Section 13(3A), but before the secured creditor has replied to that representation?
audio_script: Can a secured creditor take possession of a secured asset under Section 13(4) if the borrower has submitted a representation under Section 13(3A), but before the secured creditor has replied to that representation?
option_a: Yes, because the 60 days have lapsed.
option_b: No, the secured creditor must first respond to the representation within 15 days before proceeding under Section 13(4).
option_c: Yes, representation under Section 13(3A) does not suspend enforcement actions.
option_d: No, submission of representation permanently bars SARFAESI action.
explanation: Section 13(3A) mandates that the secured creditor must consider the representation and communicate the reasons for non-acceptance within 15 days before taking any measures under Section 13(4).

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities

audio_script: What is the legal nature of security created over movable assets like a vehicle financed through a retail vehicle loan?
option_a: Pledge
option_b: Hypothecation
option_c: Mortgage
option_d: Assignment
explanation: Under Section 2(n) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, a charge created on movable property existing or future, where possession remains with the debtor, is termed as 'Hypothecation'.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: In accordance with RBI regulations distinguishing between NBFCs categorized as deposit-taking (NBFC-D) and non-deposit-taking (NBFC-ND), what is the mandatory minimum Net Owned Fund (NOF) requirement prescribed for a new company to commence and carry on the business of non-banking financial institution accepting public deposits?
audio_script: In accordance with RBI regulations distinguishing between deposit-taking and non-deposit-taking NBFCs, what is the mandatory minimum Net Owned Fund requirement prescribed for a new company to commence and carry on the business of non-banking financial institution accepting public deposits?
option_a: Rs. 2 करोड़
option_b: Rs. 10 करोड़
option_c: Rs. 20 करोड़
option_d: Rs. 100 करोड़
explanation: As per RBI Master Directions, the minimum Net Owned Fund (NOF) required for specialized categories and new NBFC-D (Deposit taking) is generally scaled up, and specifically for CICs and standard registrations, the baseline for NBFC-D is established at Rs. 20 crore to ensure higher solvency and depositor protection.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Regarding the operational duties of a Debt Recovery Agent (DRA), can a certified DRA delegate recovery visits or negotiation tasks to an uncertified sub-agent or family member?
audio_script: Regarding the operational duties of a Debt Recovery Agent, can a certified DRA delegate recovery visits or negotiation tasks to an uncertified sub-agent or family member?
option_a: Yes, delegation is permitted if the sub-agent is supervised indirectly over the phone.
option_b: Yes, family members can assist in field visits provided they carry an authorization letter from the DRA.
option_c: No, the principle of non-delegation applies strictly; recovery duties and client interactions must be executed personally by the certified DRA.
option_d: No restrictions exist on delegation as long as the primary DRA takes ultimate legal responsibility for the recovery outcome.
explanation: Under the Code of Conduct for DRAs, certification is personal and non-transferable. The rule of non-delegation applies strictly, meaning that only the certified DRA is authorized to conduct recovery visits, contact borrowers, and handle negotiations. Outsourcing or delegating these duties to uncertified persons violates regulatory compliance.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: An NBFC-Digital Lender disburses a personal loan through a Lending Service Provider (LSP). As per the standardized Key Fact Statement (KFS) mandate, which of the following components must compulsorily be factored into the calculation and explicit disclosure of the Annual Percentage Rate (APR)?
audio_script: An NBFC Digital Lender disburses a personal loan through a Lending Service Provider. As per the standardized Key Fact Statement mandate, which of the following components must compulsorily be factored into the calculation and explicit disclosure of the Annual Percentage Rate?
option_a: Only the principal interest rate charged by the lender on reducing balance method.
option_b: All-inclusive cost of digital loans including interest rate, mandatory upfront/back-end LSP fees, and non-refundable insurance charges recovered upfront.
option_c: Interest rate plus penal charges levied strictly for past delayed installments.
option_d: Interest rate and GST component on loan processing fees, excluding partner platform charges.
explanation: The RBI mandates that the Annual Percentage Rate (APR) must capture the total cost of the digital loan, which includes all-inclusive cost components such as interest rate, processing fees, insurance charges, and any other fees mandatorily recovered upfront or bundled through the LSP, expressed on an annual basis.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Which specific statutory enactment governs the legal consequences and criminal liabilities arising from the dishonour of cheques due to insufficiency of funds in the drawer's bank account?
audio_script: Which specific statutory enactment governs the legal consequences and criminal liabilities arising from the dishonour of cheques due to insufficiency of funds in the drawer's bank account?
option_a: The Indian Contract Act, 1872
option_b: The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
option_c: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
option_d: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
explanation: Section 138, which deals with the dishonour of cheques for insufficiency of funds, is a statutory provision incorporated under Chapter XVII of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: What is the time frame within which the District Magistrate or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate is expected to dispose of an application filed by a secured creditor under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, as per statutory amendments?
audio_script: What is the time frame within which the District Magistrate or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate is expected to dispose of an application filed by a secured creditor under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, as per statutory amendments?
option_a: 30 days, extendable up to an aggregate of 60 days
option_b: 15 days strictly
option_c: 90 days with no extensions
option_d: 6 months
explanation: Under Section 14, the DM/CMM shall pass an order within 30 days from the date of application, which can be extended for further periods up to an aggregate of 60 days for reasons recorded in writing.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: During location verification of a borrower by a Debt Recovery Agent, which of the following practices is considered a violation of the RBI Fair Practices Code?
audio_script: During location verification of a borrower by a Debt Recovery Agent, which of the following practices is considered a violation of the RBI Fair Practices Code?
option_a: Visiting the borrower's declared residential or business address during permissible daytime hours.
option_b: Disclosing the details of the borrower's loan default to neighbors or employers during the verification visit.
option_c: Carrying an official identity card issued by the hiring bank or authorized agency.
option_d: Verifying the address details provided in the loan application form.
explanation: RBI guidelines strictly prohibit DRAs from violating borrower privacy. Disclosing loan default details to third parties, including neighbors, relatives, or employers during location verification, constitutes severe harassment and a breach of the Code of Conduct.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In personal unsecured loans, what is the primary legal recourse available to a bank when a borrower defaults, given that no tangible collateral is held?
audio_script: In personal unsecured loans, what is the primary legal recourse available to a bank when a borrower defaults, given that no tangible collateral is held?
option_a: Invoke the SARFAESI Act to seize personal assets
option_b: File a civil suit for recovery under the Code of Civil Procedure or approach the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT)
option_c: Directly auction the borrower's residential property without court intervention
option_d: Seize the borrower's salary through the police
explanation: Since unsecured personal loans do not have collateral to invoke SARFAESI, banks must file a summary or regular civil suit, or approach the DRT (if the debt threshold is met under the RDDBFI Act) for a recovery certificate and subsequent execution.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In the context of the Rule in Clayton's Case governing running current accounts, how are the debits and credits chronologically appropriated when determining the liability of a deceased or retiring partner's estate?
audio_script: In the context of the Rule in Clayton's Case governing running current accounts, how are the debits and credits chronologically appropriated when determining the liability of a deceased or retiring partner's estate?
option_a: Latest credits are appropriated against the latest debits
option_b: First item of credit is applied to extinguish the first item of debt
option_c: All debits are aggregated and paid proportionately from all subsequent deposits
option_d: Credits are always appropriated towards disputed liabilities first
explanation: The Rule in Clayton's Case establishes the 'first-in, first-out' (FIFO) principle for running current accounts, meaning that the earliest credit entry is applied to extinguish the earliest debit entry on the account.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Why is recording details in the daily register crucial for recovery agencies under regulatory frameworks?
audio_script: Why is recording details in the daily register crucial for recovery agencies under regulatory frameworks?
option_a: To calculate employee monthly salaries only
option_b: To maintain an auditable trail of customer interactions and prevent harassment complaints
option_c: To share borrower data publicly
option_d: To increase advertising revenue
explanation: Maintaining a daily register provides an official audit trail, ensuring that all recovery actions adhere to ethical guidelines and protecting against allegations of harassment.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act applies when a cheque is dishonoured by the bank primarily due to which of the following reasons?
audio_script: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act applies when a cheque is dishonoured by the bank primarily due to which of the following reasons?
option_a: The cheque is torn or mutilated
option_b: Insufficient funds in the account or exceeding the arrangement
option_c: Difference in the signature of the account holder
option_d: The drawer has expired
explanation: Section 138 specifically penalizes the dishonour of a cheque for insufficiency of funds in the account, or because it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement with that bank.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

explanation: Call recordings must be preserved for at least 6 months primarily to serve as verifiable audit trails for investigating complaints, resolving disputes, and ensuring accountability during recovery interactions.

OVDs include the passport, driving licence, proof of possession of Aadhaar number, voter's ID card, job card issued by NREGA, and letter issued by the National Population Register.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under the Scale Based Regulation (SBR) framework introduced by the RBI for Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), which specific layer encompasses NBFC-Peer to Peer Lending Platforms (NBFC-P2P), NBFC-Account Aggregators (NBFC-AA), Non-Operative Financial Holding Companies (NOFHC), and NBFCs up to an asset size of INR 1000 crore, irrespective of whether they hold public funds or not?
audio_script: Under the Scale Based Regulation framework introduced by the RBI for Non-Banking Financial Companies, which specific layer encompasses NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, NOFHC, and NBFCs up to an asset size of INR 1000 crore?
option_a: Top Layer
option_b: Upper Layer
option_c: Base Layer
option_d: Middle Layer
explanation: Under the RBI's Scale Based Regulation (SBR) framework, the Base Layer (BL) comprises NBFCs-P2P, NBFCs-AA, Non-Operative Financial Holding Companies (NOFHC), and NBFCs with asset size below INR 1000 crore, specifically focusing on systemic risk containment and regulatory proportionality.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In the context of securities under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which specific section governs a Registered Mortgage (also known as a Simple Mortgage), and what is the mandatory requirement for its execution and perfection compared to an Equitable Mortgage?
audio_script: In the context of securities under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which specific section governs a Registered Mortgage, also known as a Simple Mortgage, and what is the mandatory requirement for its execution and perfection compared to an Equitable Mortgage?
option_a: Governed by Section 58(b); requires registration under the Indian Registration Act, 1908, irrespective of the principal amount secured.
option_b: Governed by Section 58(f); requires physical delivery of title deeds in notified towns only.
option_c: Governed by Section 58(a); does not require compulsory registration if the value is below one hundred rupees.
option_d: Governed by Section 58(c); requires a conditional sale agreement registered within 30 days.
explanation: A Simple Mortgage (Registered Mortgage) is defined under Section 58(b) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Under Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, any mortgage deed that creates an interest in immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards must be compulsorily registered, making registration mandatory for perfection.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

explanation: The Upper Layer of NBFCs is populated based on a scale and scoring methodology (taking into account size, interconnectedness, complexity, etc.) evaluated by the RBI. The Top Layer remains practically empty and is populated only if the RBI assesses extreme systemic risk from specific Upper Layer entities.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-22-Item01] When a bank branch receives a Garnishee Order Nisi issued under Order XXI Rule 46 of the Civil Procedure Code, what specific funds are attached?

option_d: All independent accounts belonging to the customer's immediate blood relatives
explanation: A Garnishee Order Nisi attaches only the debts due or accruing due at the time of service. It does not attach future credits or uncleared cheques.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

option_c: Due to mutilation of the physical instrument

explanation: Section 138 specifically applies when the cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) principles and RBI guidelines on recovery agents, a DRA contacts the guarantor regarding a borrower's defaulted retail loan. During the call, the guarantor asks for the exact outstanding principal, interest breakup, and the borrower's recent salary slip submitted to the bank. What is the legally compliant course of action for the DRA?
audio_script: Under the DPDP principles and RBI guidelines on recovery agents, a DRA contacts the guarantor regarding a borrower's defaulted retail loan. During the call, the guarantor asks for the exact outstanding principal, interest breakup, and the borrower's recent salary slip submitted to the bank. What is the legally compliant course of action for the DRA?
option_a: Disclose the total outstanding principal and interest breakup as the guarantor is jointly liable, but withhold the salary slip.
option_b: Disclose all requested financial details since the guarantor has a legal stake in the debt repayment.
option_c: Refuse to disclose any specific financial profile details or salary documents of the borrower to the guarantor without explicit written consent from the borrower, as it violates data privacy.
option_d: Share the salary slip and loan breakup with the guarantor only if the guarantor threatens legal action against the bank.
explanation: Under DPDP principles and banking confidentiality norms, a borrower's financial profile, including salary slips and detailed account breakdowns, cannot be disclosed to third parties—including guarantors—without explicit, verifiable consent from the principal borrower, even though the guarantor has legal liability for the guaranteed amount.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: A Debt Recovery Agent (DRA) acting on behalf of XYZ Bank visits a borrower's workplace to collect an overdue installment without prior written notice and discusses the debt with the borrower's immediate supervisor. According to the RBI Fair Practices Code for Lenders regarding debt collection and prohibition of visiting unnotified workplaces, what specific regulatory violation has occurred?
audio_script: A DRA visits a borrower's workplace without prior notice and discusses the debt with their supervisor. What RBI Fair Practices Code violation has occurred?
option_a: Violation of the mandatory 48-hour prior written intimation rule and breach of borrower privacy at the workplace
option_b: Violation of the absolute prohibition on visiting a borrower's workplace under any circumstances
option_c: Violation of the RBI guideline mandating that workplace visits can only occur after 30 days of continuous default
option_d: No violation has occurred if the debt is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA)
explanation: Under the RBI Fair Practices Code and Guidelines on Recovery Agents, lenders and their agents are prohibited from visiting a borrower's workplace unnotified. Visits must respect privacy, and discussing debt with third parties like employers/supervisors is strictly prohibited, while workplace visits generally require prior intimation/consent and are restricted to prevent harassment.

option_a: Individual written notice served directly to the Reserve Bank of India

explanation: Section 45 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, mandates that public notice of dissolution must be given to absolve partners from liability for subsequent acts, except in the case of a deceased or insolvent partner or a dormant partner who was not known to be a partner.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: In a debt recovery dispute referred to the Lok Adalat under Section 20 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, a settlement is reached and an award is passed under Section 21. The borrower later intends to challenge this award on merits through an appeal before the High Court. What is the legal position regarding the appealability of this Lok Adalat award under Section 21?
audio_script: In a debt recovery dispute referred to the Lok Adalat under Section 20 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, a settlement is reached and an award is passed under Section 21. The borrower later intends to challenge this award on merits through an appeal before the High Court. What is the legal position regarding the appealability of this Lok Adalat award under Section 21?
option_a: The award can be appealed within 30 days before the High Court with leave of the court.
option_b: The award is deemed to be a decree of a civil court and is final, hence no appeal lies against it to any court.
option_c: The award can be appealed only on questions of substantive law within 90 days.
option_d: The award is non-binding and can be reopened by filing a fresh suit in the Debt Recovery Tribunal.
explanation: Under Section 21(2) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, every award made by a Lok Adalat shall be final and binding on all the parties to the dispute, and no appeal shall lie to any court against the award. It is deemed to be a decree of a civil court.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

explanation: Section 25 lists modes such as attachment/sale of property, arrest/detention, and appointment of a receiver. Direct criminal prosecution and sentencing to rigorous imprisonment for fraud is handled by courts under criminal law, not directly as a recovery mode under Section 25.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) debt recovery scenario, the Karta mortgages joint family property for a business loan without establishing 'legal necessity' (Aghama/Vyavahara). Subsequently, a total partition of the HUF takes place under Hindu law. As a Debt Recovery Agent (DRA), how does this partition impact the liability of the minor coparceners, and who bears the ultimate burden of proving legal necessity when the bank enforces the mortgage?
audio_script: In an HUF debt recovery scenario, the Karta mortgages property without legal necessity, followed by a total partition. How does this partition impact minor coparceners, and who bears the burden of proving legal necessity?
option_a: Minors are personally liable to the extent of their share received upon partition; the burden of proving legal necessity lies entirely on the minor coparceners to invalidate the mortgage.
option_b: Minors are not personally liable, and their divided shares remain immune from the debt; the burden of proving legal necessity lies strictly on the creditor bank seeking to enforce the mortgage against joint family assets.
option_c: Minors have unlimited personal liability post-partition; the burden of proving the absence of legal necessity rests on the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) appointed receiver.
option_d: Minors' liability is restricted to pre-partition profits only, and the burden of proof shifts to the Karta to disprove personal liability.
explanation: Under Hindu law, upon a partition, minor coparceners do not incur personal liability for debts contracted by the Karta, and their respective shares allotted on partition are not liable for ancestral debts unless incurred for 'legal necessity' or 'benefit of the estate'. When a creditor bank seeks to enforce a mortgage created by the Karta over joint family property, the burden of proof lies squarely on the bank (creditor) to establish that the loan and subsequent mortgage were executed for a valid legal necessity binding on all coparceners, including minors.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In a registered partnership firm operating a manufacturing unit, Partner 'A' executes a promissory note in the firm's name for a standard business loan, but explicitly outside the usual course of the firm's trading business, and without express authority from other partners. Under Section 19 and 20 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, what is the extent of the firm's liability to the lending bank?
audio_script: In a registered partnership firm operating a manufacturing unit, Partner A executes a promissory note in the firm's name for a standard business loan, but explicitly outside the usual course of the firm's trading business, and without express authority from other partners. Under Section 19 and 20 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, what is the extent of the firm's liability to the lending bank?
option_a: The firm is strictly liable as implied authority covers all financial instruments executed by any partner.
option_b: The firm is not liable unless the bank proves that the partner had express usage authority or ratified the act.
option_c: The firm is jointly and severally liable only if the loan amount does not exceed twenty-five percent of the firm's capital.
option_d: The firm's liability is limited to the personal assets of Partner 'A' only, excluding the firm's assets.
explanation: Under Section 19(1) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the act of a partner which is done to carry on, in the usual way, business of the kind carried on by the firm binds the firm (implied authority). However, Section 20 allows partners to contractually restrict implied authority. Furthermore, if an act is outside the usual course of business, the firm is not bound unless the third party (bank) has knowledge of express authority or ratifies it.

question_text: In the recovery of unsecured personal loans, if a borrower makes a part-payment or signs a written acknowledgment of debt after the expiry of the original limitation period of 3 years under the Limitation Act, 1963, what is the legal consequence regarding the limitation period?
audio_script: In the recovery of unsecured personal loans, if a borrower makes a part-payment or signs a written acknowledgment of debt after the expiry of the original limitation period of 3 years under the Limitation Act, 1963, what is the legal consequence regarding the limitation period?
option_a: A fresh limitation period of 3 years starts from the date of such acknowledgment or part-payment under Section 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act, provided it is done before the expiry of the original period.
option_b: Part-payment or acknowledgment after the expiry of the original 3-year limitation period cannot revive the debt, and the debt becomes completely unenforceable as a time-barred debt.
option_c: Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act allows a time-barred debt to be revived through a signed written promise to pay, creating a fresh enforceable contract.
option_d: Both A and C are legally applicable depending on whether it is a part-payment (Sec 19) or a written promise (Sec 25(3)).
explanation: Under Section 18 (Acknowledgment) and Section 19 (Part-payment), the action must occur *before* the expiration of the prescribed limitation period to extend it. However, under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, a debtor can sign a written promise to pay a time-barred debt in whole or in part, which constitutes a valid contract capable of reviving the time-barred debt.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under the Master Directions on Frauds - Classification and Reporting by commercial banks, within how many days of a retail personal loan account turning into a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) due to suspected fraudulent diversion of funds must the Joint Lenders' Forum (JLF) or bank classify the account as 'Fraud'?

explanation: RBI Master Directions on Frauds stipulate the framework primarily for large credit portfolios (usually borrower accounts of INR 5 crore and above for fraud classification timelines, while general NPA guidelines apply to retail). Specifically, the strict time-bound forensic audit and fraud tagging mandates (like the 60-day rule) are targeted at large consortiums/multiple banking accounts rather than standalone retail personal loans.

audio_script: As per RBI Master Circular on Credit Card Operations, from which exact point in time must credit card issuers calculate the overdue status of a credit card account to ensure uniform NPA classification across all lending institutions?
option_a: From the date when the minimum amount due is unpaid for 30 consecutive days

If it remains unpaid beyond the due date, it is classified as overdue immediately on the day following the due date.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: When does the standard 3-year limitation period under the Limitation Act, 1963, typically begin to tick for a demand promissory note payable on demand?

explanation: For a promissory note payable on demand, Article 34 of the Limitation Act, 1963, stipulates that the 3-year limitation period begins to run from the date of the promissory note itself (i.e., its execution date).

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: How do Permanent Lok Adalats established under Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 differ from regular Lok Adalats regarding dispute resolution when a settlement fails between parties?
audio_script: How do Permanent Lok Adalats established under Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 differ from regular Lok Adalats regarding dispute resolution when a settlement fails between parties?
option_a: Permanent Lok Adalats dissolve the case and direct parties to Civil Courts.
option_b: Permanent Lok Adalats have the power to decide the dispute on merits if conciliation fails.
option_c: Permanent Lok Adalats can only handle criminal compounding matters.
option_d: Permanent Lok Adalats require mandatory consent from both parties for rendering an award after conciliation failure.
explanation: Unlike regular Lok Adalats which can only pass awards based on a settlement between parties (and return the case to court if no settlement is reached), Permanent Lok Adalats under Section 22C(8) have the statutory authority to adjudicate and decide the dispute on merits if the conciliation proceedings fail, provided the dispute does not relate to an offense not compoundable.

option_d: Documenting the borrower's financial constraints accurately and submitting a factual report to the bank.
explanation: RBI Fair Practices Code strictly prohibits DRAs from resorting to intimidation, harassment, public humiliation, or undue pressure, especially when dealing with vulnerable borrowers facing genuine hardships.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: How does 'Clayton's Rule' (Devaynes v. Noble) apply to a running cash credit or overdraft account of a defaulting borrower when determining the limitation period and the recovery of historical debts?
audio_script: How does Clayton's Rule apply to a running cash credit or overdraft account of a defaulting borrower when determining the limitation period and the recovery of historical debts?
option_a: Credits paid into a running account are legally appropriated to pay off the newest debts incurred first, leaving the oldest debts intact.
option_b: First-in, first-out rule applies, implying that the earliest debit item in the account is offset by the earliest credit item paid into the account.
option_c: All payments made by the customer are exclusively appropriated towards statutory interest charges, leaving the principal debt entirely outside the scope of appropriation.
option_d: The rule mandates that the bank must freeze the account immediately upon the first default, making Clayton's rule inapplicable to banking transactions.
explanation: Clayton's Rule establishes the 'first-in, first-out' principle for running accounts. In the absence of specific appropriation by the customer or bank, the first credit entry pays off the first debit entry. This becomes critical in determining which parts of a debt are time-barred under the Limitation Act.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: If a debtor makes a part-payment towards the principal amount of a term loan via a cheque, and the cheque is honored after the original 3-year limitation period has expired, does Section 19 save the limitation?
audio_script: If a debtor makes a part-payment towards the principal amount of a term loan via a cheque, and the cheque is honored after the original 3-year limitation period has expired, does Section 19 save the limitation?
option_a: Yes, because cheque clearance relates back to the date of presentation
option_b: No, the payment or acknowledgment must be made before the expiration of the prescribed limitation period
option_c: Yes, provided the bank manager approves an extension
option_d: No, because part-payment is only valid for mortgages under Section 19
explanation: Under both Section 18 and Section 19 of the Limitation Act 1963, the acknowledgment or part-payment *must* be made before the expiration of the prescribed limitation period. Once time-barred, a subsequent payment does not revive limitation unless supported by a fresh contract under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act.

option_c: NBFC-Peer to Peer (P2P) Lending Platforms
option_d: NBFCs designated as Layer-4 and Top Layer entities based on a scoring methodology
explanation: Under the SBR framework, the Top Layer (the highest tier) is ideally empty and populated only when the RBI is of the opinion that there is a substantial increase in systemic risk from specific NBFCs in the Upper Layer, which are identified using a quantitative scoring methodology.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: A borrower defaults on a term loan on January 1, 2021. On December 15, 2023, the borrower signs a balance confirmation letter acknowledging the debt. Up to what date is the limitation period extended under Section 18 of the Limitation Act 1963?
audio_script: A borrower defaults on a term loan on January 1, 2021. On December 15, 2023, the borrower signs a balance confirmation letter acknowledging the debt. Up to what date is the limitation period extended under Section 18 of the Limitation Act 1963?
option_a: January 1, 2024
option_b: December 15, 2026
option_c: December 15, 2033
option_d: January 1, 2033
explanation: Since the acknowledgment was made on December 15, 2023 (within the original 3-year limitation expiring on January 1, 2024), a fresh limitation period of 3 years starts from the date of signing, extending the limitation up to December 15, 2026.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Can a corporate body be prosecuted if an electronic fund transfer instruction issued on its behalf is dishonoured under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007?
audio_script: Can a corporate body be prosecuted if an electronic fund transfer instruction issued on its behalf is dishonoured under Section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007?
option_a: No, only individual account holders can be prosecuted.
option_b: Yes, companies and persons in charge of the company's business can be held liable.
option_c: Only the bank can be penalized.
option_d: Corporate bodies are completely immune from criminal liability under this Act.
explanation: Under the provisions incorporated into the PSS Act (mirroring Section 141 of the NI Act), offences by companies hold both the company and the responsible persons in charge liable for the dishonour.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: In the context of Permanent Lok Adalats established under Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the maximum pecuniary value of the dispute regarding public utility services that the Permanent Lok Adalat can take cognizance of, prior to the 2015 amendment removing the cap?
audio_script: In the context of Permanent Lok Adalats established under Section 22B of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the maximum pecuniary value of the dispute regarding public utility services that the Permanent Lok Adalat can take cognizance of?
option_a: Up to Rs. 10 Lakhs
option_b: Up to Rs. 20 Lakhs
option_c: Up to Rs. 1 Crore
option_d: Jurisdiction is unlimited up to any amount as per the amended statute
explanation: Initially, Permanent Lok Adalats had a monetary ceiling of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 22C(1). However, via the Legal Services Authorities (Amendment) Act, 2002/subsequent updates, the central government enhanced/removed the limit, and currently, Permanent Lok Adalats for public utility services can adjudicate disputes up to any pecuniary limit specified by the Central Government, effectively removing the rigid cap.

option_d: Minor savings accounts operated by parents

The employer demands details of the outstanding loan amount and default history to evaluate the employee's financial reliability. What is the legally compliant course of action for the DRA?
audio_script: Under DPDP principles and RBI recovery guidelines, a DRA contacts a borrower's employer who demands loan default details. What should the DRA do?
option_a: Disclose the total outstanding amount and default period since the employer has a legitimate interest in the employee's financial conduct.
option_b: Refuse to disclose any financial profile details, as sharing borrower data with employers without explicit consent violates non-disclosure and privacy norms.
option_c: Disclose only the principal outstanding amount while withholding the specific default duration or legal notices issued.
option_d: Share the details strictly on the condition that the employer provides a written undertaking of confidentiality.
explanation: According to Data Privacy guidelines and Digital Personal Data Protection principles, a borrower's financial profile, loan status, and default history constitute sensitive personal data. Sharing such details with third parties, including employers or relatives, without explicit, informed consent from the borrower constitutes a severe breach of confidentiality and the RBI Code of Conduct for Recovery Agents.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: A secured creditor issues a demand notice under Section 13(2) and takes symbolic possession under Section 13(4). Subsequently, the authorized officer publishes an auction notice on November 10 for an e-auction scheduled on December 5. On November 15, the borrower deposits the entire dues, including all costs, charges, and expenses incurred by the secured creditor. What is the legal validity of the borrower's redemption under Section 13(8) post the 2016 amendment?
audio_script: A borrower tenders all dues after the auction notice is published. Is the redemption valid under Section 13-8?
option_a: Valid, because the borrower cleared the entire dues prior to the actual date of the e-auction.
option_b: Invalid, because under Section 13(8) as amended in 2016, the right of redemption is terminated upon the publication of the auction notice.
option_c: Valid, provided the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) grants special permission upon an application filed under Section 17.
option_d: Invalid, unless 50 percent of the outstanding penal interest is additionally paid by the borrower.
explanation: Post the 2016 amendment to Section 13(8) of the SARFAESI Act, the borrower's right to redeem the secured asset ceases strictly once the auction notice or notice for inviting tenders is published. Since the borrower tendered the amount on November 15, which is after the publication date of November 10, the redemption is legally invalid without the explicit consent of the secured creditor.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy (RDB) Act, 1993, an appeal against an order passed by the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) must be filed before the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) within how many days, and what is the standard pre-deposit percentage required to entertain the appeal?
audio_script: According to the RDB Act, what is the timeline to file an appeal before the DRAT against a DRT order, and what is the standard pre-deposit requirement?

option_b: Within 30 days, with a pre-deposit of 50% of the debt amount determined by the DRT

option_d: Within 15 days, with a pre-deposit of 10% of the debt amount determined by the DRT
explanation: As per Section 20 of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy (RDB) Act, 1993, an appeal to the DRAT must be filed within 30 days from the date of receipt of the DRT's order. Additionally, under Section 21, the appellant is required to deposit 50% of the debt determined by the DRT (which DRAT may reduce to a minimum of 25% for reasons to be recorded in writing) for the appeal to be entertained.

explanation: As per Section 13(3A) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, on receipt of the notice under Section 13(2), the borrower may make a representation or raise objections within 60 days of the notice. Note that the borrower has 60 days to respond to the 13(2) notice overall, but specifically, the timeline to reply to representations under 13(3A) is 15 days from receipt of the representation.

audio_script: At what stage can an offense under Section 138 be compounded after conviction, and what are the applicable cost guidelines?

explanation: As per the landmark Supreme Court ruling in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H., offenses under Section 138 are compoundable even at the appellate stage. However, to discourage delayed settlements, if compounding is sought at the appellate or revision stage, a graded cost of 15% of the cheque amount is generally levied as costs to be deposited with the Legal Services Authority.

question_text: In the context of the banker's right of set-off, which of the following scenarios legally prohibits a bank from exercising this right without prior notice or specific authorization?
audio_script: In the context of the banker's right of set-off, which of the following scenarios legally prohibits a bank from exercising this right without prior notice or specific authorization?
option_a: A single savings bank account held by an individual who has defaulted on their personal term loan with the same branch.
option_b: A joint account where the debt is owed by all account holders jointly, and the credit balance is also held in the exact same joint names and capacities.
option_c: A credit balance in a partner's personal account being set off against a debt owed by the partnership firm.
option_d: A matured fixed deposit receipt held solely by the borrower, where the deposit was pledged as collateral security.
explanation: The right of set-off requires 'mutuality', meaning the debts must be due in the same right and capacity. A partner's personal account and a partnership firm's account are held in different capacities, hence a bank cannot set off a partner's personal credit balance against a firm's debt (or vice versa) without specific, valid authorization.

audio_script: According to RBI guidelines on prudential norms and asset classification, how is a genuine hardship resulting in temporary cash flow mismatch distinguished from a willful default during borrower counseling?
option_a: Willful default involves intentional non-payment despite capacity to pay and diversion of funds, whereas genuine hardship stems from involuntary job loss or unforeseen medical emergencies.
option_b: Genuine hardship is declared when the loan amount exceeds INR 50 lakhs, while willful default applies to any retail loan below this threshold.
option_c: Willful default is legally established only if the borrower fails to respond to notices under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act within 30 days.
option_d: Genuine hardship applies exclusively to agricultural loans under Priority Sector Lending norms, while willful default applies only to corporate borrowers.
explanation: RBI Master Circulars define a willful default as intentional non-payment, fund diversion, or siphoning despite adequate repayment capacity. In contrast, borrower counseling for genuine hardship identifies involuntary factors such as sudden medical crises, business failure without fraud, or job loss, which qualify the borrower for restructuring rather than penal action.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, what are the statutory timelines regarding the issuance of the demand notice by the payee and the payment period allowed for the drawer after receiving the notice?
audio_script: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, what are the statutory timelines for issuing a demand notice and the subsequent payment period allowed to the drawer? Let's look at the correct timelines. The payee must issue a demand notice in writing within 30 days of receiving the bank's return memo. Following this, the drawer is given 15 days from the receipt of the notice to clear the dues. Therefore, the correct option is B.
option_a: The payee must issue the notice within 15 days of receiving the return memo, and the drawer is allowed 30 days to make the payment.
option_b: The payee must issue the notice within 30 days of receiving the return memo, and the drawer is allowed 15 days from the receipt of notice to make the payment.
option_c: The payee must issue the notice within 30 days of receiving the return memo, and the drawer is allowed 30 days from the receipt of notice to make the payment.
option_d: The payee must issue the notice within 45 days of receiving the return memo, and the drawer is allowed 15 days from the receipt of notice to make the payment.
explanation: As per Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the payee or holder in due course must make a demand for the payment of the amount by giving a notice in writing to the drawer within 30 days of receiving information (return memo) from the bank regarding the dishonor of the cheque. The drawer is then given 15 days from the receipt of the notice to make the payment. If the drawer fails to make the payment within this 15-day period, the cause of action arises.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Under the RBI Guidelines and IBA Code of Conduct, under what conditions is a Debt Recovery Agent (DRA) permitted to contact a borrower's family members or workplace?
audio_script: Listen to the following question on recovery ethics. Under the RBI Guidelines and IBA Code of Conduct, when is a Debt Recovery Agent permitted to contact a borrower's family members or workplace? Review the options carefully. Option A: When the borrower fails to respond to three consecutive calls. Option B: Only with prior consent, or if untraceable, solely to get contact details without disclosing debt information. Option C: To verify employment or secure a reference guarantee. Option D: With written authorization from the recovery agency's manager.
option_a: Whenever the borrower fails to respond to more than three consecutive phone calls on their personal mobile number.
option_b: Only with the prior consent of the borrower, or if the borrower is untraceable, strictly for obtaining location/contact details without disclosing any information regarding the debt.
option_c: At any time during business hours to verify the borrower's employment status or to request family members to clear the outstanding dues.
option_d: If authorized by a written internal order from the recovery agency's branch manager, irrespective of the borrower's consent.
explanation: Under the RBI guidelines and the IBA Code of Conduct, recovery agents must respect the privacy of borrowers. Contacting workplace colleagues or family members is strictly prohibited unless prior consent is obtained, or the borrower is genuinely untraceable. Even when untraceable, the contact must be strictly limited to obtaining the borrower's location or updated phone number, without revealing any details about the debt or loan default.

These are Passport, Driving Licence, Aadhaar, Voter ID, NREGA Job Card, and NPR Letter. The PAN Card is not listed as an OVD under these directions because it does not contain the holder's address.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under the legal framework governing Hindu Undivided Families (HUF) in India, when the Karta avails a bank loan for a family business or legal necessity, what is the extent of liability of the Karta and the other coparceners?
audio_script: In a Hindu Undivided Family, when the Karta takes a loan for family necessity or business, the liability of the Karta is unlimited, meaning his personal properties can be attached. On the other hand, the liability of other coparceners is limited only to their share in the HUF property, unless they have personally signed the loan documents as co-borrowers or guarantors.
option_a: The liability of both the Karta and all coparceners is unlimited and extends to their personal individual assets.
option_b: The liability of the Karta is unlimited (extending to his personal assets), while the liability of the other coparceners is limited only to their share in the HUF property.
option_c: The liability of the Karta is limited to his share in the HUF property, while the other coparceners have unlimited personal liability.
option_d: The bank cannot recover the debt from the HUF property; recovery can only be made from the Karta's personal salary or income.
explanation: Under Hindu Law, the Karta has the implied authority to contract debts for family business or legal necessity. In such cases, the Karta's liability is personal and unlimited. However, the liability of the other coparceners is limited only to their undivided share in the joint family property, unless they have specifically made themselves personally liable by executing the loan documents.

audio_script: A DRA contacts a corporate borrower's employer to ascertain the borrower's current salary and whereabouts after default exceeding 90 days. question_text: A surety guarantees the repayment of a cash credit facility extended by a bank to the principal debtor. Thus, the surety is discharged.

explanation: According to Clayton's Rule, in a running current account, the first item on the credit side is applied to extinguish the first item on the debit side in chronological order ('first in, first out').

question_text: If a debt becomes time-barred under the Limitation Act, 1963 (i.e., the 3-year limitation period expires without any acknowledgment or payment), what is the legal status of the debt?

option_c: The bank can still file a civil suit as a matter of right.
option_d: The borrower faces immediate criminal imprisonment.
explanation: The Limitation Act bars the remedy (filing a suit in a court of law) after the prescribed period expires, but it does not extinguish the underlying debt or moral obligation, which is why banks can still appropriate certain rights or accept voluntary payments.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under Hindu Law, when a Karta of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) avails a business loan for the legal necessity of the family and defaults, what is the extent of liability of the Karta and the other coparceners?
audio_script: Welcome, candidates. Let us understand the liability structure in an HUF. When a Karta takes a loan for family necessity or business, his liability is unlimited, meaning his personal assets can also be attached. However, the liability of other coparceners is strictly limited only to their share in the HUF property. Thus, the correct option is B.
option_a: The Karta and all adult coparceners are personally liable to the full extent of their personal assets.
option_b: The Karta has unlimited personal liability, whereas the liability of other coparceners is strictly limited only to their share in the HUF property.
option_c: Only the Karta is liable to the extent of his share in the HUF property, and other coparceners have no liability whatsoever.
option_d: The liability of both the Karta and the coparceners is limited to their respective shares in the HUF property, and no personal assets can be attached.
explanation: In a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF), the Karta has the implied authority to manage family business and contract debts for legal necessity. In the event of default, the Karta is personally liable (unlimited liability), while the liability of other coparceners is limited to their share in the joint family property, unless they have signed the loan agreement in their individual capacity.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: A registered partnership firm engaged in debt recovery operations has two active partners, X and Y. Partner X retires from the firm on January 10, 2023. However, neither X nor the remaining partners give a public notice of X's retirement in the Official Gazette and in at least one vernacular newspaper. On March 15, 2023, Partner Y executes a high-risk promissory note in the name of the firm with a commercial bank, borrowing funds for a speculative venture. When the bank initiates recovery proceedings against the firm, X contends he is not liable as he retired prior to the execution of the instrument. Applying Section 32 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, what is the legal position of Partner X regarding this debt?
audio_script: A partner retires without giving public notice. Are they liable for subsequent firm debts?
option_a: X is completely absolved of liability because his actual retirement predated the execution of the promissory note.
option_b: X remains liable to the bank for the debt because he failed to issue a public notice of his retirement as mandated by Section 32, making third parties deal with the firm on the assumption he was still a partner.
option_c: X is liable only if the bank can prove that X personally benefited from the loan proceeds.
option_d: X's liability is restricted strictly to trade creditors existing on the exact date of his retirement, excluding banking credit facilities.
explanation: Under Section 32(3) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, a retiring partner continues to be liable to third parties for any acts done by any of the partners after his retirement until public notice of his retirement is given. Since X failed to issue the statutory public notice, he remains liable to the bank for transactions entered into post-retirement.
