question_text: Under the RBI Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets, when evaluating a borrower's application for debt restructuring due to financial distress, a Debt Recovery Agent must understand the classification criteria. Which of the following specifically characterizes a 'willful default' as per RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters, as opposed to genuine hardship?
audio_script: Under the RBI Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets, when evaluating a borrower's application for debt restructuring due to financial distress, a Debt Recovery Agent must understand the classification criteria. Which of the following specifically characterizes a 'willful default' as per RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters, as opposed to genuine hardship?
option_a: The borrower has defaulted on loan repayments due to unexpected job loss and acute medical emergencies.
option_b: The borrower has the capacity to pay but has deliberately withheld payment, or has diverted funds for purposes other than for which the finance was availed.
option_c: The borrower's business enterprise suffered structural losses due to an industry-wide recession beyond their control.
option_d: The borrower filed for formal insolvency under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code due to operational insolvency.
explanation: According to the RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters, a willful default occurs broadly when a unit has defaulted despite having the capacity to pay, or has diverted/siphoned off funds, or disposed of movable/immovable assets given for secure interest without bank approval. Job loss, medical emergencies, and industry recessions constitute genuine hardship rather than willful default.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: When a Debt Recovery Agent encounters a borrower who demonstrates a clear 'willful default' status under RBI Master Circular guidelines, what is the appropriate regulatory approach?

explanation: Willful defaulters have the capacity to repay but intentionally withhold payments; therefore, banks and recovery agents must deploy standard enforcement and legal recovery mechanisms rather than hardship counseling.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: A borrower defaults on a secured loan facility availed from an eligible NBFC. The outstanding principal, interest, and other dues total Rs. 25 Lakhs. The NBFC's total balance sheet asset size is Rs. 150 Crore. Can the NBFC invoke the provisions of Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002?
audio_script: A borrower defaults on a secured loan facility availed from an eligible NBFC. The outstanding principal, interest, and other dues total Rs. 25 Lakhs. The NBFC's total balance sheet asset size is Rs. 150 Crore. Can the NBFC invoke the provisions of Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002?
option_a: No, because the default amount must be at least Rs. 50 Lakhs regardless of asset size.
option_b: No, because the asset size of the NBFC must be a minimum of Rs. 500 Crore.
option_c: Yes, because the NBFC meets the minimum asset size threshold of Rs. 100 Crore and the minimum default claim threshold of Rs. 20 Lakhs.
option_d: Yes, but only after obtaining prior written approval from the High Court having jurisdiction.
explanation: An NBFC is eligible to act as a 'secured creditor' under the SARFAESI Act if its asset size is Rs. 100 Crore or more and the minimum default claim is Rs. 20 Lakhs or more. Since this NBFC has an asset size of Rs. 150 Crore (> Rs. 100 Crore) and a default claim of Rs. 25 Lakhs (> Rs. 20 Lakhs), it is legally eligible to issue a demand notice under Section 13(2).

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: When a secured creditor intends to take possession of secured assets under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, and encounters resistance or requires assistance, under which section can they approach the District Magistrate (DM) or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) for taking physical possession?
audio_script: When a secured creditor intends to take possession of secured assets under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, and encounters resistance or requires assistance, under which section can they approach the District Magistrate (DM) or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) for taking physical possession?

option_b: Section 15

explanation: Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 empowers the secured creditor to apply to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or District Magistrate within whose jurisdiction the asset is situated to obtain possession of the asset.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: If a borrower submits a representation under Section 13(3A) objecting to the Section 13(2) notice, and the secured creditor rejects the representation, can the secured creditor immediately proceed with taking possession under Section 13(4)?
audio_script: If a borrower submits a representation under Section 13(3A) objecting to the Section 13(2) notice, and the secured creditor rejects the representation, can the secured creditor immediately proceed with taking possession under Section 13(4)?
option_a: Yes, immediately after communicating the rejection
option_b: No, the creditor must wait for an additional 30 days after communicating the rejection before taking action under Section 13(4)
option_c: No, they must file a suit in the Civil Court first
option_d: Yes, but only after obtaining prior written permission from the RBI
explanation: Once the secured creditor considers the representation and communicates the reasons for non-acceptance to the borrower, they can proceed to take measures under Section 13(4). However, Section 13(3A) explicitly clarifies that the communication of reasons does not confer any right on the borrower to approach the DRT under Section 17 until Section 13(4) measures are actually taken.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

question_text: A borrower availed a term loan and defaulted. After 2 years and 10 months from the date of default, the borrower signs a balance confirmation letter acknowledging the debt. audio_script: A borrower availed a term loan and defaulted. After 2 years and 10 months from the date of default, the borrower signs a balance confirmation letter acknowledging the debt. explanation: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act 1963, when an acknowledgement of liability has been signed in writing before the expiration of the prescribed period for a suit, a fresh period of limitation computes from the time when the acknowledgement was signed. For a money claim, this fresh period is 3 years.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: In the context of debt recovery and Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, if a principal borrower's debt becomes time-barred under the Limitation Act, what is the legal impact on the liability of the surety?
audio_script: In the context of debt recovery and Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, if a principal borrower's debt becomes time-barred under the Limitation Act, what is the legal impact on the liability of the surety?
option_a: The surety's liability remains enforceable indefinitely regardless of the principal debt status
option_b: The surety's liability is generally extinguished because the surety's liability is co-extensive and cannot exceed that of the principal debtor
option_c: The surety becomes the principal debtor automatically for a further period of three years
option_d: The creditor can recover the debt from the surety only through an arbitration tribunal
explanation: Since the surety's liability under Section 128 is co-extensive with the principal debtor, if the principal debt is time-barred and cannot be recovered legally, the surety's liability is also extinguished, as the surety cannot be held liable for a debt that is no longer legally recoverable from the principal debtor.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Under Clayton's Rule (established in the famous case Devaynes v. Noble), how are withdrawals and deposits appropriated in a running current account when a debt is continuous?
audio_script: Under Clayton's Rule, established in Devaynes versus Noble, how are withdrawals and deposits appropriated in a running current account when a debt is continuous?
option_a: The latest deposit is appropriated against the latest withdrawal.
option_b: The earliest withdrawal is extinguished or paid off by the earliest subsequent deposit.
option_c: All deposits are distributed proportionally across all outstanding debits.
option_d: Withdrawals and deposits are segregated, preventing any mutual set-off.
explanation: Clayton's Rule dictates the appropriation of payments in a running current account, establishing the presumption that the first item on the debit side of the account is the item paid off or reduced by the first item on the credit side ('first in, first out').

question_text: Under the Scale Based Regulation (SBR) framework introduced by the Reserve Bank of India for NBFCs, which layer specifically includes all deposit-taking NBFCs (NBFC-D) regardless of their asset size, along with non-deposit-taking NBFCs with an asset size of Rs. 1,000 crore and above?

option_a: Mutilation of the physical cheque leaf
option_b: Difference in signatures or words
option_c: Insufficiency of funds in the account or exceeding arrangement
option_d: Death or insolvency of the account holder
explanation: Section 138 specifically applies when a cheque is drawn for the discharge of any debt or other liability and is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: [CBT-27-Item16] Under the IIBF Code of Ethics for Recovery Agents, what must an agent explicitly display to a borrower before commencing any debt recovery communication?
audio_script: Question 16. Under the IIBF Code of Ethics for Recovery Agents, what must an agent explicitly display to a borrower before commencing any debt recovery communication?
option_a: Identity Card issued by the agency/bank and an authentic copy of the Bank's Authorisation Letter
option_b: A certified criminal complaint receipt issued by the jurisdictional Magistrate
option_c: A non-bailable attachment warrant copy approved by the District Police Head
option_d: A complete loan statement showing other defaulting borrowers in the district
explanation: An agent must display an authentic Identity Card and the bank's written Authorisation Letter before initiating any recovery dialogue.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: [CBT-27-Item17] Under RBI's Master Directions on Digital Lending, what is the mandatory requirement regarding the Key Fact Statement (KFS)?
audio_script: Question 17. Under RBI's Master Directions on Digital Lending, what is the mandatory requirement regarding the Key Fact Statement (KFS)?
option_a: A standardized KFS containing the Annual Percentage Rate (APR) and recovery mechanisms must be provided prior to agreement execution
option_b: KFS is optional for short-term micro loans below Rs 20,000
option_c: KFS can be dispatched within 30 days after first loan disbursement
option_d: KFS is only mandatory for corporate entity borrowers with turnover exceeding Rs 100 Crore
explanation: Under RBI Digital Lending Directions, a standardized KFS with full disclosure of APR and cooling-off terms must be provided to the borrower prior to agreement execution.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: [CBT-27-Item18] Under RBI Directions on Default Loss Guarantee (DLG / FLDG) in Digital Lending, what is the maximum permissible portfolio cap on such guarantee arrangements?
audio_script: Question 18. Under RBI Directions on Default Loss Guarantee (DLG / FLDG) in Digital Lending, what is the maximum permissible portfolio cap on such guarantee arrangements?
option_a: 5% of the total outstanding loan portfolio backing the arrangement
option_b: 15% of the aggregate disbursed principal value
option_c: 25% subject to approval by the Regulated Entity's Board of Directors
option_d: 50% for all secured priority sector advances
explanation: RBI Directions on Default Loss Guarantee in Digital Lending stipulate that total DLG cover on any outstanding loan portfolio shall not exceed 5%.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: [CBT-27-Item19] Under RBI Master Directions, what are the statutory eligibility thresholds for an NBFC to enforce security interests under the SARFAESI Act, 2002?
audio_script: Question 19. Under RBI Master Directions, what are the statutory eligibility thresholds for an NBFC to enforce security interests under the SARFAESI Act, 2002?
option_a: Asset size of Rs 100 Crore and above, with a minimum default claim threshold of Rs 20 Lakh
option_b: Asset size of Rs 500 Crore and above, with a minimum default claim threshold of Rs 1 Crore
option_c: Asset size of Rs 50 Crore and above, with a minimum default claim threshold of Rs 5 Lakh
option_d: Asset size of Rs 1,000 Crore with zero net Non-Performing Assets
explanation: NBFCs with an asset size of Rs 100 Crore and above are notified as financial institutions under the SARFAESI Act with a minimum debt enforcement threshold of Rs 20 Lakh.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: What is the statutory timeline mandated under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016 for the completion of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) from the date of admission of the application, including any permissible extensions?
audio_script: What is the statutory timeline mandated under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 for the completion of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process from the date of admission of the application, including any permissible extensions?
option_a: 180 days only
option_b: 270 days maximum including extensions
option_c: 330 days maximum including any extension and litigation time
option_d: 365 days maximum
explanation: As per Section 12 of the IBC 2016, the CIRP shall be mandatorily completed within a period of 180 days from the date of admission of the application, extendable by the Adjudicating Authority up to a maximum of 90 days. However, the total time-limit for CIRP including extensions and time taken in legal proceedings must not exceed 330 days.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: In the context of First Loss Default Guarantee (FLDG) arrangements, how must Regulated Entities (REs) invoke and honor the guarantee invoked against an LSP when defaults occur?
audio_script: In the context of First Loss Default Guarantee (FLDG) arrangements, how must Regulated Entities (REs) invoke and honor the guarantee invoked against an LSP when defaults occur?
option_a: Invocation must be done within a maximum of 90 days of default, and the LSP must honor it through adjustments or direct payouts.
option_b: REs can recover defaults from FLDG only after completing all legal proceedings against the borrower.
option_c: LSPs are required to maintain the entire portfolio value in an escrow account prior to loan disbursement.
option_d: FLDG invocation is restricted only to corporate borrowers, excluding retail digital loans.
explanation: Regulated Entities must ensure that invocation of FLDG is done within a maximum overdue period of 90 days, and the default must be honored by the LSP without delay as per the contractual terms.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-27-Item20] Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following cases can a bank NOT exercise its statutory General Lien?
audio_script: Question 20. Under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in which of the following cases can a bank NOT exercise its statutory General Lien?
option_a: On gold ornaments or securities left expressly for safe custody or for an ear-marked trust purpose
option_b: On proceeds of credit bills deposited for general collection without restrictions
option_c: On surplus proceeds remaining after the sale of an earlier pledged security
option_d: On mature fixed deposits standing in the borrower's own individual name
explanation: A banker's general lien applies strictly to securities bailed in the ordinary course of business. Valuables left specifically for safe custody or dedicated trust purposes are exempt from lien.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: What is the primary role of a Lending Service Provider (LSP) partnering with a Regulated Entity under RBI norms?
audio_script: What is the primary role of a Lending Service Provider partnering with a Regulated Entity under RBI norms?
option_a: To independently sanction loans and bear credit risk
option_b: To act as an agent of the RE providing customer acquisition, pricing, or recovery services
option_c: To operate independent deposit-taking schemes
option_d: To bypass RBI regulations for speedier loan processing
explanation: LSPs are agents engaged by Regulated Entities to carry out specific digital lending functions such as customer acquisition, underwriting support, pricing, or recovery, but they do not bear ultimate credit risk or independently sanction loans without RE oversight.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-27-Item21] What legal principle governs the Right of Set-off exercisable by a lending institution against a customer's deposit accounts?
audio_script: Question 21. What legal principle governs the Right of Set-off exercisable by a lending institution against a customer's deposit accounts?
option_a: Mutuality of debts where claims are due to and from the same parties in the exact same legal capacity
option_b: A compulsory prior clearance certificate obtained from the local Debt Recovery Tribunal
option_c: An irrevocable court warrant issued by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate
option_d: The requirement that the customer must be declared an insolvent by a civil court
explanation: Set-off requires mutuality of debts—the debts must be between the same parties in the same legal right and capacity (e.g., individual credit cannot be set off against partnership dues).

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-27-Item22] When a bank branch receives a Garnishee Order Nisi issued under Order XXI Rule 46 of the Civil Procedure Code, what specific funds are attached?
audio_script: Question 22. When a bank branch receives a Garnishee Order Nisi issued under Order XXI Rule 46 of the Civil Procedure Code, what specific funds are attached?
option_a: Only the cleared credit balance due or accruing due at the exact moment the order is served on the bank
option_b: All future salary credits and remittances credited to the account over the subsequent 6 months
option_c: Uncleared cheques and bills deposited for collection that have not yet been realized
option_d: All independent accounts belonging to the customer's immediate blood relatives
explanation: A Garnishee Order Nisi attaches only the debts due or accruing due at the time of service. It does not attach future credits or uncleared cheques.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: During a negotiation under the RBI Fair Practices Code for Lenders, a debtor expresses severe financial distress and outright denial of the debt amount due to unapplied waivers promised verbally by a previous branch manager. Which de-escalation tactic and communication strategy should the Debt Recovery Agent (DRA) employ first?
audio_script: Listen to the borrower's concerns completely without interruption, acknowledge their emotional distress regarding the verbal promises, and steer the conversation back to documented ledger statements to negotiate a mutually acceptable One-Time Settlement (OTS) within RBI guidelines.
option_a: Threaten immediate legal action under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 to force acknowledgment of the debt.
option_b: Practice active listening by letting the borrower vent, validate their frustration without admitting liability, and calmly review the written loan agreement and statement of accounts.
option_c: Disconnect the call immediately as verbal promises made by branch managers are legally invalid under Section 92 of the Indian Evidence Act.
option_d: Demand immediate lump-sum payment of the full outstanding amount, rejecting any discussion on waivers.
explanation: Active listening and de-escalation require acknowledging the borrower's emotional state and grievances without conceding legal positions, followed by a factual review of written documentation as mandated by RBI recovery norms.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: What is the mandatory minimum cool-off / look-up period that Regulated Entities must provide to borrowers for digital loans, enabling them to exit the loan without penalty?
audio_script: What is the mandatory minimum cool-off / look-up period that Regulated Entities must provide to borrowers for digital loans, enabling them to exit the loan without penalty?
option_a: 1 to 3 days
option_b: A period determined by the RE, typically ranging between 3 to 7 days
option_c: 14 days
option_d: 30 days
explanation: RBI guidelines stipulate that REs shall provide a cool-off / look-up period during which the borrowers can exit digital loans by paying principal and proportionate APR. The duration of this period is determined by the RE's board-approved policy, typically set between 3 to 7 days.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [Set #27-Q095] Under Article 62 of the Limitation Act, 1963, what is the prescribed period of limitation for enforcing payment of money secured by a mortgage or charge upon immovable property?

option_a: 12 Years from the date the money sued for becomes due

option_c: 30 Years for all registered commercial institutions
option_d: 5 Years from the classification of account as NPA
explanation: Article 62 of the Limitation Act 1963 provides a limitation period of 12 years to enforce payment of money secured by a mortgage or charge upon immovable property.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities

explanation: Officially Valid Documents (OVDs) under RBI KYC Directions include Passport, Driving Licence, Proof of Aadhaar, Voter ID, NREGA Job Card, and NPR Letter.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, what is the maximum imprisonment term to which a drawer can be sentenced upon conviction for a dishonoured cheque, or fine up to twice the amount of the cheque, or both?

option_a: Up to 6 months
option_b: Up to 1 year
option_c: Up to 2 years
option_d: Up to 7 years
explanation: Section 138 specifies that anyone convicted of dishonour of cheques shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Which of the following conditions is mandatory for exercising the banker's right of set-off on multiple accounts?
audio_script: Which of the following conditions is mandatory for exercising the banker's right of set-off on multiple accounts?
option_a: The accounts must be held by the customer in the same capacity and right
option_b: The accounts can be held in entirely different capacities, such as personal and trust
option_c: Notice must be given to the borrower after the adjustment is completed without exception
option_d: The debts in the accounts must be contingent and future
explanation: A fundamental requirement for set-off is that the debts must be mutual and the accounts must be held by the customer in the exact same right and capacity.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-27-Item24] As per RBI Master Directions on KYC, what is the mandatory periodic updation (re-KYC) requirement for accounts categorized under 'High Risk'?
audio_script: Question 24. As per RBI Master Directions on KYC, what is the mandatory periodic updation (re-KYC) requirement for accounts categorized under 'High Risk'?
option_a: At least once every 2 years
option_b: At least once every 5 years
option_c: At least once every 8 years
option_d: At least once every 10 years
explanation: Periodic re-KYC must be conducted at least once every 2 years for high risk, 8 years for medium risk, and 10 years for low risk accounts.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Under the RBI Digital Lending Guidelines, who is directly responsible for the disbursement of loan proceeds to the borrower's bank account without passing through any Lending Service Provider (LSP) pool account?
audio_script: Under the RBI Digital Lending Guidelines, who is directly responsible for the disbursement of loan proceeds to the borrower's bank account without passing through any Lending Service Provider pool account?
option_a: Lending Service Provider (LSP)
option_b: Regulated Entity (RE)
option_c: Payment Aggregator
option_d: Recovery Agent
explanation: According to RBI Digital Lending Guidelines, loan disbursement must be executed directly from the bank account of the Regulated Entity (RE) to the bank account of the borrower, without any passthrough or pooling account of the Lending Service Provider (LSP) or any third party.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-27-Item25] In the case of a contract entered into with a Minor for a recovery loan, what is the fundamental legal status under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Mohori Bibee precedent)?
audio_script: Question 25. In the case of a contract entered into with a Minor for a recovery loan, what is the fundamental legal status under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Mohori Bibee precedent)?
option_a: The contract is void ab initio (void from the very beginning) and unenforceable
option_b: The contract is voidable strictly at the option of the lending bank
option_c: The contract becomes legally binding as soon as the minor attains majority
option_d: The minor's natural parents are automatically liable to liquidate the debt
explanation: As established in Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, an agreement with a minor is void ab initio and no contractual liability or debt recovery suit can arise against a minor.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: [CBT-27-Item26] Under the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, what is the legal position regarding daughters as coparceners in a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)?
audio_script: Question 26. Under the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, what is the legal position regarding daughters as coparceners in a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF)?
option_a: A daughter is a coparcener by birth in her own right with the same rights and liabilities as a son
option_b: A daughter only acquires coparcenary status after the demise of the Karta
option_c: A daughter cannot be a coparcener and cannot be allotted ancestral partition shares
option_d: A daughter's coparcenary rights are limited strictly to self-acquired movable assets
explanation: Under the 2005 amendment to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, daughters have the exact same coparcenary rights and liabilities by birth as sons.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: If a borrower lodges a formal complaint regarding abusive language or harassment over a recovery call, what critical compliance artifact must the recovery agency retrieve to verify the interaction?
audio_script: If a borrower lodges a formal complaint regarding abusive language or harassment over a recovery call, what critical compliance artifact must the recovery agency retrieve to verify the interaction?
option_a: The agent's personal diary notes

option_c: The neighbor's witness statement
option_d: The collection target sheet of the agency
explanation: To investigate complaints of harassment or improper conduct, the mandatory archived audio recordings—which must be preserved for at least 6 months—serve as the primary audit trail for banks and regulatory compliance checks.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-27-Item27] Under Section 26D of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, what is the statutory restriction on a secured creditor if it fails to register its security interest on the CERSAI portal?
audio_script: Question 27. Under Section 26D of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, what is the statutory restriction on a secured creditor if it fails to register its security interest on the CERSAI portal?
option_a: The secured creditor cannot exercise any enforcement rights of taking possession or sale under Chapter III of the Act
option_b: The underlying loan contract automatically gets converted into an unsecured promissory grant
option_c: The borrower is granted a 12-month statutory moratorium on all interest payments
option_d: The presiding officer of the DRT is mandated to dismiss the recovery certificate with costs
explanation: Section 26D explicitly debars secured creditors from exercising any SARFAESI enforcement powers unless the security interest is duly registered with CERSAI.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-27-Item28] Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, what is the legal effect of a written and signed acknowledgment of liability by the borrower before the limitation period expires?
audio_script: Question 28. Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, what is the legal effect of a written and signed acknowledgment of liability by the borrower before the limitation period expires?
option_a: A fresh period of limitation begins to run from the exact date when the acknowledgment was signed
option_b: The total statutory limitation period is permanently doubled for all co-borrowers
option_c: The loan liability is deemed to be an executed Civil Court decree without trial
option_d: The bank acquires direct powers to attach the borrower's movable assets without notice
explanation: A written and signed acknowledgment of debt before the expiration of the limitation period starts a fresh period of limitation from that date under Section 18.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Which legal doctrine governs the appropriation of payments in a running current account where debits and credits are continuous, presuming that the first item paid in is the first item paid out?
audio_script: Which legal doctrine governs the appropriation of payments in a running current account where debits and credits are continuous, presuming that the first item paid in is the first item paid out?
option_a: Rule of Set-off
option_b: Clayton's Rule
option_c: Rule of General Lien
option_d: Subrogation Rule
explanation: Clayton's Rule applies to running current accounts, establishing the presumption that the earliest debt is discharged or paid off by the earliest credit entry.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: In the context of borrower counseling by Debt Recovery Agents, if a retail borrower exhibits genuine hardship (such as sudden unemployment or permanent disability), what is the primary regulatory recourse provided under the RBI guidelines before initiating coercive recovery actions?
audio_script: In the context of borrower counseling by Debt Recovery Agents, if a retail borrower exhibits genuine hardship (such as sudden unemployment or permanent disability), what is the primary regulatory recourse provided under the RBI guidelines before initiating coercive recovery actions?
option_a: Immediate classification of the account as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) without notice and seizure of assets.
option_b: Exploration of a viable restructuring plan or resolution framework such as tenor extension or moratorium under the RBI Prudential Framework for Stressed Assets.
option_c: Forced liquidation of personal guarantees without formal notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act.
option_d: Filing an immediate criminal complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act disregarding the hardship.
explanation: RBI guidelines emphasize empathetic borrower counseling and require lending institutions and their agents to explore restructuring options (such as rescheduling payments, extending tenors, or granting moratoriums) for borrowers facing genuine, temporary hardships before resorting to harsh enforcement actions.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: When interacting with a borrower who is exhibiting strong defensive denial regarding their financial default under RBI Fair Practices Code guidelines, what is the primary communication objective of a Debt Recovery Agent?
audio_script: When interacting with a borrower who is exhibiting strong defensive denial regarding their financial default under RBI Fair Practices Code guidelines, what is the primary communication objective of a Debt Recovery Agent?
option_a: To challenge their statements aggressively and establish the legal validity of the debt immediately
option_b: To practice active listening and acknowledge their emotional state without validating the avoidance of the debt
option_c: To bypass the borrower entirely and serve immediate legal notices at their workplace
option_d: To offer immediate write-offs of the principal amount to close the account quickly
explanation: Active listening and emotional acknowledgment help de-escalate tension and overcome debt denial while maintaining professional boundaries aligned with the RBI Fair Practices Code.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Which of the following fundamental distinctions correctly differentiates a Working Capital facility from a Term Loan?
audio_script: Which of the following fundamental distinctions correctly differentiates a Working Capital facility from a Term Loan?
option_a: Working capital is meant for acquiring fixed assets, whereas term loans finance day-to-day operational expenses.
option_b: Working capital is revolving credit meant to finance short-term operating cycles, whereas term loans are meant for capital expenditure with a structured repayment schedule.
option_c: Working capital requires collateral security under the SARFAESI Act, whereas term loans are strictly clean advances.
option_d: Working capital is governed by RBI prudential norms, whereas term loans are regulated exclusively by SEBI guidelines.
explanation: Working capital facilities (like cash credit or overdraft) finance short-term operational gaps and revolve as goods are bought and sold, whereas term loans are extended for acquiring fixed assets and are repaid via fixed periodic installments.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: During a telephonic recovery interaction, a borrower becomes increasingly agitated, using abusive language. According to RBI guidelines and standard de-escalation tactics, how should the DRA respond?
audio_script: During a telephonic recovery interaction, a borrower becomes increasingly agitated, using abusive language. According to RBI guidelines and standard de-escalation tactics, how should the DRA respond?
option_a: Return the hostility to establish dominance and ensure compliance
option_b: Maintain a calm tone, state professional boundaries firmly, and offer to reschedule the conversation when the borrower is calm
option_c: Disconnect the call immediately and blacklist the borrower's phone number permanently without reporting
option_d: Threaten immediate police intervention for verbal abuse over the phone
explanation: De-escalation tactics require DRAs to maintain a professional, calm demeanor, reiterate boundaries, and provide an opportunity for a constructive dialogue later.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: According to the RBI Master Circular on Housing Finance, what is the maximum permissible Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio stipulated for individual housing loans up to Rs. 30 lakhs, and what is the mandatory minimum risk weight for such loans under standard asset classification?
audio_script: According to the RBI Master Circular on Housing Finance, what is the maximum permissible Loan-to-Value ratio stipulated for individual housing loans up to Rs. 30 lakhs, and what is the mandatory minimum risk weight for such loans under standard asset classification?

option_d: LTV up to 75%, Minimum Risk Weight of 50%
explanation: As per RBI regulatory guidelines for individual housing loans up to Rs. 30 lakhs, the maximum LTV ratio is capped at 90%, and the standard asset risk weight is pegged at 35% to incentivize affordable housing credit.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-27-Item29] Under Article 62 of the Limitation Act, 1963, what is the period of limitation for a bank to file a suit to enforce payment of money secured by a mortgage upon immovable property?
audio_script: Question 29. Under Article 62 of the Limitation Act, 1963, what is the period of limitation for a bank to file a suit to enforce payment of money secured by a mortgage upon immovable property?

explanation: Article 62 of the Limitation Act 1963 prescribes a 12-year limitation period to enforce payment of money secured by a mortgage or charge upon immovable property.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-27-Item30] Under Article 55 of the Limitation Act, 1963, what is the limitation period for initiating legal action for breach of contract on an unsecured promissory note?

explanation: For breach of simple contract or recovery of money on an unsecured basis / demand promissory note, the limitation period is 3 years under Article 55.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: According to the RBI Fair Practices Code for lenders and recovery agents, which of the following is strictly prohibited during recovery negotiations?
audio_script: According to the RBI Fair Practices Code for lenders and recovery agents, which of the following is strictly prohibited during recovery negotiations?
option_a: Explaining the legal consequences of default under the SARFAESI Act
option_b: Using intimidation, harassment, or persistent molestation, including calling relatives or employers repeatedly
option_c: Offering flexible installment options to clear overdue amounts
option_d: Providing official bank receipts for payments collected
explanation: RBI strictly prohibits harassment, intimidation, public humiliation, and contacting third parties like employers or unrelated relatives regarding the borrower's debt.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: When a customer submits an Aadhaar number for identification, what must banks ensure regarding the Aadhaar number as per UIDAI and RBI guidelines?

option_a: Print the full Aadhaar number on all bank passbooks

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: As per the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) guidelines on Digital Lending issued in September 2022, what is the mandatory timeline and protocol regarding the cooling-off/look-up period provided to borrowers for digital loans disbursed through Digital Lending Apps (DLAs)?
audio_script: As per the RBI digital lending guidelines of September 2022, what is the mandatory cooling-off period and protocol for borrowers of digital loans?
option_a: A uniform 3-day cooling-off period during which borrowers can exit by paying only the proportionate APR without any penalty.
option_b: A cooling-off period determined by the lender, which must not be less than 7 days, during which borrowers can prepay the principal and proportionate APR without penalty.
option_c: A standardized cooling-off/look-up period determined by the Board of the Regulated Entity (RE), during which the borrower shall be given an option to exit the digital loan without any penalty by paying the principal and proportionate APR, up to a maximum of 7 days.
option_d: No cooling-off period is mandated for digital loans below rupees one lakh, but a mandatory 14-day period applies to loans above rupees one lakh.
explanation: According to the RBI Guidelines on Digital Lending (Para 4.10), Regulated Entities (REs) must provide a cooling-off / look-up period during which the borrowers can exit the digital loan without any penalty by paying the principal and the proportionate APR. The exact period is determined by the Board of the RE, subject to a maximum limit prescribed by the guidelines (which is 7 days for loans with a tenure of 7 days or more, though specifically phrased as determined by the Board up to a maximum limit based on the regulatory framework).

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: Who bears the ultimate responsibility under RBI guidelines if a Lending Service Provider (LSP) engaged by a Regulated Entity (RE) resorts to coercive recovery practices?
audio_script: Who bears the ultimate responsibility under RBI guidelines if a Lending Service Provider (LSP) engaged by a Regulated Entity (RE) resorts to coercive recovery practices?
option_a: Only the third-party recovery agency hired by the LSP
option_b: The individual collection agent directly
option_c: The Regulated Entity (RE), as outsourcing of recovery does not absolve the RE from its regulatory responsibilities
option_d: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI)
explanation: Under RBI outsourcing and digital lending guidelines, the Regulated Entity (RE) retains ultimate accountability and responsibility for compliance, including adherence to fair practices in recovery, even when digital lending and recovery operations are outsourced to LSPs.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Can a creditor directly initiate legal recovery proceedings or demand payment from the surety under Section 128 without first suing the principal debtor?
audio_script: Can a creditor directly initiate legal recovery proceedings or demand payment from the surety under Section 128 without first suing the principal debtor?
option_a: No, the creditor must first exhaust all remedies against the principal debtor
option_b: Yes, because the surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor, making the surety liable immediately upon default
option_c: No, unless special written permission is obtained from the Reserve Bank of India
option_d: Yes, but only after a mandatory waiting period of 90 days post-default
explanation: Because the surety's liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor under Section 128, the surety is considered a principal debtor regarding liability. The creditor can sue the surety directly without first suing the principal debtor, unless contractually agreed otherwise.

question_text: When a bank creates a charge via a 'Hypothecation Deed' over movable assets like book debts or inventory under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest (SARFAESI) Act, 2002, which legal characteristic differentiates it fundamentally from a Pledge?
audio_script: When a bank creates a charge via a Hypothecation Deed over movable assets like book debts or inventory under the SARFAESI Act, 2002, which legal characteristic differentiates it fundamentally from a Pledge?
option_a: Hypothecation involves creation of a charge over movable property where neither ownership nor physical or constructive possession is transferred to the lender.
option_b: Hypothecation requires the physical locking and keying of the goods under the bank's exclusive lock and key mechanism.
option_c: Hypothecation can only be executed for immovable properties exceeding a statutory valuation threshold of ten lakh rupees.
option_d: Hypothecation grants the lender an immediate right of private sale under Section 176 of the Indian Contract Act without invoking SARFAESI provisions.
explanation: Hypothecation is defined under Section 2(1)(n) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 as a charge in or upon any movable property, existing or future, created by a borrower in favour of a secured creditor without delivery of possession of the property to such creditor. Unlike a pledge, possession remains with the borrower.

question_text: In the context of a running current account with multiple distinct debts, how does the rule established in Clayton's Case (Devaynes v. Noble) allocate incoming credits deposited by the customer?
audio_script: In the context of a running current account with multiple distinct debts, how does the rule established in Clayton's Case allocate incoming credits deposited by the customer?
option_a: Credits are applied to the newest debt first.
option_b: Credits are applied to discharge the earliest (oldest) debt first in point of time.
option_c: Credits are distributed equally across all active liabilities.
option_d: Credits are exclusively reserved for statutory dues and penal charges.
explanation: The rule in Clayton's Case dictates that in a running account, every payment made by the debtor is applied to extinguish the earliest debt incurred (first in, first out basis), unless there is an express agreement or circumstance indicating a contrary intention.

question_text: A term loan account became irregular and was classified as NPA on June 15, 2018. The borrower made a part payment of Rs. 25,000 towards the principal on August 10, 2020, but did not sign any written acknowledgment. What will be the fresh limitation period for filing a recovery suit for the money claim under the Limitation Act, 1963?
audio_script: A term loan account became an NPA on June 15, 2018. The borrower made a part payment on August 10, 2020, without signing a written acknowledgment. What is the fresh limitation period for filing a recovery suit under the Limitation Act, 1963?
option_b: August 10, 2023
option_d: August 10, 2032
explanation: Under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963, where payment on account of a debt is made before the expiration of the prescribed period by the debtor, a fresh period of limitation computes from the time when the payment was made. Since the part payment was made on August 10, 2020 (within the original 3-year period expiring June 15, 2021), a fresh 3-year period starts from August 10, 2020, making it valid up to August 10, 2023.

question_text: Under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which specific type of mortgage requires compulsorily registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, regardless of the principal sum secured, and involves the transfer of interest in the specific immovable property without delivery of possession?
audio_script: Under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which specific type of mortgage requires compulsorily registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, regardless of the principal sum secured, and involves the transfer of interest in the specific immovable property without delivery of possession?
option_a: Equitable Mortgage by deposit of title deeds
option_b: Simple Mortgage
option_c: English Mortgage
option_d: Mortgage by Conditional Sale
explanation: A Simple Mortgage (defined under Section 58(b) of the TP Act) does not involve delivery of possession, but because it creates a right in the mortgagee to cause the property to be sold, it requires compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act irrespective of the amount. Equitable mortgages (deposit of title deeds) restricted to notified towns are exempt from compulsory registration of the memorandum under certain judicial interpretations, whereas Simple, English, and Conditional mortgages require registration if value exceeds 100 rupees, but Simple mortgage has no delivery of possession unlike English mortgage where property is absolutely transferred subject to re-transfer.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: A Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) issues a final recovery certificate against a defaulting borrower for an amount of Rs. 35 Lakhs. The borrower is aggrieved by the order and wishes to file an appeal before the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) under Section 20 of the RDB Act, 1993. What is the mandatory pre-deposit amount required to be deposited by the appellant for the appeal to be entertained by DRAT?
audio_script: A borrower wants to appeal against a DRT order of Rs 35 Lakhs before the DRAT under Section 20. What is the mandatory pre-deposit percentage required?
option_a: 25% of the debt due as determined by the DRT
option_b: 50% of the amount of debt so due, which can be reduced to 25% by the Appellate Tribunal for reasons to be recorded in writing
option_c: 75% of the total claim made by the bank in the original application
option_d: 100% of the certificate amount deposited in an escrow account
explanation: Under Section 20 of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy (RDB) Act, 1993, no appeal shall be entertained by the DRAT unless the appellant deposits 50% of the amount of debt due as determined by the DRT. However, the DRAT has the discretion to reduce this amount, for reasons to be recorded in writing, to not less than 25% of the debt.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: If a debtor fails to comply with the 30-day appeal window under Section 20 of the RDB Act, 1993, can the DRAT entertain an appeal beyond this period?

explanation: The DRAT may entertain an appeal after the expiry of the 30-day period if the appellant satisfies the appellate tribunal that there was sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal within the stipulated time.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: A term loan account defaulted on June 15, 2018. On May 10, 2021, the borrower signed a balance confirmation letter admitting the liability. Subsequently, no further payments were made. Up to what date can the bank legally file a summary suit for recovery of money under the Limitation Act, 1963?
audio_script: A term loan defaulted on June 15, 2018. A balance confirmation letter was signed on May 10, 2021. Up to what date can the bank legally file a suit for recovery under the Limitation Act?
explanation: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, an acknowledgment of liability in writing signed by the party against whom the claim is made before the expiration of the prescribed period creates a fresh period of limitation. Since the acknowledgment was made on May 10, 2021 (within the original 3-year limitation period ending June 15, 2021), a fresh 3-year period starts from May 10, 2021, extending the limitation date to May 10, 2024.

option_b: Total Fixed Assets plus Inventory minus Term Loan borrowings.
option_c: Gross Profit minus Operational Expenses.
option_d: Total Bank Borrowings minus Paid-up Capital and Reserves.
explanation: The working capital gap is the difference between total current assets and current liabilities (excluding bank borrowings). It represents the total requirement of funds for operations that need to be met through net working capital and bank finance.

option_a: Base Layer

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Term loans sanctioned by commercial banks are primarily intended to finance which of the following?

option_a: Day-to-day electricity bills and staff salaries

option_c: Immediate trade creditors for short cycles

explanation: Term loans are medium-to-long-term credit facilities extended for capital expenditure, such as purchasing fixed assets for business expansion, modernization, or setting up new projects.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: As per RBI Digital Lending Guidelines, who bears the ultimate responsibility and obligation for paying fees, charges, or commissions to the Lending Service Providers (LSPs) engaged by a Regulated Entity (RE)?
audio_script: As per RBI Digital Lending Guidelines, who bears the ultimate responsibility and obligation for paying fees, charges, or commissions to the Lending Service Providers engaged by a Regulated Entity?
option_a: The borrower, by way of an explicit add-on fee included in the annualized percentage rate (APR).
option_b: The LSP itself, by adjusting it against the collection float generated during loan recovery.
option_c: The Regulated Entity (RE) directly, and these charges cannot be recovered from the borrower by the LSP under the guise of additional fees.
option_d: Shared equally between the borrower and the RE based on the tripartite agreement executed at the time of onboarding.
explanation: RBI guidelines explicitly state that the fees, charges, etc., payable to the LSP shall be paid directly by the Regulated Entity (RE) and shall not, under any circumstances, be charged by the LSP to the borrower.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

explanation: As per the notifications issued under Section 2(1)(m)(iv) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, NBFCs with a minimum asset size of Rs 100 Crore and above are eligible to be notified as financial institutions for enforcing security interest.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In retail personal loans, which default pattern typically indicates systemic or structural default behavior as opposed to transient liquidity mismatch?

option_a: Single delayed payment due to technical bank holiday issues
option_b: Missing the EMI due date by exactly two days once a year
option_c: Progressive movement through SMA-0, SMA-1, and SMA-2 categories culminating in NPA classification
option_d: Prepayment of the loan facility before the completion of tenure
explanation: Progressive migration through SMA categories (SMA-1 for 31-60 days and SMA-2 for 61-90 days overdue) reflects continuous default patterns indicating severe financial distress or structural inability to pay, unlike one-off technical delays.

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: Which of the following best describes the obligation of a Debt Recovery Agent (DRA) regarding a borrower's personal and financial data?

option_d: Data can be shared with neighbors to locate the borrower
explanation: DRAs are bound by strict data privacy and non-disclosure rules. Borrower information must be kept confidential and cannot be disclosed to unauthorized third parties or colleagues who are not directly involved in the recovery process.

option_d: Direct recovery and collection agents strictly

explanation: RBI guidelines on Fair Practices Code strictly stipulate that recovery telecalling must be confined strictly between 08:00 hours (8:00 AM) and 19:00 hours (7:00 PM).

module: Module C: Code of Conduct & Ethics
question_text: A customer has registered their mobile number under the National Do Not Call (NDNC) registry / Customer Preference Registry. Under RBI and TRAI guidelines, can recovery agents contact this customer for debt collection via telephonic calls?
audio_script: A customer has registered their mobile number under the National Do Not Call registry. Under RBI and TRAI guidelines, can recovery agents contact this customer for debt collection via telephonic calls?

explanation: Transactional and service calls, including calls made by regulated banks and their authorized recovery agents for the recovery of bonafide dues, are statutorily exempt from the restrictions of the National Do Not Call (NDNC) registry, provided they adhere to prescribed calling hours and ethical codes.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In the context of working capital finance, which RBI directive governs the assessment and monitoring of working capital limits under the Maximum Permissible Bank Finance (MPBF) or cash budget system, originally recommended by which committee?

option_a: Tandon Committee

explanation: The Tandon Committee (1974), appointed by the RBI, recommended norms for inventory and receivables and introduced the Maximum Permissible Bank Finance (MPBF) system to assess working capital requirements of borrowers.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

option_b: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act (SARFAESI) Section 13(4)

explanation: The RBI guidelines on Fair Practices Code and Managing Risks and Code of Conduct in Outsourcing of Financial Services explicitly prohibit banks and their agents from resorting to intimidation, harassment, public humiliation, or contacting family members in ways that violate borrower privacy.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: When evaluating the core principles of sound lending, how does a banker distinguish between a working capital loan and a term loan regarding the source of repayment?
audio_script: When evaluating the core principles of sound lending, how does a banker distinguish between a working capital loan and a term loan regarding the source of repayment?
option_a: Working capital loans are repaid from liquidation of current assets/cash flows, whereas term loans are repaid from future projected operational profits.
option_b: Working capital loans are repaid through capital subsidies, whereas term loans are repaid through secondary collateral liquidation.
option_c: Working capital loans are repaid from long-term capital investments, whereas term loans are repaid from daily cash sales.
option_d: There is no distinction; both are repaid strictly from the liquidation of primary immovable fixed assets.
explanation: Working capital loans are designed to finance short-term operational requirements (current assets) and are repaid through the normal cash cycle and realization of current assets like inventory and receivables. Conversely, term loans are extended for acquiring fixed assets and are repaid out of the future generation of operational profits over a medium to long-term amortization schedule.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Within what timeframe must a complaint be filed in writing before the competent Magistrate by the payee after the expiry of the 15-day notice period following the dishonour of an electronic fund transfer / NACH mandate under Section 25?
audio_script: Within what timeframe must a complaint be filed in writing before the competent Magistrate by the payee after the expiry of the 15-day notice period following the dishonour of an electronic fund transfer / NACH mandate under Section 25?
option_a: Within 30 days of the cause of action (expiry of 15 days notice)
option_b: Within 60 days of the bank return memo
option_c: Within 90 days of the presentation date
option_d: Within 1 year of the loan agreement signing
explanation: Mirroring the provisions of Section 138/142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act made applicable via Section 25 of the PSS Act, the complaint must be made within one month (30 days) of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to sub-section (1) (i.e., expiry of the 15-day notice period).

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives
question_text: In accordance with RBI regulatory guidelines on Scale Based Regulation, what is the primary regulatory distinction regarding capital adequacy requirements (CRAR) between an NBFC-ND (Non-Deposit taking) in the Base Layer and an NBFC-D (Deposit taking)?
audio_script: In accordance with RBI regulatory guidelines on Scale Based Regulation, what is the primary regulatory distinction regarding capital adequacy requirements between an NBFC-ND in the Base Layer and an NBFC-D?
option_a: NBFC-ND Base Layer has no minimum CRAR requirement, while NBFC-D must maintain 15 percent.
option_b: NBFC-ND Base Layer is subject to a minimum CRAR of 10 percent, whereas NBFC-D is subject to 15 percent.
option_c: Both NBFC-ND Base Layer and NBFC-D are subject to a uniform minimum CRAR of 15 percent, but NBFC-D has stricter public deposit ceilings.
option_d: NBFC-ND Base Layer must maintain a minimum CRAR of 15 percent, while NBFC-D must maintain 20 percent.
explanation: Under the SBR framework, NBFC-NDs in the Base Layer are subject to a reduced minimum CRAR of 10 percent to ease compliance for smaller entities, whereas NBFC-D (deposit-taking) entities are required to maintain a minimum CRAR of 15 percent.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: A cheque issued by a debtor towards the repayment of a bank loan is dishonoured due to 'funds insufficient'. option_a: November 25th
option_b: November 30th
option_c: December 10th
option_d: December 25th
explanation: The cause of action arises on the day after the 15-day payment window ends (November 11th). The complaint must be filed within one month (30 days) from that date, which makes December 10th the final deadline for filing the complaint under Section 142(b).

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In the context of lending principles, which of the following refers to the bank's requirement that a loan must be repaid from the generated cash flows of the borrower's business rather than through the forced liquidation of securities?
audio_script: In the context of lending principles, which of the following refers to the bank's requirement that a loan must be repaid from the generated cash flows of the borrower's business rather than through the forced liquidation of securities?
option_a: Principle of Liquidity
option_b: Principle of Safety
option_c: Principle of Purpose
option_d: Principle of Profitability
explanation: The Principle of Purpose dictates that loans must be granted for productive and legitimate purposes so that they generate adequate income for timely repayment, ensuring the borrower does not depend on the sale of securities.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 13(3A) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, if the secured creditor rejects the representation or objection made by the borrower against the 60-day notice under Section 13(2), within how many days must the creditor communicate the reasons for such non-acceptance to the borrower?
audio_script: Under Section 13 subsection 3A of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, if the secured creditor rejects the representation or objection made by the borrower against the 60-day notice under Section 13(2), within how many days must the creditor communicate the reasons for such non-acceptance to the borrower?

explanation: According to Section 13(3A) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, if the borrower makes a representation or raises any objection in response to the Section 13(2) notice, the secured creditor must consider it and, if not acceptable, communicate the reasons within 15 days of receipt of such representation or objection.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: Which canon of sound lending ensures that the bank's funds are deployed in such a manner that they can be easily converted into cash without incurring losses in times of unexpected liquidity demands?

explanation: The Principle of Liquidity ensures that banks maintain sufficient liquid assets and easily realizable securities to meet sudden withdrawal demands from depositors without facing a liquidity crunch.

option_d: The bank acquires direct powers to attach the borrower's movable assets without notice
explanation: A written and signed acknowledgment of debt before the expiration of the limitation period starts a fresh period of limitation from that date under Section 18.

option_d: Loss Asset

An NPA remains in the 'Sub-standard' category for a period up to 12 months (or exceeding 90 days up to 180 days in older contexts, but formally sub-standard applies when NPA for up to 12 months).

option_d: Individual retail investors directly

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: A borrower defaulted on a cash credit facility on 15th April 2020. On 10th January 2023, the borrower makes a partial payment of Rs. 50,000 towards the loan account and signs a balance confirmation letter. According to the Limitation Act, 1963, what will be the fresh limitation period for filing a recovery suit, and under which section does this extension apply?
audio_script: A borrower defaulted on a cash credit facility on 15th April 2020. On 10th January 2023, the borrower makes a partial payment of Rs. 50,000 towards the loan account and signs a balance confirmation letter. According to the Limitation Act, 1963, what will be the fresh limitation period for filing a recovery suit, and under which section does this extension apply?
option_a: 3 years from 10th January 2023, under Section 18 for acknowledgment and Section 19 for part payment
option_b: 12 years from 15th April 2020, under Section 19 for mortgage debt
option_c: 3 years from 15th April 2023, under Section 5 for condonation of delay
option_d: 12 years from 10th January 2023, under Section 18 for registered mortgage
explanation: Under the Limitation Act, 1963, for a money claim (cash credit facility), the standard limitation period is 3 years from the date of default (15th April 2020). However, Section 18 (acknowledgment of liability in writing) and Section 19 (payment on account of debt) both apply here, providing a fresh limitation period of 3 years starting from the date of such payment/acknowledgment (10th January 2023).

audio_script: Which regulatory principle governs the prohibition of Debt Recovery Agents from disclosing a borrower's debt status to neighbors, employers, or unrelated third parties?

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: A borrower defaulted on a cash credit facility on 15th January 2021. On 10th January 2024, the borrower signs a balance confirmation letter admitting the liability. According to the Limitation Act 1963, what is the fresh limitation period for filing a money recovery suit?
audio_script: A borrower defaulted on a cash credit facility on 15th January 2021. On 10th January 2024, the borrower signs a balance confirmation letter admitting the liability. According to the Limitation Act 1963, what is the fresh limitation period for filing a money recovery suit?

explanation: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act 1963, where, before the expiration of the prescribed period for a suit of property or right, an acknowledgement of liability has been made in writing signed by the party against whom such right is claimed, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the acknowledgement was so signed. Since it is a money claim, the fresh period is 3 years starting from 10th January 2024.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: According to Section 133 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what effect does any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor have on the surety?
audio_script: According to Section 133 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what effect does any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor have on the surety?
option_a: It discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance.
option_b: It has no legal effect, and the surety remains liable for all past and future amounts.
option_c: It automatically converts the guarantee into a continuing indemnity bond.
option_d: It increases the surety's liability in direct proportion to the monetary variance.
explanation: Section 133 provides that any variance, made without the surety's consent, in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor, discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: [CBT-29-Item04] Under Section 21 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the legal nature and finality of an Award passed by a Lok Adalat in a debt settlement?

option_a: It is deemed to be a decree of a Civil Court, final and binding on all parties, and strictly non-appealable

option_d: It has no binding effect unless the borrower ratifies it through an affidavit
explanation: A Lok Adalat award is deemed to be a decree of a Civil Court under Section 21 of the LSA Act. Because it is founded on mutual consent, no appeal lies against it.

explanation: Data privacy rules and the Code of Conduct dictate that borrower information must be protected and not disclosed to third parties or even internal colleagues who are not officially assigned to manage that specific account.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 128, since the liability of the surety is co-extensive with the principal debtor, can a bank directly sue the surety for recovery without suing the principal debtor first?
audio_script: Under Section 128, since the liability of the surety is co-extensive with the principal debtor, can a bank directly sue the surety for recovery without suing the principal debtor first?
option_a: No, the bank must always exhaust remedies against the principal debtor first.
option_b: Yes, the creditor can sue the surety directly as the liability is co-extensive.
option_c: No, the surety is only liable after legal insolvency of the principal debtor.
option_d: Yes, but only with prior written permission from the RBI.
explanation: Because the surety's liability is co-extensive under Section 128, the surety is liable on default, and the creditor may proceed against the surety directly without exhausting remedies against the principal debtor first.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities

option_a: To serve as the bank's profit commission charged upfront on the sanctioned loan amount.

option_c: To pay the legal fees associated with the registration of charges under the CERSAI portal.
option_d: To comply with the statutory liquidity ratio requirements mandated under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act.
explanation: The margin is the percentage of the asset's value not financed by the bank, which the borrower must fund themselves. It acts as a safety cushion for the lender against market price fluctuations and depreciation of the collateral.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework

question_text: If a borrower fails to maintain the stipulated margin on inventory and book debts under a working capital cash credit facility, what immediate operational impact does it have on the account?

explanation: A drop in inventory or receivables reduces the Drawing Power (DP). If the outstanding balance exceeds this reduced DP, the excess drawing is classified as irregular, and banks typically levy penal interest on such overdrawn amounts as per RBI guidelines.

audio_script: According to RBI prudential norms on margin requirements and valuation of securities for term loans, what is the regulatory implication if a bank discovers that the collateral margin has eroded below the stipulated minimum?
option_a: The bank must immediately write off the entire asset as a Loss Asset irrespective of the borrower's repayment track record.
option_b: The bank is mandated to revalue the security at least once a quarter and call for top-up securities or additional cash margins to restore the original margin level to mitigate unsecured exposure risks.
option_c: The bank can unilaterally convert the term loan into an equity holding in the borrower's company under Section 19 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
option_d: Margin erosion has no regulatory consequence as long as the loan account is categorized as Standard.
explanation: Prudential banking principles and RBI guidelines dictate that safety in lending relies heavily on maintaining adequate margins. If market fluctuations or asset degradation cause the margin to drop below sanctioned stipulations, banks must insist on top-up security or cash margins to protect against potential shortfalls upon default.

module: Module A: General Banking & Securities
question_text: In the assessment of working capital requirements under the traditional Maximum Permissible Bank Finance (MPBF) approach as recommended by the Tandon Committee, what is the precise treatment of 'Core Current Assets' (also known as Hard Core Working Capital) while calculating the Net Working Capital (NWC) gap?
audio_script: In the assessment of working capital requirements under the traditional MPBF approach as recommended by the Tandon Committee, what is the precise treatment of Core Current Assets while calculating the Net Working Capital gap?
option_a: Core Current Assets are financed entirely through short-term bank borrowings and spontaneous current liabilities.
option_b: Core Current Assets are treated as a permanent investment of the firm, similar to fixed assets, and must be financed through long-term sources such as equity or term loans.
option_c: Core Current Assets are ignored in the MPBF calculation and deducted directly from total inventory before assessing current assets.
option_d: Core Current Assets are funded exclusively through trade creditors and provisions without requiring any long-term margin.
explanation: According to the Tandon Committee guidelines on working capital finance, Core Current Assets (the minimum level of raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods, and receivables that must be maintained at all times to keep production going) represent a permanent lock-up of funds. Therefore, they must be treated like fixed assets and financed through long-term funds (equity and long-term debt) rather than short-term bank credit.

question_text: In evaluating the 'Margin Requirement' principle of good lending, if a borrower pledges government securities with a face value of INR 1,00,000 and a market value of INR 95,000 against a loan, and the bank stipulates a margin of 15% on the market value, what is the maximum loan amount the bank can disburse?
audio_script: In evaluating the Margin Requirement principle of good lending, if a borrower pledges government securities with a face value of one lakh and a market value of ninety-five thousand against a loan, and the bank stipulates a margin of fifteen percent on the market value, what is the maximum loan amount the bank can disburse?
explanation: Margin is calculated on the current market value of the security. Market Value = INR 95,000. Margin = 15% of 95,000 = INR 14,250. Maximum loan amount = Market Value minus Margin = 95,000 - 14,250 = INR 80,750.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: A secured creditor issues a demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002. The borrower submits a detailed representation under Section 13(3A) on the 45th day from the date of the notice. What is the legal obligation of the secured creditor regarding the 60-day timeline before taking measures under Section 13(4)?
audio_script: A secured creditor issues a demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002. The borrower submits a detailed representation under Section 13(3A) on the 45th day from the date of the notice. What is the legal obligation of the secured creditor regarding the 60-day timeline before taking measures under Section 13(4)?
option_a: The 60-day period automatically gets extended by another 15 days from the date of receipt of the representation.
option_b: The secured creditor must still wait for the completion of the original 60 days from the demand notice, and communicating the reply within 15 days of the representation does not invalidate the original 60-day expiry.
option_c: The secured creditor can immediately take measures under Section 13(4) as soon as the 15-day reply is dispatched, regardless of the initial 60 days.
option_d: The demand notice becomes null and void, requiring a fresh 60-day notice to be served.
explanation: Section 13(3A) clarifies that the communication of reasons for non-acceptance of a representation does not confer upon the borrower any right to approach the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) under Section 17 unless the secured creditor has actually taken recourse to measures under Section 13(4). The original 60-day statutory timeline under Section 13(2) remains the baseline, and the reply under Section 13(3A) must be sent within 15 days of receiving the representation without necessarily extending the basic 60-day notice window unless mandated by specific judicial precedents, but the core rule is that 13(4) measures cannot be taken before the expiry of the 60 days from the 13(2) notice.

option_c: Summarizing the borrower's statements to ensure complete clarity before proposing solutions
option_d: Allowing adequate pauses for the borrower to respond without cutting them off
explanation: Interrupting a borrower prevents effective communication, violates active listening rules, and creates barriers to resolving the default amicably.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act 1963, what is the legal consequence if acknowledgment of liability in respect of a debt is made in writing and signed by the debtor before the expiration of the original limitation period?
audio_script: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act 1963, what is the legal consequence if acknowledgment of liability in respect of a debt is made in writing and signed by the debtor before the expiration of the original limitation period?
option_a: A fresh limitation period starts to compute from the date the acknowledgment was signed
option_b: The entire debt is completely written off and cancelled
option_c: The interest rate on the debt is legally halved
option_d: The loan transforms automatically from secured to unsecured
explanation: Section 18 of the Limitation Act 1963 provides that where, before the expiration of the prescribed limitation period for any suit or application, an acknowledgment of liability has been made in writing signed by the party against whom the property or right is claimed, a fresh limitation period shall be computed from the time when the acknowledgment was so signed.

module: Module D: NBFCs, Digital Lending & Co-operatives

option_b: Responsibility for timely servicing and NPA recognition remains with the Regulated Entity irrespective of FLDG invoke

option_d: NPA classification is suspended until the 90-day guarantee invocation period expires
explanation: Invocation of FLDG cannot do away with the Regulated Entity's responsibility of following standard regulatory guidelines, including timely provisioning and NPA recognition. The RE must recognize NPAs at the individual borrower level irrespective of invocation of the guarantee.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework
question_text: Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, what is the current pecuniary jurisdiction (ceiling on the total value of assets/debt involved) up to which a Lok Adalat can exercise jurisdiction to settle bank recovery disputes before litigation?

option_a: Rs 10 Lakhs

option_c: Rs 50 Lakhs
option_d: No monetary limit for pre-litigation cases
explanation: While Permanent Lok Adalats have a specific statutory ceiling for public utility services disputes, regular Lok Adalats under the LSA Act, 1987 have no upper monetary limit for cases referred in the pre-litigation stage, though traditionally specified limits apply to certain referrals. For general bank recovery disputes brought to pre-litigation Lok Adalats, there is no upper ceiling cap.
