question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q048] With respect to the statutory 5-year record retention rule under the PMLA, 2002, and the RBI Master Direction on KYC, identify the INCORRECT statement regarding the exact timeline and scope of records to be maintained by a scheduled commercial bank.
audio_script: Question 48. With respect to the statutory 5-year record retention rule under the PMLA, 2002, and the RBI Master Direction on KYC, identify the INCORRECT statement regarding the exact timeline and scope of records to be maintained by a scheduled commercial bank.
option_a: Records pertaining to the identification of the customer and their address must be maintained for at least five years after the business relationship has ended or account has been closed.
option_b: Records of all domestic and international transactions, including both the text and metadata necessary to reconstruct individual transactions, must be maintained for a period of five years from the date of the transaction.
option_c: If a customer account is subjected to an ongoing litigation, internal investigation, or a formal notice from an enforcement agency (like ED or FIU-IND), the 5-year retention clock is paused, and records must be retained until the final conclusion of the legal proceedings, even if it exceeds five years.
option_d: All records corresponding to Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) filed with the FIU-IND, along with internal analysis notes, must be archived for exactly 5 years from the date the STR was acknowledged by the FIU-IND.
explanation: While the standard statutory retention period is 5 years, RBI Master Directions and PMLA rules require that records relating to STRs and matters under investigation must be retained beyond the standard 5-year period until the law enforcement or competent authority confirms that the case has been fully closed or resolved.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q073] A domestic corporate customer structured as a private limited company approaches a bank for credit facilities. During the Beneficial Ownership (BO) identification process as per Rule 9 of the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, the bank discovers that no single natural person holds more than 10% of the shares. However, an individual exercises ultimate effective control over the management and financial decisions through voting rights and shareholder agreements. What is the correct threshold and classification for identifying the Beneficial Owner in this scenario?
audio_script: Question 73. A domestic corporate customer structured as a private limited company approaches a bank for credit facilities. During the Beneficial Ownership (BO) identification process as per Rule 9 of the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, the bank discovers that no single natural person holds more than 10% of the shares. However, an individual exercises ultimate effective control over the management and financial decisions through voting rights and shareholder agreements. What is the correct threshold and classification for identifying the Beneficial Owner in this scenario?
option_a: Since nobody holds above 25% (or 10% for companies), the identity of the natural person exercising control through other means (control) must be determined as the Beneficial Owner.
option_b: The company is exempt from BO identification because shareholdings are fragmented below the statutory percentage threshold.
option_c: The Managing Director of the company defaults automatically as the sole Beneficial Owner regardless of shareholding or control.
option_d: The bank must treat the corporate entity itself as the beneficial owner without looking behind the corporate veil.
explanation: As per PML Rules, for companies, the beneficial owner is the natural person(s) who, whether acting alone or together, or through one or more juridical person, has a controlling ownership interest (>= 10%) or exercises control through other means. If no natural person is identified through shareholding, the natural person exercising control through other means must be identified.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q091] In accordance with the guidelines on freezing of assets under Section 51A of the UAPA Act and orders issued by the Central Government, if an entity or individual challenges the freezing order, what is the appropriate recourse for the banking institution?
audio_script: Question 91. In accordance with the guidelines on freezing of assets under Section 51A of the UAPA Act and orders issued by the Central Government, if an entity or individual challenges the freezing order, what is the appropriate recourse for the banking institution?
option_a: Unfreeze the account immediately upon receiving a written legal notice from the customer's advocate.
option_b: Refer the representation and documents to the designated authority or nodal ministry appointed under the UAPA guidelines while maintaining the freeze status.
option_c: Transfer the disputed funds to an escrow account managed by the bank's legal department pending internal review.
option_d: Obtain a direct clearance certificate from the local district magistrate before restoring normal account operations.
explanation: Banks cannot independently unfreeze assets designated under Section 51A of UAPA. Any representations or challenges by customers must be forwarded to the designated authority for review and instruction.

module: Module D: Transaction Monitoring, Sanctions & Red Flags
question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q095] A foreign respondent bank ('Bank X') utilizes its account with an Indian correspondent bank ('Bank Y') to provide banking services to its own downstream respondent customers ('Bank Z'), which Bank Y does not have a direct relationship with. This arrangement is known as a nested correspondent relationship. What is the primary AML risk and compliance requirement under RBI/FATF guidelines for Bank Y regarding this arrangement?
audio_script: Question 95. A foreign respondent bank ('Bank X') utilizes its account with an Indian correspondent bank ('Bank Y') to provide banking services to its own downstream respondent customers ('Bank Z'), which Bank Y does not have a direct relationship with. This arrangement is known as a nested correspondent relationship. What is the primary AML risk and compliance requirement under RBI/FATF guidelines for Bank Y regarding this arrangement?
option_a: Bank Y must compel Bank X to disclose the identities of all retail depositors of Bank Z under Section 12 of the PMLA.
option_b: Bank Y must satisfy itself that Bank X has performed adequate due diligence on, and applies ongoing monitoring to, the direct customers (Bank Z) having access to the correspondent account, and can provide relevant customer identification data upon request.
option_c: Nested relationships are strictly prohibited by the RBI Master Direction on KYC; hence Bank Y must terminate the account immediately upon discovery.
option_d: Bank Y is legally indemnified from all AML violations since the primary liability rests solely with Bank X's home country regulator.
explanation: Nested correspondent banking involves the use of a correspondent bank's account by other financial institutions (nested institutions). Under RBI KYC guidelines and FATF standards, the correspondent bank (Bank Y) must ensure that the respondent bank (Bank X) has verified the identity of and performed ongoing due diligence on the customers having direct access to the accounts of the correspondent bank (nested institutions like Bank Z) and is able to provide relevant customer due diligence information upon request.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q056] Which of the following restrictions applies to a 'Small Account' opened under simplified KYC norms in terms of total credits in a financial year?

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q026] An authorized reporting entity successfully identifies a suspicious transaction relating to potential terrorist financing during routine monitoring on a Tuesday. audio_script: AMLKYC-CBT07-Q026. An authorized reporting entity successfully identifies a suspicious transaction relating to potential terrorist financing during routine monitoring on a Tuesday. According to the statutory and regulatory guidelines governing Financial Intelligence Unit - India (FIU-IND) reporting timelines, what is the exact deadline by which the Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) must be filed?
option_a: Within 7 working days from the date of establishment of suspicion
option_b: Within 7 days from the date of occurrence of the transaction
option_c: Within 3 working days from the date of confirmation by the Principal Officer
option_d: By the 15th day of the succeeding calendar month
explanation: According to the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 and FIU-IND guidelines, Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) must be furnished to the Director, FIU-IND, within 7 working days of establishing that the transaction is suspicious. (Note: Cash Transaction Reports and Cross-Border Wire Transfer Reports are submitted by the 15th of the succeeding month).

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q050] In evaluating a complex corporate group structure for Beneficial Ownership (BO) determination under the PML Rules, a company has three corporate layers holding shares. Entity X holds 28% shares in the client company, Entity Y holds 15% through a trust, and Entity Z holds 12% directly. Furthermore, an individual 'Mr. A' exercises ultimate effective control over Entity X through a shareholders' agreement. Which of the following correctly outlines the BO determination requirement for this client?
audio_script: Question 50. In evaluating a complex corporate group structure for Beneficial Ownership (BO) determination under the PML Rules, a company has three corporate layers holding shares. Entity X holds 28% shares in the client company, Entity Y holds 15% through a trust, and Entity Z holds 12% directly. Furthermore, an individual 'Mr. A' exercises ultimate effective control over Entity X through a shareholders' agreement. Which of the following correctly outlines the BO determination requirement for this client?
option_a: Mr. A must be identified as the Beneficial Owner based on control, but Entities X, Y, and Z need not be looked through because none individually holds more than the 25% statutory threshold for companies.
option_b: Only Entity X is the beneficial owner because it crosses the 25% shareholding threshold; Mr. A's control is irrelevant since he does not hold direct shares.
option_c: Beneficial ownership must include any individual holding controlling ownership interest (25% for companies, 15% for partnership/trusts) AND any individual exercising control through other means such as voting rights or management agreements (like Mr. A).
option_d: The bank is required to identify beneficial owners only if the aggregate foreign direct investment exceeds 50% of the company's total paid-up capital.
explanation: Under PML Rules (Rule 9(3)), beneficial ownership for a company includes a natural person who holds controlling ownership interest (25% or more shares/capital/profits) AND/OR who exercises control through other means (management control, voting rights, shareholder agreements). Mr. A qualifies via control, and threshold tracking applies as per rules.

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework in India
question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q032] Which of the following official documents is NOT classified among the officially valid documents (OVDs) under the PMLA for establishing identity?
audio_script: Question 32. Which of the following official documents is NOT classified among the officially valid documents (OVDs) under the PMLA for establishing identity?
option_a: Passport
option_b: Ration Card
option_c: Driving Licence
option_d: Voter's Identity Card
explanation: The 6 Officially Valid Documents (OVDs) under PMLA include: Passport, Driving Licence, Proof of possession of Aadhaar number, Voter's ID card, Job card issued by NREGA signed by a State Government officer, and Letter issued by the National Population Register containing details of name and address. Ration card is not a standalone OVD.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q075] A Compliance Officer is evaluating whether an individual qualifies as a Politically Exposed Person (PEP) under the RBI KYC guidelines. Which of the following categories of individuals is NOT classified under the definition of PEPs?
audio_script: Question 75. A Compliance Officer is evaluating whether an individual qualifies as a Politically Exposed Person (PEP) under the RBI KYC guidelines. Which of the following categories of individuals is NOT classified under the definition of PEPs?
option_a: Persons entrusted with prominent public functions by a foreign country, including heads of States or of Governments, senior politicians, and senior judicial officials.
option_b: Senior executives of state-owned corporations and important political party officials.
option_c: Middle-level administrative officers working in municipal corporations with standard clerical duties and no discretionary policy-making powers.
option_d: Senior government officials holding executive positions in defense and regulatory bodies.
explanation: PEPs are individuals who are or have been entrusted with prominent public functions in India or abroad, such as heads of States/Governments, senior politicians, senior government/judicial/military officers, senior executives of state-owned corporations, and important political party officials. Middle-level administrative officers with standard clerical duties do not meet this high-ranking threshold.

option_a: Instantly freeze all operations in the account permanently

option_c: Place partial freezing or restrictions on operations after giving adequate notice, ensuring the customer can still approach the bank to complete KYC
option_d: Transfer the account balance to the Reserve Bank of India
explanation: RBI guidelines specify that if a customer fails to submit KYC documents during periodic updates, banks can impose partial freezing (allowing only credits or restricting debits) after serving adequate notice, ensuring the account is not abruptly closed without recourse.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q023] Under the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 (as amended), what is the exact statutory timeline for banking institutions to maintain and preserve records of all cash transactions, international wire transfers, and identity documents (such as PAN, Aadhaar, or officially valid documents) from the date of cessation of the transaction or termination of the business relationship, respectively?
audio_script: Question 23. Under the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 (as amended), what is the exact statutory timeline for banking institutions to maintain and preserve records of all cash transactions, international wire transfers, and identity documents (such as PAN, Aadhaar, or officially valid documents) from the date of cessation of the transaction or termination of the business relationship, respectively?
option_a: A minimum of 2 years from the date of transaction and 3 years from business termination.
option_b: A minimum of 5 years from the date of transaction and 5 years after the business relationship has ended or account has been closed.
option_c: A minimum of 10 years from the date of transaction and 10 years after the business relationship has ended or account has been closed.
option_d: Indefinitely for all transactions exceeding INR 10 Lakhs, and 5 years for other accounts.
explanation: Rule 8 of the PML Rules, 2005 mandates that banks must maintain records of all prescribed transactions and customer identification records for a period of at least five years from the date of the transaction and from the date of cessation of the business relationship, respectively.

explanation: According to Section 12 of the PMLA, records pertaining to customer identification and transaction history must be maintained for a period of at least five years from the date of cessation of the business relationship between the client and the reporting entity.

audio_script: Question 92. While conducting transaction monitoring, a compliance officer observes that a newly onboarded non-resident corporate account is receiving high-value inward remittances from high-risk jurisdictions known for weak AML controls, which are immediately swept out to multiple beneficiary accounts in tax havens. explanation: Under Rule 7 and Rule 8 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, when transactions are identified as suspicious (such as rapid movement of funds to tax havens from high-risk jurisdictions), an STR must be filed with FIU-IND within 7 days of verifying the suspicion.

option_d: Value averaging

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q089] Under the institutional mechanism for implementing UNSCR 1988 regarding the Taliban sanctions regime, what is the primary obligation of a Scheduled Commercial Bank upon identifying a potential name match in its existing customer database?
audio_script: Question 89. Under the institutional mechanism for implementing UNSCR 1988 regarding the Taliban sanctions regime, what is the primary obligation of a Scheduled Commercial Bank upon identifying a potential name match in its existing customer database?
option_a: Freeze the account and notify the United Nations Security Council directly via email within 48 hours.
option_b: Halt all credit transactions, permit debit transactions for legal fees, and submit a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) to FIU-IND.
option_c: Verify the match against the updated list provided by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), freeze the assets immediately without prior notice, and communicate the action to the designated authority.
option_d: Seek approval from the bank's Board of Directors before applying any operational restrictions on the account.
explanation: Banks must cross-reference customer databases with the consolidated lists provided by the MHA implementing UNSCR 1267 and 1988, executing immediate asset freezing and reporting compliance without tipping off the customer.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q052] What is the statutory timeline prescribed under the PML Rules for reporting Cash Transaction Reports (CTR) by banks to the Financial Intelligence Unit - India (FIU-IND)?

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q047] Section 24 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, introduces the principle of 'Burden of Proof' in the context of trial of an offence of money-laundering. In this regard, which of the following statements correctly defines how the burden shifts between the prosecution and the accused?
audio_script: Question 47. Section 24 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, introduces the principle of 'Burden of Proof' in the context of trial of an offence of money-laundering. In this regard, which of the following statements correctly defines how the burden shifts between the prosecution and the accused?
option_a: The prosecution must conclusively prove beyond reasonable doubt that the property involved was acquired through scheduled offences before the accused is asked to provide any explanation.
option_b: In the case of any person charged with the offence of money-laundering under Section 3, the Authority or Court shall, unless the contrary is proved, presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money-laundering, and the burden of proving that they are not rests on the accused.
option_c: The burden of proof rests entirely on the FIU-IND to establish the nexus between the STR generated and the ultimate laundering activity without any legal presumptions.
option_d: The burden of proof applies strictly to banking institutions to prove that adequate CDD was performed, but does not shift to the accused individual regarding the source of wealth.
explanation: Section 24 of the PMLA mandates that when a person is charged with the offence of money-laundering, the Court or Adjudicating Authority shall, unless the contrary is proved, presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money-laundering, thereby shifting the burden of proving that they are untainted property onto the accused.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT07-Q099] A foreign branch of an Indian bank processes a cross-border wire transfer of USD 15,000 originating from a non-account holder. audio_script: Question 99. A foreign branch of an Indian bank processes a cross-border wire transfer of USD 15,000 originating from a non-account holder. Under the FATF Recommendation 16 and correspondent banking standards, if the intermediary or beneficiary financial institution identifies that the incoming wire transfer lacks required originator information (e.g., missing address or account number), what immediate course of action is prescribed?
option_a: Process the transaction immediately, credit the beneficiary account, and file a retrospective STR after 30 days if the customer complains.
option_b: Adopt risk-based policies for executing, rejecting, or suspending wire transfers lacking required originator or beneficiary information, and take appropriate follow-up action, which may include issuing a Request for Information (RFI) or freezing/rejecting the transfer.
option_c: Transfer the funds to the central bank's suspense account and liquidate the foreign exchange into local currency without notifying the originator bank.

explanation: Under FATF Recommendation 16, beneficiary financial institutions must have effective risk-based policies and procedures for determining when to execute, reject, or suspend a wire transfer lacking required originator or beneficiary information, and for taking appropriate follow-up action.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT08-Q052] Which of the following official documents is NOT included in the list of six Officially Valid Documents (OVDs) specified under Rule 2(1)(d) of the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules for individual KYC?
audio_script: Question 52. Which of the following official documents is NOT included in the list of six Officially Valid Documents (OVDs) specified under Rule 2(1)(d) of the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules for individual KYC?

question_text:
[AMLKYC-CBT08-Q047] In the context of legal proceedings under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, Section 24 deals with the 'Burden of Proof'. Evaluate the following propositions concerning how the burden shifts between the prosecution and the accused during a trial for money laundering:
1. Where any person is accused of an offense under Section 3, the burden of proving that proceeds of crime are untainted property shall lie upon the accused.
2. In proceedings relating to proceeds of crime seized or frozen under the Act, in the case of any other person claiming the property, the burden of proving that it is not tainted property lies squarely on the enforcement authorities.
3. The statutory presumption under Section 24 applies only after the prosecution discharges its initial burden of establishing a prima facie link between the accused and the property derived from a scheduled offense.

audio_script:
Question 47. In the context of legal proceedings under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, Section 24 deals with the 'Burden of Proof'. Evaluate the following propositions concerning how the burden shifts between the prosecution and the accused during a trial for money laundering:
1. Where any person is accused of an offense under Section 3, the burden of proving that proceeds of crime are untainted property shall lie upon the accused.
2. In proceedings relating to proceeds of crime seized or frozen under the Act, in the case of any other person claiming the property, the burden of proving that it is not tainted property lies squarely on the enforcement authorities.
3. The statutory presumption under Section 24 applies only after the prosecution discharges its initial burden of establishing a prima facie link between the accused and the property derived from a scheduled offense.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
option_a: 1 and 3 only
option_b: 1 only
option_c: 2 and 3 only
explanation: Statement 1 is true: under Section 24(a) of PMLA, the burden of proving that proceeds of crime are untainted property lies on the accused. Statement 3 is true as established by judicial interpretations (e.g., Vijay Madanlal Choudhary case), where the initial foundational facts regarding the scheduled offense and acquisition of property must be shown before reverse burden provisions fully apply. Statement 2 is incorrect because under Section 24(b), in the case of any other person claiming the property, the burden of proving that the property is not tainted property lies on such claimant, not on the enforcement authorities.

I. Gathering sufficient information about the respondent bank to fully understand the nature of its business and to determine from publicly available information the reputation of the bank and the quality of supervision.

audio_script:
Question 94. An Indian scheduled commercial bank is evaluating a correspondent banking relationship with a foreign respondent bank located in a high-risk jurisdiction. According to the RBI Master Directions on KYC and PMLA guidelines, which of the following due diligence requirements are mandatory before entering into or continuing such a relationship? 
I. Gathering sufficient information about the respondent bank to fully understand the nature of its business and to determine from publicly available information the reputation of the bank and the quality of supervision.
II. Assessing the respondent bank's Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) controls.
III. Obtaining approval from the Board of Directors or senior management prior to establishing new correspondent relationships.
IV. Ensuring that the respondent bank does not permit its accounts to be used by shell banks (Nested Correspondent Banking).

audio_script:
Question 72. Consider the following statements regarding the Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) and operational protocols for Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) under the Indian AML framework:
1. The definition of PEPs under RBI Master Directions includes individuals entrusted with prominent public functions by a foreign country, including heads of states/governments, senior politicians, senior government/judicial/military officers, and senior executives of state-owned corporations.
2. Family members and close associates of PEPs must be subjected to the same EDD measures as the PEP themselves, even if the account is held in the individual family member's name.
3. Once an individual ceases to be a PEP based on a risk-based assessment, the bank can immediately exempt the account from all transaction monitoring protocols without retaining historical tracking.
Which of the above statements are TRUE?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
option_d: 1, 2 and 3
explanation: Statement 1 is correct as it accurately reflects the FATF and RBI definition of PEPs. Statement 2 is correct because EDD measures applicable to PEPs also extend to their family members and close associates. Statement 3 is incorrect because even when a person is no longer a PEP, banks must continue to apply a risk-based approach, taking into account the continuing risk posed by the individual, and monitoring cannot simply be abandoned without a thorough risk evaluation.

[AMLKYC-CBT08-Q095] In the context of the FATF Travel Rule for cross-border and domestic wire transfers, which of the following statements regarding the required originator and beneficiary information is/are INCORRECT under the PMLA framework?
I. For cross-border wire transfers exceeding USD/EUR 1,000, the ordering financial institution must include accurate originator information (name, account number, and address) and beneficiary information.
II. Batch transfers containing cross-border wire transfers must contain required and accurate originator information, but individual beneficiary information is exempted if the batch file is routed through an FATF-compliant jurisdiction.
III. Intermediary financial institutions must ensure that all originator and beneficiary information accompanying a wire transfer is retained along with the transfer.
IV. Domestic wire transfers must always be accompanied by originator information such as name and account number, or a unique transaction reference number if an account number does not exist, which permits traceability back to the originator.
audio_script:
Question 95. In the context of the FATF Travel Rule for cross-border and domestic wire transfers, which of the following statements regarding the required originator and beneficiary information is/are INCORRECT under the PMLA framework?
I. For cross-border wire transfers exceeding USD/EUR 1,000, the ordering financial institution must include accurate originator information (name, account number, and address) and beneficiary information.
II. Batch transfers containing cross-border wire transfers must contain required and accurate originator information, but individual beneficiary information is exempted if the batch file is routed through an FATF-compliant jurisdiction.
III. Intermediary financial institutions must ensure that all originator and beneficiary information accompanying a wire transfer is retained along with the transfer.
IV. Domestic wire transfers must always be accompanied by originator information such as name and account number, or a unique transaction reference number if an account number does not exist, which permits traceability back to the originator.
option_a: II only
option_b: I and III only
option_c: I, II and IV only
option_d: II and III only
explanation: Statement II is incorrect because batch files containing cross-border wire transfers must contain required and accurate originator information AND fully validated beneficiary information; individual wire transfers within a batch cannot be exempted from carrying beneficiary details simply because of routing through compliant jurisdictions.

option_c: Take risk-based steps to either obtain the missing originator information before processing or execute a targeted query, and consider filing an STR if the lack of complete data points towards potential money laundering or sanctions evasion.
option_d: Convert the wire transfer into cash and require the beneficiary to clear KYC manually at the branch before crediting the account.
explanation: Under the FATF Travel Rule (Recommendation 16) and RBI guidelines, cross-border wire transfers must be accompanied by accurate and meaningful originator information. If mandatory information is missing, the beneficiary bank must exercise risk-based policies—which may include querying the ordering institution, restricting/rejecting the transfer, and filing an STR.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT08-Q097] Regarding Nested Correspondent Banking relationships, which of the following statements correctly articulates the compliance risks and mandatory safeguards required by the FATF and RBI guidelines?
audio_script: Question 97. Regarding Nested Correspondent Banking relationships, which of the following statements correctly articulates the compliance risks and mandatory safeguards required by the FATF and RBI guidelines?
option_a: Nested correspondent banking occurs when a respondent bank provides downstream correspondent services to other financial institutions using its own accounts with a correspondent bank. The primary risk is opacity, requiring the correspondent bank to verify that the respondent bank does not permit shell banks to use these nested services and that the respondent conducts due diligence on downstream users.
option_b: Nested correspondent banking is strictly prohibited under PMLA rules for all Authorized Dealer Category-I banks in India, and any indirect access granted to third-party financial institutions results in immediate license revocation.
option_c: Nested correspondent banking refers exclusively to vostro accounts held by foreign central banks, which require simplified due diligence (SDD) under all circumstances.
option_d: Nested correspondent accounts are permitted only when the downstream institution is domiciled in a Financial Action Task Force (FATF) member country, exempting the primary correspondent bank from monitoring transactions passing through the nested chain.
explanation: Nested correspondent banking involves a third-party financial institution using the correspondent banking relationship through the respondent bank's account. This introduces transparency risks. Correspondent banks must ensure that respondent banks screen downstream users and prohibit access to shell banks.

The client company is owned through a chain of intermediaries where a trust holds 15% voting shares, a partnership firm holds 12%, and an individual holds 11% beneficial interest through a closely-held foreign entity. audio_script: Question 50. A compliance officer at a foreign bank operating in India is analyzing a complex multi-layered corporate structure to determine Ultimate Beneficial Ownership (UBO) for a new corporate client seeking credit facilities. The client company is owned through a chain of intermediaries where a trust holds 15% voting shares, a partnership firm holds 12%, and an individual holds 11% beneficial interest through a closely-held foreign entity. Considering the RBI Master Direction on KYC thresholds for companies, trusts, and partnerships, which of the following analytical assertions regarding threshold identification is legally precise?
option_a: The threshold for identifying beneficial ownership in a company is 25%, in a partnership firm is 15%, and in a trust, it is the author, trustee, beneficiaries with 15% or more interest, and protector.
option_b: The threshold for identifying beneficial ownership in a company is 10%, in a partnership firm is 10%, and in a trust, it is any individual holding any controlling ownership interest.
option_c: The threshold for identifying beneficial ownership in a company is 25%, in a partnership firm is 15%, and in a trust, it is any beneficiary holding 10% or more interest.
option_d: Beneficial ownership rules apply exclusively to individual retail accounts; corporate entities are exempt from UBO tracing if they are listed on a recognized stock exchange.
explanation: According to the RBI Master Direction on KYC (which operationalizes PML Rules), for a company, the beneficial owner is the natural person(s) who, whether acting alone or together, or through one or more juridical person, has ownership of/entitlement to more than 25% of shares or capital or profits of the company. For a partnership firm, it is the natural person(s) who, whether acting alone or together, has ownership of/entitlement to more than 15% of capital or profits of the partnership. For a trust, the identification includes the author, the trustee, the protector, the beneficiaries with 15% or more interest in the trust, and any other natural person exercising ultimate effective control over the trust through a chain of control or ownership.

question_text:
[AMLKYC-CBT08-Q046] Under Section 5 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, the Director or any other officer not below the rank of Deputy Director (authorized by the Director) has the power to attach property involved in money laundering. Consider the following statements regarding the statutory conditions and timelines for provisional attachment:
1. The officer must have reason to believe (to be recorded in writing based on material in possession) that any person is in possession of any proceeds of crime and such proceeds of crime are likely to be concealed, transferred, or dealt with in any manner which may result in frustrating any proceedings relating to confiscation.
2. The provisional attachment order under Section 5(1) shall cease to have effect after the expiry of a period of 180 days from the date of the order or on the date an order is passed by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 8(3).
3. The provisional attachment order requires prior approval of a judicial magistrate of the first class before it is served upon the person in possession of the property.
Which of the statements given above are INCORRECT?
audio_script:
Question 46. Under Section 5 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, the Director or any other officer not below the rank of Deputy Director (authorized by the Director) has the power to attach property involved in money laundering. Consider the following statements regarding the statutory conditions and timelines for provisional attachment:
1. The officer must have reason to believe (to be recorded in writing based on material in possession) that any person is in possession of any proceeds of crime and such proceeds of crime are likely to be concealed, transferred, or dealt with in any manner which may result in frustrating any proceedings relating to confiscation.
2. The provisional attachment order under Section 5(1) shall cease to have effect after the expiry of a period of 180 days from the date of the order or on the date an order is passed by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 8(3).
3. The provisional attachment order requires prior approval of a judicial magistrate of the first class before it is served upon the person in possession of the property.
Which of the statements given above are INCORRECT?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 3 only
option_c: 2 and 3 only
explanation: Statement 3 is incorrect because a provisional attachment order under Section 5(1) of PMLA does NOT require prior approval of a judicial magistrate; it requires the recording of 'reasons to believe' in writing based on material in possession and can be issued directly by the authorized officer (not below Deputy Director), subject to subsequent confirmation by the Adjudicating Authority. Statements 1 and 2 are accurate reflections of Section 5(1) and Section 5(3) of the PMLA.

[AMLKYC-CBT08-Q021] The Wolfsberg Group Anti-Money Laundering Principles for Private Banking emphasize specific controls regarding Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs). Consider the following statements regarding PEP identification and account monitoring under these principles:
I. Private banks must establish a specific, automated or rigorous manual risk-based screening process to identify PEPs at the inception of the relationship and upon any material change in account ownership.

audio_script:
Question 21. The Wolfsberg Group Anti-Money Laundering Principles for Private Banking emphasize specific controls regarding Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs). Consider the following statements regarding PEP identification and account monitoring under these principles:
I. Private banks must establish a specific, automated or rigorous manual risk-based screening process to identify PEPs at the inception of the relationship and upon any material change in account ownership.
II. The decision to open or maintain an account for a PEP or their close associates (RAs) must always be escalated to and approved by business line management only, without mandatory involvement of compliance or senior management.
III. Private banks should conduct enhanced ongoing monitoring of PEP relationships, commensurate with the high risks associated with public officials and their wealth.
Which of the above statements are TRUE?
option_a: I and II only
option_b: II and III only
option_c: I and III only
option_d: I, II, and III
explanation: Statement I is true as Wolfsberg Principles require rigorous screening for PEPs. Statement III is true as enhanced ongoing monitoring is mandatory for PEPs. question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT08-Q049] An audit team reviewing a Tier-1 urban branch of a nationalized bank discovers that during an ongoing investigation by the Enforcement Directorate into a high-profile corporate fraud, the branch disposed of and destroyed physical account opening forms, customer ledger sheets, and inward wire transfer instructions relating to an account closed 4 years and 2 months ago. The branch manager argues that since the account was closed over 4 years ago and internal operational guidelines suggested archiving only for 3 years, the destruction was compliant. From an AML legal framework perspective, evaluate this action:
audio_script: Question 49. An audit team reviewing a Tier-1 urban branch of a nationalized bank discovers that during an ongoing investigation by the Enforcement Directorate into a high-profile corporate fraud, the branch disposed of and destroyed physical account opening forms, customer ledger sheets, and inward wire transfer instructions relating to an account closed 4 years and 2 months ago. The branch manager argues that since the account was closed over 4 years ago and internal operational guidelines suggested archiving only for 3 years, the destruction was compliant. From an AML legal framework perspective, evaluate this action:
option_a: The branch manager is fully protected since internal bank guidelines supersede statutory rules upon account closure.
option_b: The destruction constitutes a severe statutory violation under PMLA Rules and RBI directions because records must be retained for a minimum of 5 years post-account closure, and destruction during an active investigation may additionally attract obstruction of justice or tampering charges.
option_c: Destruction is permitted after 3 years under the Limitation Act for banking contracts.
option_d: The 5-year retention rule applies only to digital logs, whereas physical records can be shredded after 2 years.
explanation: Under the PML Rules, 2005, and RBI KYC Master Directions, the statutory obligation requires retention of records for at least 5 years following the termination of the business relationship (account closure). Disposing of records at 4 years and 2 months violates this mandate. Additionally, destroying documents while an investigation by law enforcement is active can lead to penal consequences under PMLA and criminal laws for destruction of evidence.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT08-Q096] A branch of a foreign bank in Mumbai detects a complex Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML) scheme involving an import transaction from an associate entity in a tax haven. The transaction involves massive over-invoicing of specialized industrial machinery accompanied by discrepancies between the bills of lading and shipping manifests, coupled with early settlement using low-cost trade finance facilities. Under RBI and FIU-IND guidelines, what is the primary regulatory and operational vulnerability exploited in this TBML typology, and what immediate action is mandated?
audio_script: Question 96. A branch of a foreign bank in Mumbai detects a complex Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML) scheme involving an import transaction from an associate entity in a tax haven. The transaction involves massive over-invoicing of specialized industrial machinery accompanied by discrepancies between the bills of lading and shipping manifests, coupled with early settlement using low-cost trade finance facilities. Under RBI and FIU-IND guidelines, what is the primary regulatory and operational vulnerability exploited in this TBML typology, and what immediate action is mandated?
option_a: The vulnerability is capital flight through legitimate customs channels; the bank must immediately execute a unilateral freeze on the importer's operating accounts under PMLA Section 12.
option_b: The vulnerability is the movement of value across international borders through price manipulation of goods; the bank must evaluate the commercial rationale, verify shipping documents rigorously, and file a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) with FIU-IND without notifying the customer.
option_c: The vulnerability is structured cash deposits used to fund LC margins; the bank must report the transaction as a Cash Transaction Report (CTR) within 7 working days.
option_d: The vulnerability is the abuse of nested correspondent accounts; the bank must report the foreign respondent bank to the Reserve Bank of India's Department of Banking Supervision while maintaining status quo on the local importer.
explanation: TBML relies heavily on misrepresentation of the quantity, value, or quality of imports/exports (over/under-invoicing) to transfer value illicitly. Banks are mandated to scrutinize trade transactions for economic rationale, reconcile trade documents, and file an STR with FIU-IND maintaining 'tipping-off' confidentiality.

Which of the following combinations of penalties can the Director legally impose on the banking company, its designated director, or its employees under Section 13(2)(d)?
audio_script: Question 45. An authorized branch of a scheduled commercial bank in Mumbai fails to maintain records of transactions and to furnish information to the Director, FIU-IND, as required under Section 12 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002. In an adjudication proceeding initiated under Section 13(2) of the PMLA, the Director, FIU-IND, intends to impose monetary penalties for the systemic failure. Which of the following combinations of penalties can the Director legally impose on the banking company, its designated director, or its employees under Section 13(2)(d)?
option_a: A penalty of not less than Rs. 10,000 but which may extend to Rs. 1 Lakh for each failure.
option_b: A penalty ranging from Rs. 1 Lakh to Rs. 1 Crore for each failure, depending on the gravity of the violation.
option_c: A fixed penalty of Rs. 5 Lakhs per branch irrespective of the number of non-compliant transactions.
option_d: Criminal imprisonment up to 3 years along with a mandatory forfeiture of the bank's operational license.
explanation: Under Section 13(2)(d) of the PMLA, 2002 (as amended), if the Director, FIU-IND, finds that a reporting entity or its designated director or any of its employees has failed to comply with the obligations under Section 12 (maintenance of records, furnishing of information), the Director may impose a monetary penalty of not less than ten thousand rupees but which may extend to one lakh rupees for each failure. Note: While Section 13(2)(a) through (d) outlines various disciplinary actions including warnings and directions to audit, the specific quantum of monetary penalty for Section 12 failures under the statutory framework ranges from Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 1 Lakh per failure.

In the context of international information exchange governed by the Egmont Group principles, which of the following protocols is INCORRECT regarding cross-border FIU-to-FIU intelligence sharing?
audio_script: Question 22. The Egmont Group of Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs) serves as the apex global network for enhancing cooperation and information exchange among national FIUs to combat money laundering and terrorist financing. In the context of international information exchange governed by the Egmont Group principles, which of the following protocols is INCORRECT regarding cross-border FIU-to-FIU intelligence sharing?
option_a: Information exchanged between FIUs can be used for administrative, investigative, or prosecutorial purposes without prior consent of the disclosing FIU.
option_b: Requests for information must be handled with the highest standards of confidentiality, matching or exceeding the domestic protections of the requesting and requested jurisdictions.
option_c: An FIU should not refuse to provide assistance to another FIU merely because the request is considered to involve fiscal matters such as tax evasion.
option_d: The information received from a foreign FIU cannot be transferred or disseminated to third-party law enforcement agencies without the prior explicit consent of the disclosing FIU.
explanation: According to Egmont Group principles for information exchange, information provided by one FIU to another cannot be used for administrative, investigative, or judicial purposes outside the scope specified in the original request, nor can it be disseminated to third parties without the prior express consent of the disclosing FIU. Therefore, statement A is incorrect because prior consent is strictly mandatory.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT08-Q023] A scheduled commercial bank in India receives an urgent order from the central government under Section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967, directing the immediate freezing of all accounts associated with an individual listed in the UNSC 1267 Consolidated Sanctions List. audio_script: Question 23. A scheduled commercial bank in India receives an urgent order from the central government under Section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967, directing the immediate freezing of all accounts associated with an individual listed in the UNSC 1267 Consolidated Sanctions List. Concurrently, the branch manager discovers that the designated individual has initiated an RTGS transfer out of the country just 10 minutes prior to the freezing order receipt. What is the precise statutory obligation of the Principal Officer under PMLA and UAPA guidelines?
option_a: Allow the transaction to clear since it was initiated before the physical receipt of the freezing order at the branch level.
option_b: Immediately block all funds, prevent any further debits or credits, notify the regulatory authorities and FIU-IND immediately regarding the attempted transaction and freeze action, without tipping off the customer.
option_c: Inform the account holder immediately via telephone about the impending freeze to comply with principles of natural justice before executing the freeze.
option_d: Reverse the transaction internally but transfer the balance to an unlisted nominee account controlled by the bank.
explanation: Under Section 51A of the UAPA and RBI guidelines on freezing orders, banks must immediately freeze funds of designated individuals/entities without prior notice (to prevent tipping off). Any attempted transactions post-receipt or ongoing matching triggers must be immediately reported to the FIU-IND and relevant national authorities while ensuring absolute confidentiality.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT08-Q048] As per Rule 10 of the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, read with the RBI Master Direction on KYC, what is the mandatory statutory timeline for which reporting entities must retain records pertaining to customer identification and transaction documents after the business relationship has ended or the account has been closed?
audio_script: Question 48. As per Rule 10 of the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, read with the RBI Master Direction on KYC, what is the mandatory statutory timeline for which reporting entities must retain records pertaining to customer identification and transaction documents after the business relationship has ended or the account has been closed?
option_a: At least 3 years from the date of closure of the account.
option_b: At least 5 years from the date of cessation of the transaction or termination of the business relationship.
option_c: At least 8 years from the date of the last transaction recorded in the account ledger.
option_d: Indefinitely, until explicit clearance is issued by the Enforcement Directorate and FIU-IND jointly.
explanation: Rule 10 of the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 mandates that reporting entities shall maintain all necessary records of transactions, both domestic and international, for at least five years from the date of transaction between the client and the reporting entity. Furthermore, records pertaining to the identification of the customer and their address (e.g., KYC documents) must be maintained for at least five years after the business relationship has ended or account has been closed, whichever is later.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT08-Q024] In accordance with the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and RBI Master Direction on KYC, what is the exact statutory timeline for maintaining records of all domestic and international cash transactions, including Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) and underlying customer identification documents, from the date of cessation of the transaction or termination of the business relationship?
audio_script: Question 24. In accordance with the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and RBI Master Direction on KYC, what is the exact statutory timeline for maintaining records of all domestic and international cash transactions, including Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) and underlying customer identification documents, from the date of cessation of the transaction or termination of the business relationship?
option_a: Minimum of 3 years from the date of transaction closure
option_b: Minimum of 5 years from the date of cessation of the business relationship or transaction
option_c: Minimum of 10 years from the date of cessation of the business relationship or transaction
option_d: Indefinitely until special clearance is received from the Supreme Court of India
explanation: As per Rule 3 and Rule 10 of the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and RBI instructions, banking companies are mandated to maintain records of all customer identification data, account files, and business correspondence, as well as records of transactions (both domestic and international), for a minimum period of 5 years. However, records pertaining to identification, CDD, and transactions relating to investigations must be retained for at least 10 years (often interpreted and mandated as 5 to 10 years depending on specific operational rules; specifically, Rule 10 mandates that records referred to in clause (f) of sub-rule (1) of rule 3—identity records—shall be maintained for not less than 5 years after the business relationship is ended, but RBI guidelines and PMLA amendments often mandate keeping transaction and KYC records for 5 to 10 years. Let's align with the standard PMLA Rule 10 which specifies 5 years, wait, let's verify standard IIBF question answers: PMLA specifies 'at least five years' under Rule 10(1), but many compliance manuals state 5 years after business ends. Let's double check if 5 years is the correct statutory minimum under PML Rules). Wait, PML Rules Rule 10 states: 'The records referred to in clause (a) of sub-rule (1) of rule 3 shall be maintained for a period of five years... and records referred to in clause (f) of sub-rule (1) of rule 3 shall be maintained for a period of five years after the business relationship has ended...' Therefore, the correct statutory period under PML Rules is 5 years.

audio_script: Question 24. A high-net-worth individual approaches a private banking branch seeking to open an account. During the due diligence process, the compliance officer discovers that the applicant is a close family member (spouse) of a politically exposed person (PEP) holding a senior ministerial office in a neighboring high-risk jurisdiction. Additionally, the applicant requests complete anonymity in all bank statements and intends to execute frequent, high-value wire transfers through shell companies. How should the compliance officer evaluate and manage this relationship under the RBI Master Direction on KYC and the Wolfsberg Private Banking Principles?
option_a: Reject the account outright because all PEP-related accounts with anonymity requests are strictly barred by criminal statute under Indian law.
option_b: Classify the account as High-Risk, subject it to Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD), obtain mandatory Senior Management approval, verify the explicit Source of Wealth and Source of Funds, and decline the request for anonymity.
option_c: Accept the account with simplified due diligence (SDD) since the applicant is a family member and not the primary PEP office holder.
option_d: Approve the account under a restricted internal code name to protect the privacy rights of the PEP family member while filing a daily CTR.
explanation: Under RBI guidelines and Wolfsberg Principles, PEPs and their family members/close associates automatically attract High-Risk classification. Banks must conduct Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD), obtain Senior Management approval before onboarding, meticulously establish the Source of Wealth and Source of Funds, and monitor transactions continuously. Anonymity requests violate basic KYC tenets and must be rejected.

audio_script: Question 97. A corporate client engaged in metal imports submits bills of lading and letters of credit to an authorized dealer bank. question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT09-Q072] A domestic corporate entity classified as a private limited company approaches a bank branch for credit facilities. The shareholding pattern reveals that an overseas entity incorporated in a high-risk jurisdiction holds 28% of the voting power, while three resident individuals hold 24% each. The Chief Compliance Officer is tasked with determining the Beneficial Owner (BO) for the purpose of applying Customer Due Diligence (CDD) under Rule 9 of the PML Rules. What is the precise statutory determination of the Beneficial Owner?
audio_script: Question 72. A domestic corporate entity classified as a private limited company approaches a bank branch for credit facilities. The shareholding pattern reveals that an overseas entity incorporated in a high-risk jurisdiction holds 28% of the voting power, while three resident individuals hold 24% each. The Chief Compliance Officer is tasked with determining the Beneficial Owner (BO) for the purpose of applying Customer Due Diligence (CDD) under Rule 9 of the PML Rules. What is the precise statutory determination of the Beneficial Owner?
option_a: The resident individual holding the highest single shareholding percentage (24%) because the corporate shareholding is below the 25% threshold.
option_b: The natural person(s) who holds a controlling ownership interest of not less than 25% of the shares or capital or profits of the juridical person, which in this case points to the overseas corporate entity, requiring the bank to look through to the natural persons controlling that entity.
option_c: Only the Managing Director and the statutory auditors of the private limited company, irrespective of shareholding thresholds.
option_d: No Beneficial Owner needs to be identified since no single natural person holds 50% or more of the voting rights.
explanation: Under Rule 9(3) of the PML Rules, for a company, the beneficial owner is the natural person(s) who, whether acting alone or together, or through one or more juridical person, has a controlling ownership interest of not less than 25%. Since the corporate entity holds 28%, the bank must look through the corporate structure to identify the natural person exercising control.

Upon reviewing its database, the compliance department discovers that the designated terrorist holds a joint savings account with a completely innocent family member, along with a sole proprietorship current account used for active business operations. option_a: Freeze only the portion of the joint account corresponding to the designated individual's proportionate financial contribution, while keeping the sole proprietorship account operational for trade.

audio_script: Question 20. An IIBF-certified compliance officer is evaluating a complex corporate structure involving a multi-layered offshore holding company registered in a tax haven, where an individual holds 18% of the voting shares directly, but through a series of covert shareholder agreements and discretionary trusts, effectively exercises dominant control over management decisions and profits. According to the Master Direction on KYC (RBI) read with the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, which of the following determinations regarding Beneficial Ownership (BO) is legally sound?
option_a: The individual is not a Beneficial Owner because the direct equity holding is below the mandatory 25% threshold for companies.
option_b: The individual qualifies as a Beneficial Owner under the 'control' criterion, regardless of the fact that the direct equity holding is 18%.
option_c: The offshore holding company itself must be registered as the sole Beneficial Owner since individual tracking is impossible across tax havens.
option_d: The individual only qualifies as a Beneficial Owner if they also serve as the statutory auditor or registered director of the entity.

The 'control' test operates independently of the percentage thresholds.

An Indian bank's trade finance department observes an import transaction where the description of goods on the commercial invoice is extremely vague ('General Industrial Machinery Parts'), the shipping route involves multiple unnecessary transshipments through high-risk secrecy jurisdictions, and the payment is routed through a third party unrelated to the bill of lading. option_b: Classify it as a high-risk Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML) red flag case requiring immediate filing of an internal Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) and potential freezing/withholding of document release pending FIU-IND guidance.

question_text:
[AMLKYC-CBT09-Q046] Consider the following statements regarding the statutory Burden of Proof under Section 24 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, in the context of an adjudication or trial involving an entity suspected of layering illicit funds through complex trade transactions:
I. In any proceeding relating to proceeds of crime under this Act, the authority or court shall, unless the contrary is proved, presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money laundering.
II. In the case of any other person charged with the offense of money laundering under Section 3, the burden of proving that the proceeds of crime are untainted property lies entirely on the prosecution and never shifts to the accused.
III. The statutory reversal of the burden of proof applies only after the FIU-IND establishes a prima facie case that the assets were acquired via scheduled offenses.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
audio_script:
Question 46. Consider the following statements regarding the statutory Burden of Proof under Section 24 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, in the context of an adjudication or trial involving an entity suspected of layering illicit funds through complex trade transactions:
I. In any proceeding relating to proceeds of crime under this Act, the authority or court shall, unless the contrary is proved, presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money laundering.
II. In the case of any other person charged with the offense of money laundering under Section 3, the burden of proving that the proceeds of crime are untainted property lies entirely on the prosecution and never shifts to the accused.
III. The statutory reversal of the burden of proof applies only after the FIU-IND establishes a prima facie case that the assets were acquired via scheduled offenses.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
option_a: I only
option_b: I and III only
option_c: II and III only
option_d: I, II, and III
explanation: Under Section 24(a) of the PMLA, in any proceedings relating to proceeds of crime, the court or authority shall, unless the contrary is proved, presume that such proceeds are involved in money laundering. Section 24(b) explicitly places the burden of proving that the proceeds of crime are untainted property on the *accused* person, not the prosecution, once proceedings under the Act have commenced.

audio_script: Question 15. Which of the following is NOT categorized as an 'Officially Valid Document' (OVD) for KYC purposes under the PML Rules?
option_a: Passport
option_b: Driving Licence
option_c: Ration Card issued by the State Government
option_d: Voter's Identity Card issued by the Election Commission of India
explanation: The 6 OVDs defined under the PMLA rules are: Passport, Driving Licence, proof of possession of Aadhaar number, Voter's Identity Card, job card issued by NREGA signed by a State Government officer, and letter issued by the National Population Register containing details of name and address. Ration cards are no longer recognized as standalone OVDs.

module: Module A: Anti-Money Laundering Overview
question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT09-Q014] An authorized reporting entity suspects that a series of complex, structured cash transactions conducted by a high-risk corporate client are linked to the proceeds of a scheduled offense under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002. As per the statutory mandate and FIU-IND guidelines, what is the exact timeline within which the Principal Officer of the reporting entity must furnish a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) to the Financial Intelligence Unit - India (FIU-IND) from the date of establishing suspicion?
audio_script: AMLKYC-CBT09-Q014. An authorized reporting entity suspects that a series of complex, structured cash transactions conducted by a high-risk corporate client are linked to the proceeds of a scheduled offense under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002. As per the statutory mandate and FIU-IND guidelines, what is the exact timeline within which the Principal Officer of the reporting entity must furnish a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) to the Financial Intelligence Unit - India (FIU-IND) from the date of establishing suspicion?
option_a: Within 7 working days of establishing suspicion
option_b: Within 3 working days of establishing suspicion
option_c: Within 15 days from the close of the relevant month
option_d: Within 30 days of the transaction date
explanation: According to the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and FIU-IND guidelines, Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) must be furnished strictly within 7 working days of arriving at a conclusion that the transactions are suspicious. (Note: Cash Transaction Reports (CTRs) and Cross Border Wire Transfer Reports (CBWTRs) are required to be submitted by the 15th day of the succeeding month).

module: Module A: Anti-Money Laundering Overview
question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT09-Q023] An exhaustive audit of an Authorised Dealer (AD) Category-I bank branch reveals systemic failures in reporting transactions under the PMLA framework. Specifically, the branch failed to report 15 instances of suspicious transactions involving complex cross-border wire transfers and trade-based trade misinvoicing, despite internal alerts generated by the transaction monitoring system. According to the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 and FIU-IND directives, within what exact timeframe must a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) be filed by a banking institution from the date of initial detection of suspicion by the Principal Officer?
audio_script: Question 23. An exhaustive audit of an Authorised Dealer (AD) Category-I bank branch reveals systemic failures in reporting transactions under the PMLA framework. Specifically, the branch failed to report 15 instances of suspicious transactions involving complex cross-border wire transfers and trade-based trade misinvoicing, despite internal alerts generated by the transaction monitoring system. According to the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 and FIU-IND directives, within what exact timeframe must a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) be filed by a banking institution from the date of initial detection of suspicion by the Principal Officer?
option_a: Within 7 working days from the date of occurrence of the transaction
option_b: Within 7 working days from the date of establishing suspicion by the Principal Officer
option_c: Within 3 working days from the date of establishing suspicion by the Principal Officer
option_d: Within 30 calendar days from the close of the respective month
explanation: As per the PML Rules (Rule 8), the Principal Officer of a banking company must furnish a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) to the Director, FIU-IND, not later than 7 working days from the date of establishing that the transaction is suspicious. The timeline begins from the date the suspicion is formally established by the bank's Principal Officer/AML team, not the date of the transaction.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT09-Q074] An Indian bank receives an updated consolidated list of individuals and entities subject to sanctions under Section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967. The compliance unit runs a batch matching algorithm against the bank's entire customer database. A tentative 'false positive' match occurs for a savings bank account holding INR 15 lakhs. What is the precise statutory obligation and protocol the bank must execute pursuant to the order of the Central Government and RBI guidelines?
audio_script: Question 74. An Indian bank receives an updated consolidated list of individuals and entities subject to sanctions under Section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967. The compliance unit runs a batch matching algorithm against the bank's entire customer database. A tentative 'false positive' match occurs for a savings bank account holding INR 15 lakhs. What is the precise statutory obligation and protocol the bank must execute pursuant to the order of the Central Government and RBI guidelines?
option_a: Immediately freeze the funds/financial assets without delay and without prior notice to the customer, and simultaneously submit a detailed report to the Central Nodal Officer (UAPA) and the FIU-IND.
option_b: Wait for the customer to initiate a transaction before freezing the account, and allow withdrawals up to INR 50,000 pending confirmation.
option_c: Notify the customer via registered post giving 14 days' time to prove that they are not the designated individual before initiating any freeze action.
option_d: Report the matter exclusively to local law enforcement police stations while keeping the account fully operational for normal banking transactions.
explanation: Under Section 51A of the UAPA and RBI guidelines, banks must ensure immediate freezing of funds, financial assets, or economic resources of designated individuals/entities without prior notice, followed by prompt reporting to the designated authorities.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT09-Q007] Which stage of money laundering is considered the most vulnerable for law enforcement agencies because physical cash is introduced into the regulated financial system?
audio_script: Question 7. Which stage of money laundering is considered the most vulnerable for law enforcement agencies because physical cash is introduced into the regulated financial system?
option_a: Placement
option_b: Layering
option_c: Integration
option_d: Consolidation
explanation: Placement is the initial stage where illicit cash is first introduced into the financial system (e.g., deposited into bank accounts). Because large amounts of physical cash are handled here, it leaves a paper trail and is the most vulnerable point for detection.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT09-Q049] An internal AML investigator identifies a complex web of transactions involving a shell company account where funds are rapidly transferred across multiple accounts within the same bank on the same day just below the cash transaction reporting threshold, followed by outward international wire transfers. The Principal Officer decides to file an STR. Under Section 14 of the PMLA, 2002, and related statutory protections, which of the following legal protections is explicitly guaranteed to the bank, its directors, and its employees?
audio_script: Question 49. An internal AML investigator identifies a complex web of transactions involving a shell company account where funds are rapidly transferred across multiple accounts within the same bank on the same day just below the cash transaction reporting threshold, followed by outward international wire transfers. The Principal Officer decides to file an STR. Under Section 14 of the PMLA, 2002, and related statutory protections, which of the following legal protections is explicitly guaranteed to the bank, its directors, and its employees?
option_a: Complete immunity from civil and criminal proceedings for furnishing information in good faith to the FIU-IND, even if the suspicion ultimately proves unfounded.
option_b: Indemnity from the Reserve Bank of India against any liquidity shortages arising from the freezing of the accounts under investigation.
option_c: Automatic waiver of all corporate tax liabilities for the financial year in which the STR was generated.
option_d: Exemption from conducting subsequent annual KYC updates for any account associated with the reported entity.
explanation: Section 14 of the PMLA, 2002, provides that no suit, prosecution, or other legal proceeding shall lie against any reporting entity, its directors, officers, or employees for furnishing information in good faith to the Director (FIU-IND) in compliance with STR filing obligations, protecting them even if the suspicion turns out to be incorrect.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT09-Q047] The Director, FIU-IND, conducts an inspection of a reporting entity (a major commercial bank) under Section 13 of the PMLA, 2002, and discovers systemic failures in maintaining prescribed client records and filing timely Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs). The Director imposes a monetary penalty on the reporting entity and its Principal Officer. Which of the following represents the statutory maximum penalty limits and appellate framework governing such an order under Section 13?
audio_script: Question 47. The Director, FIU-IND, conducts an inspection of a reporting entity (a major commercial bank) under Section 13 of the PMLA, 2002, and discovers systemic failures in maintaining prescribed client records and filing timely Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs). The Director imposes a monetary penalty on the reporting entity and its Principal Officer. Which of the following represents the statutory maximum penalty limits and appellate framework governing such an order under Section 13?
option_a: Maximum penalty of up to Rs. 1,00,000 for each failure, appealable directly to the Supreme Court of India within 30 days.
option_b: Penalty ranging from Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 1,00,000 for each failure, appealable to the PMLA Appellate Tribunal established under Section 25 within 45 days.
option_c: Up to 10% of the total assets of the bank, appealable exclusively to the Reserve Bank of India Board for Financial Supervision.
option_d: A fixed penalty of Rs. 5,00,000 per branch, appealable to the High Court having jurisdiction over the registered office.
explanation: Under Section 13(2)(d) of the PMLA, 2002, the Director, FIU-IND, may impose a monetary penalty not less than ten thousand rupees but may extend to one lakh rupees for each failure (amended periodically via notifications, but historically and structurally categorized under Section 13 penalties). Appeals against orders of the Director lie with the Appellate Tribunal (PMLA) constituted under Section 25 within the statutory 45-day window.

module: Module C: KYC Standards, Identification & CDD
question_text:
[AMLKYC-CBT09-Q071] Consider the following statements regarding the Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR) operational guidelines and uploading obligations under the Prevention of Money-laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules:
1. Reporting Entities (REs) must upload the KYC data of the customer onto the CKYCR portal within 10 days of completing the account opening/KYC process.
2. Upon successful upload and validation, the CKYCR generates a unique 14-digit CKYC Identifier (CKYRIN) which must be communicated to the customer.
3. If a customer approaches a different Reporting Entity and quotes their 14-digit CKYRIN, the new RE can fetch the KYC records directly from the CKYCR, eliminating the need to collect fresh KYC documents unless there is a change in customer information.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
audio_script:
Question 71. Consider the following statements regarding the Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR) operational guidelines and uploading obligations under the Prevention of Money-laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules:
1. Reporting Entities (REs) must upload the KYC data of the customer onto the CKYCR portal within 10 days of completing the account opening/KYC process.
2. Upon successful upload and validation, the CKYCR generates a unique 14-digit CKYC Identifier (CKYRIN) which must be communicated to the customer.
3. If a customer approaches a different Reporting Entity and quotes their 14-digit CKYRIN, the new RE can fetch the KYC records directly from the CKYCR, eliminating the need to collect fresh KYC documents unless there is a change in customer information.
Which of the statements given above are TRUE?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
explanation: All three statements are accurate. REs are mandated to upload KYC records to CKYCR within 10 days of the customer onboarding process. The registry issues a unique 14-digit CKYRIN, which facilitates seamless retrieval of KYC data by other REs, preventing repetitive documentation.

Under RBI Master Directions on KYC and PML Rules, which combination of due diligence measures is MANDATORY before establishing or continuing this relationship?
audio_script: Question 94. An Indian authorized dealer bank maintains a correspondent banking relationship with a foreign respondent bank in a high-risk jurisdiction. Under RBI Master Directions on KYC and PML Rules, which combination of due diligence measures is MANDATORY before establishing or continuing this relationship?
option_a: Obtaining approval from Senior Management, assessing the respondent bank's AML/CFT controls, ensuring the respondent does not permit its accounts to be used by shell banks, and verifying that the respondent performs KYC on direct customers.
option_b: Obtaining approval only from the branch manager, securing a copy of the foreign bank's annual report, and verifying their physical presence in the home jurisdiction without evaluating their AML control systems.
option_c: Filing a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) immediately upon onboarding, regardless of risk assessment, and executing a reciprocal nostro account agreement.
option_d: Conducting EDD only if the respondent bank processes cross-border wire transfers exceeding USD 10,000 equivalent daily.
explanation: Per RBI Master Directions on KYC and FATF standards for correspondent banking, covered banks must gather sufficient information on a respondent bank to understand fully the nature of the business, determine from publicly available information the reputation of the institution and the quality of supervision, assess the respondent's AML/CFT controls, obtain approval from senior management before establishing new relationships, and clearly understand respective responsibilities of each institution under the AML/CFT framework, specifically ensuring no accounts are provided to shell banks.
