question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT09-Q045] An authorized branch of a scheduled commercial bank receives an order for the attachment of property under Section 5 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, issued by the Director, FIU-IND or an authorized officer not below the rank of Deputy Director. The order indicates that the property is 'proceeds of crime'. The branch manager finds that the affected account holder has initiated immediate legal proceedings in the High Court challenging the provisional attachment order and demands that the bank permit normal operational debits pending the litigation. What is the statutory validity and correct operational stance the bank must take regarding the attachment under PMLA provisions?
audio_script: Question 45. An authorized branch of a scheduled commercial bank receives an order for the attachment of property under Section 5 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, issued by the Director, FIU-IND or an authorized officer not below the rank of Deputy Director. The order indicates that the property is 'proceeds of crime'. The branch manager finds that the affected account holder has initiated immediate legal proceedings in the High Court challenging the provisional attachment order and demands that the bank permit normal operational debits pending the litigation. What is the statutory validity and correct operational stance the bank must take regarding the attachment under PMLA provisions?
option_a: The bank must immediately freeze all debits up to the value specified in the provisional attachment order for a maximum statutory validity period of 180 days, irrespective of ongoing litigation, unless stayed by the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal.
option_b: The bank is legally obligated to lift the freeze upon receipt of a notice of writ petition from the account holder, as provisional attachment orders under Section 5 automatically abate upon judicial challenge.
option_c: The bank can permit debits if the account holder provides a third-party corporate guarantee equivalent to 150% of the attached balance.
option_d: The provisional attachment order issued under Section 5 lapses automatically after 30 days unless ratified by the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India.
explanation: Under Section 5(1) of the PMLA, 2002, the Director or designated officers can provisionally attach property for a period not exceeding 180 days if there is reason to believe that such property is proceeds of crime. The bank is legally mandated to maintain the freeze during this period unless the Adjudicating Authority under Section 8 or the Appellate Tribunal orders otherwise.

FATF calls on all members to apply Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD), and in the most serious cases, counter-measures to protect the international financial system.

audio_script: Question 50. A corporate client structured as a private limited company applies for credit facilities. During the Beneficial Ownership (BO) determination as per the Master Direction on KYC, the bank discovers that three different individual shareholders hold 12%, 11%, and 9% of the shares respectively, with no single individual holding 10% or more (the statutory threshold for companies). However, internal monitoring flags that these three individuals are close family members acting in concert through a formal voting agreement, collectively controlling 32% of the voting rights and exercising ultimate effective control through senior management positions. What is the correct compliance determination for identifying the Beneficial Owner under the PML Rules?
option_a: Since no single individual crosses the 10% statutory shareholding threshold, the company has no beneficial owner, and the bank must record the Managing Director as the default BO.
option_b: The natural persons exercising ultimate effective control through voting rights and senior management positions must be identified as beneficial owners, looking through the shareholding percentage threshold rule.
option_c: The bank must reject the account outright because family members acting in concert violate corporate governance laws.
option_d: The bank is only required to verify the identity of the shareholder holding the highest individual percentage (12%).
explanation: According to Rule 9(3) of the PML Rules and RBI Master Directions on KYC, the definition of Beneficial Owner includes the natural person who, whether acting alone or together, or through one or more juridical persons, exercises ultimate effective control over the juridical person through ownership, voting rights, or other means. Senior management and persons exercising control via voting agreements must be identified when specific ownership thresholds are not met by individuals alone.

audio_script: Question 25. A compliance officer is conducting an annual regulatory review of record retention and aggregation protocols at a major bank branch. The branch deals with Cash Transaction Reports (CTRs), Cross-Border Wire Transfer Reports (CBWTRs), and standard customer KYC records. Which of the following statements regarding statutory record maintenance timelines under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002 and PML Rules is entirely INCORRECT?
option_a: Records of all cash transactions (CTRs) must be maintained for a period of at least five years from the date of the transaction.
option_b: Records pertaining to the identification of customers (CDD documents, PAN, address proofs) and account files must be maintained for at least five years after the business relationship has ended or the account has been closed.
option_c: All records relating to Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) and underlying correspondence must be destroyed exactly three years after filing to protect customer privacy.
option_d: Where a civil or criminal proceeding or investigation by an authority (such as FIU-IND or CBI) is pending, records must be retained beyond the standard five-year window until the matter attains final judicial closure.
explanation: Statement C is INCORRECT because destroying STR records after three years violates regulatory requirements. Under PML Rules, records relating to STRs, customer identification, and transaction documents must be retained for at least 5 years (and often preserved longer if ongoing legal/regulatory investigations or proceedings require them). They cannot be destroyed prematurely.

audio_script: Question 95. A correspondent bank in Mumbai discovers that its foreign respondent bank in an offshore financial center provides 'nested correspondent banking' services to several downstream respondent banks whose identities are not fully disclosed to the Mumbai bank. Considering RBI guidelines and PML Rules on tiered relationships, how must the compliance officer evaluate this risk?
option_a: Nested relationships are implicitly prohibited for all foreign respondents; the bank must immediately terminate the main correspondent relationship without notice.
option_b: The bank must require the foreign respondent to demonstrate that it has performed appropriate due diligence and applied ongoing monitoring to downstream institutions that have direct access to the correspondent account, and that it can provide relevant customer identification data upon request.
option_c: Nested relationships do not require additional scrutiny provided the aggregate transaction volume remains within the pre-approved bilateral credit limit.
option_d: The compliance officer should bypass the foreign respondent and conduct direct onsite inspections of all downstream respondent banks in their home jurisdictions.
explanation: According to RBI guidelines and international AML standards regarding correspondent banking, when nested relationships (where a customer bank uses the correspondent's account through the respondent bank) exist, the correspondent bank must satisfy itself that the respondent bank has verified the identity of and performed ongoing due diligence on the customers having direct access to the accounts of the correspondent bank and that it is able to provide relevant customer identification data upon request to the correspondent bank.

question_text:
[AMLKYC-CBT09-Q098] Consider the following statements regarding the application of the FATF Travel Rule to domestic versus cross-border wire transfers under the Indian PMLA framework:
I. For cross-border wire transfers, ordering financial institutions must ensure that the message or instruction contains accurate and meaningful originator and beneficiary information.
II. For domestic wire transfers, the ordering institution is exempt from including originator information if the transfer is below INR 50,000.
III. Domestic wire transfers must be accompanied by originator information such as name and account number, or a unique transaction reference number, which must be made available to the beneficiary institution and appropriate authorities.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
audio_script:
Question 98. Consider the following statements regarding the application of the FATF Travel Rule to domestic versus cross-border wire transfers under the Indian PMLA framework:
I. For cross-border wire transfers, ordering financial institutions must ensure that the message or instruction contains accurate and meaningful originator and beneficiary information.
II. For domestic wire transfers, the ordering institution is exempt from including originator information if the transfer is below INR 50,000.
III. Domestic wire transfers must be accompanied by originator information such as name and account number, or a unique transaction reference number, which must be made available to the beneficiary institution and appropriate authorities.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
option_a: I and II only
option_b: I and III only
option_c: II and III only
option_d: I, II, and III
explanation: Statement I is true as cross-border transfers strictly require full originator and beneficiary details. Statement II is incorrect because even for domestic wire transfers, complete originator information must accompany the wire, or be made available via other means if batch transfers are used; complete exemption is not permitted. Statement III is true as domestic transfers must carry originator information (name, account number/unique reference) that is readily accessible to beneficiary institutions and law enforcement.

question_text:
[AMLKYC-CBT09-Q021] Consider the following statements regarding the global anti-money laundering regulatory ecosystem and international standard-setting bodies: 
1. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) issued consolidated 'Customer Due Diligence for Banks' guidelines requiring banks to adopt robust risk-based acceptance policies, explicitly prohibiting anonymous accounts or accounts in fictitious names.
2. The Wolfsberg Group Anti-Money Laundering Principles for Private Banking mandate that private banks must obtain senior management approval for establishing relationships with High-Risk Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) and must establish the source of wealth.
3. The Egmont Group of Financial Intelligence Units serves as the operational clearinghouse for international cooperation, facilitating secure information exchange regarding suspicious transactions through the Egmont Secure Web.
Which of the above statements are TRUE?
audio_script:
Question 21. Consider the following statements regarding the global anti-money laundering regulatory ecosystem and international standard-setting bodies: 
1. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) issued consolidated 'Customer Due Diligence for Banks' guidelines requiring banks to adopt robust risk-based acceptance policies, explicitly prohibiting anonymous accounts or accounts in fictitious names.
2. The Wolfsberg Group Anti-Money Laundering Principles for Private Banking mandate that private banks must obtain senior management approval for establishing relationships with High-Risk Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) and must establish the source of wealth.
3. The Egmont Group of Financial Intelligence Units serves as the operational clearinghouse for international cooperation, facilitating secure information exchange regarding suspicious transactions through the Egmont Secure Web.
Which of the above statements are TRUE?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
explanation: All three statements are accurate representations of the international AML architecture. BCBS guidelines strictly prohibit anonymous/fictitious accounts and mandate comprehensive CDD. Wolfsberg AML Principles for Private Banking specifically require enhanced due diligence, source of wealth verification, and senior management sign-off for PEP relationships. The Egmont Group facilitates secure operational intelligence sharing among global FIUs via the Egmont Secure Web.

audio_script: Question 100. In the context of correspondent banking relationships, what specific statutory duty is imposed on an Indian bank regarding 'payable-through accounts' maintained for foreign respondent banks?
option_a: The bank must ensure that the respondent bank has verified the identity of and performed ongoing due diligence on customers that have direct access to the accounts of the respondent bank and is able to provide relevant customer identification data upon request.
option_b: The bank must guarantee all trade credit facilities extended by the respondent bank to retail clients.
option_c: The bank is permitted to bypass KYC checks for retail end-users as long as the respondent bank is domiciled in a FATF-compliant jurisdiction.
option_d: Payable-through accounts are legally prohibited under Section 12 of the PMLA without prior cabinet approval.
explanation: Under RBI Master Directions on KYC and FATF recommendations governing correspondent banking, where 'payable-through accounts' (where customers of the respondent bank use the correspondent bank's account directly) are used, the respondent bank must satisfy itself that the respondent has performed KYC on direct users, maintains ongoing due diligence, and can supply KYC data to the correspondent bank upon demand.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT10-Q046] A scheduled commercial bank's compliance officer receives an attachment order under Section 5 of the PMLA, 2002, issued by the Deputy Director, freezing an operating current account held by a corporate entity suspected of generating proceeds of crime through trade-based invoicing irregularities. audio_script: Question 46. A scheduled commercial bank's compliance officer receives an attachment order under Section 5 of the PMLA, 2002, issued by the Deputy Director, freezing an operating current account held by a corporate entity suspected of generating proceeds of crime through trade-based invoicing irregularities. The corporate entity challenges the bank's compliance, stating that the order exceeds the statutory maximum provisional attachment period. Under Section 5(1) of the PMLA, what is the maximum validity period of an initial provisional attachment order before it must be confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority?
option_a: 60 days from the date of the order
option_b: 90 days from the date of the order
option_c: 180 days from the date of the order
option_d: 365 days from the date of the order
explanation: As per Section 5(1) of the PMLA, 2002, no provisional attachment of property can be made unless a complaint has been filed under Section 5 or Section 16, or an application has been filed before a court. The initial period of provisional attachment under Section 5(1) is restricted to a maximum period of 180 days from the date of the order, subject to confirmation by the Adjudicating Authority within this timeframe.

question_text:
[AMLKYC-CBT10-Q022] The Wolfsberg Group Anti-Money Laundering Principles for Private Banking establish rigorous benchmarks for managing high-net-worth clients, particularly Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs). Consider the following statements regarding PEP acceptance and account monitoring under Wolfsberg standards and RBI guidelines:
I. Approval for establishing a business relationship with a PEP must be obtained from senior management, defined as at least one level higher than the relationship manager.
II. The source of wealth and source of funds must be established and documented for all PEP relationships, not merely their initial deposits.
III. Domestic PEPs are categorically exempt from enhanced due diligence (EDD) unless they exhibit specific transaction red flags.
Which of the statements given above is/are TRUE?
audio_script:
Question 22. The Wolfsberg Group Anti-Money Laundering Principles for Private Banking establish rigorous benchmarks for managing high-net-worth clients, particularly Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs). Consider the following statements regarding PEP acceptance and account monitoring under Wolfsberg standards and RBI guidelines:
I. Approval for establishing a business relationship with a PEP must be obtained from senior management, defined as at least one level higher than the relationship manager.
II. The source of wealth and source of funds must be established and documented for all PEP relationships, not merely their initial deposits.
III. Domestic PEPs are categorically exempt from enhanced due diligence (EDD) unless they exhibit specific transaction red flags.
Which of the statements given above is/are TRUE?
option_a: I only
option_b: I and II only
option_c: II and III only
option_d: I, II, and III
explanation: Statement I is true (senior management approval is mandatory for PEPs under Wolfsberg and RBI rules). Statement II is true (establishing source of wealth and funds is a core Wolfsberg requirement for private banking PEPs). Statement III is incorrect because RBI Master Directions on KYC apply EDD measures to all PEPs (whether domestic or foreign), though risk-based categorisation determines the intensity.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT10-Q075] A senior compliance officer is analyzing a case where a customer, classified as high-risk due to involvement in international trading through shell-like structures, has been identified as a PEP. The branch has failed to obtain senior management approval prior to onboarding, and records show that the enhanced due diligence was superficial. audio_script: Question 75. A senior compliance officer is analyzing a case where a customer, classified as high-risk due to involvement in international trading through shell-like structures, has been identified as a PEP. The branch has failed to obtain senior management approval prior to onboarding, and records show that the enhanced due diligence was superficial. Under the PMLA and RBI Master Directions, what are the primary regulatory ramifications of this compliance lapse?
option_a: The bank is immune to penalties if the customer maintains a positive net balance and no STR has been generated by the FIU-IND.
option_b: The bank faces severe regulatory penalties for non-compliance with CDD and PEP protocols, potential enforcement actions under Section 13 of the PMLA for failure to maintain records and verify identity, and severe reputational damage.
option_c: The account is automatically regularized after 180 days if no suspicious transactions are reported during that period.
option_d: The liability falls exclusively on the customer, and the bank's license cannot be touched for internal procedural oversights.
explanation: Failure to adhere to mandatory KYC/AML prescriptions such as obtaining senior management approval for PEPs and conducting proper EDD represents a critical regulatory breach under the RBI Master Direction on KYC and Section 13 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), which empowers the Director of FIU-IND to impose monetary penalties, issue warnings, or direct audits for compliance failures.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT10-Q049] A designated branch receives a complex web of transactions involving a Politically Exposed Person (PEP) from a high-risk jurisdiction. The compliance department fails to conduct enhanced due diligence (EDD), and subsequent investigations by law enforcement reveal that the transactions violated UAPA Section 51A freezing mandates. The Principal Officer and the Compliance Head face regulatory scrutiny. Which of the following correctly outlines the reporting entity's obligations under Rule 8 and Rule 9 of the PML Rules regarding PEPs and UAPA implementation?
audio_script: Question 49. A designated branch receives a complex web of transactions involving a Politically Exposed Person (PEP) from a high-risk jurisdiction. The compliance department fails to conduct enhanced due diligence (EDD), and subsequent investigations by law enforcement reveal that the transactions violated UAPA Section 51A freezing mandates. The Principal Officer and the Compliance Head face regulatory scrutiny. Which of the following correctly outlines the reporting entity's obligations under Rule 8 and Rule 9 of the PML Rules regarding PEPs and UAPA implementation?
option_a: PEPs require senior management approval only at the time of onboarding; ongoing monitoring is optional under risk-based approaches.
option_b: Reporting entities must obtain senior management approval for establishing business relationships with PEPs, take reasonable measures to establish the source of wealth/funds, and maintain strict ongoing monitoring independent of standard customer risk categories.
option_c: UAPA Section 51A asset freezing mandates supersede PEP rules, allowing banks to bypass standard KYC verification if funds originate from foreign diplomatic channels.
option_d: The Principal Officer must report PEP accounts directly to the Reserve Bank of India within 24 hours of opening, irrespective of transaction activity.
explanation: Under the PML Rules and RBI Master Direction on KYC, reporting entities must formulate risk management policies to identify PEPs. This requires: (i) obtaining senior management approval prior to establishing relationships with PEPs; (ii) taking reasonable measures to establish the source of wealth and funds; and (iii) conducting enhanced ongoing monitoring of the business relationship. UAPA Section 51A mandates prompt freezing without prior notice, which operates in tandem with AML/KYC frameworks.

option_b: By complying strictly with international customs valuation standards

audio_script: Question 99. In the context of Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML) typologies, which combination of red flags observed during a documentary letter of credit transaction warrants immediate escalation and filing of a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR)?
option_a: Commodity description in the bill of lading matches the invoice precisely; shipment originates from a low-risk OECD nation.
option_b: Significant discrepancy between the declared weight of goods and the vessel's carrying capacity; routing through unassociated third-party jurisdictions; and description of goods is overly complex or vague (e.g., 'general chemical compounds').
option_c: Payment made via irrevocable letter of credit confirmed by a top-tier international prime bank.
option_d: Shipping documents presented well within the stipulated presentation period under UCP 600.
explanation: Weight discrepancies, circuitous routing via unrelated third-party countries, and vague commodity descriptions are textbook red flags for TBML schemes such as phantom shipping, short-shipping, or misrepresentation of goods.

option_a: Under-invoicing; intended to generate illicit capital flight and smuggle contraband.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT10-Q045] Under Section 13 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, the Director, FIU-IND possesses the authority to impose monetary penalties on a reporting entity (RE) or its designated director for failure to comply with obligations under Section 12. Consider the following statements regarding these powers: 1. The Director, FIU-IND can levy a fine ranging from not less than ten thousand rupees up to one lakh rupees for each failure. 2. The Director may issue a warning, direct the RE to comply with specific instructions, or send a designated officer to audit the RE. 3. audio_script: Question 45. Under Section 13 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, the Director, FIU-IND possesses the authority to impose monetary penalties on a reporting entity (RE) or its designated director for failure to comply with obligations under Section 12. Consider the following statements regarding these powers: 1. The Director, FIU-IND can levy a fine ranging from not less than ten thousand rupees up to one lakh rupees for each failure. 2. The Director may issue a warning, direct the RE to comply with specific instructions, or send a designated officer to audit the RE. 3. The compounding of offenses under Section 13 cannot be undertaken by the Director, FIU-IND, as it requires exclusive sanction from a Special Court. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 only
option_c: 1 and 3 only
option_d: 1, 2 and 3
explanation: Under Section 13(2) of the PMLA, 2002, the Director, FIU-IND may, on inquiry, impose a penalty for failure to comply with Section 12 obligations which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees but may extend to one lakh rupees for each failure. Statement 2 is correct as the Director can issue warnings, direct compliance, or order audits. Statement 3 is incorrect because the Director, FIU-IND is empowered to impose monetary penalties directly; criminal prosecution and compounding before Special Courts operate via different statutory pathways under Section 45/Section 44.

audio_script: Question 98. An Indian bank is analyzing an outward wire transfer transaction to detect potential sanctions evasion. The intermediary bank receives a message where the originator's physical address has been deliberately omitted and replaced with a generic country name, although the account number is present. How should the beneficiary/intermediary bank classify and handle this transaction under the FATF wire transfer standards?
option_a: Process the transaction normally since the account number is a unique identifier.
option_b: Treat the wire transfer as a red flag for potential sanctions stripping/evasion, execute a freeze or stop, and file an STR with FIU-IND while implementing risk-based restrictions.
option_c: Return the wire transfer to the ordering bank immediately without performing any investigation.
option_d: Call the originator directly to update the address while keeping the transaction pending for 14 working days.
explanation: Missing or truncated essential data fields (such as originator address in cross-border wires) represent a classic red flag for information stripping aimed at bypassing sanctions filters. Banks must adopt risk-based policies to freeze, reject, or halt such wires and report suspicions via STR.

option_c: Reject the account application outright without documenting reasons, as domestic PEPs pose zero risk under Indian AML regulations.

explanation: Under RBI guidelines and FATF standards, the definition of a Politically Exposed Person (PEP) extends to immediate family members (spouse, children, parents) and close associates. When a beneficial owner of a legal entity falls into this category (even as a relative of a domestic/foreign PEP), the risk is heightened. Banks must apply EDD measures, obtain senior management approval, and establish the source of wealth/funds.

The branch manager advises the customers to continue operating split transactions to avoid banking friction. When reviewed by the FIU-IND examiner, the bank is penalized under Section 13. audio_script: Question 50. A domestic scheduled bank's transaction monitoring system flags multiple accounts exhibiting structuring behavior (smurfing) just below the reporting threshold for Cash Transaction Reports (CTRs) under the PMLA rules. The branch manager advises the customers to continue operating split transactions to avoid banking friction. When reviewed by the FIU-IND examiner, the bank is penalized under Section 13. What is the precise legal threshold and aggregation principle governing CTRs that the bank failed to respect?
option_a: Transactions in cash exceeding Rs. 10 Lakhs or its equivalent in foreign currency, including all connected cash transactions that are serially integrated within one calendar month.
option_b: All cash transactions of the value of more than Rs. 10 Lakhs or its equivalent in foreign currency, and series of integrally connected cash transactions that are below Rs. 10 Lakhs where such series of transactions take place within a month.
option_c: Cash transactions exceeding Rs. 50,000 requiring PAN verification, and CTR aggregation across all accounts of the same customer aggregating to Rs. 20 Lakhs per financial quarter.
option_d: All foreign exchange transactions exceeding USD 10,000 or equivalent, aggregated over a rolling 7-day window.
explanation: Under Rule 3 read with Rule 7 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, CTRs must be furnished to FIU-IND for all cash transactions of the value of more than Rs. 10 Lakhs (or foreign currency equivalent) and all series of integrally connected cash transactions that are individually below Rs. 10 Lakhs where such series of transactions take place within a month. Branch personnel advising customers to circumvent this via structuring violates statutory anti-evasion mandates.

audio_script: Question 21. A domestic scheduled commercial bank receives an urgent freezing order under Section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967, read with the order of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), targeting an entity linked to terrorist financing. The designated entity maintains a current account, a term deposit nearing maturity with accrued interest, and a safe deposit locker. The branch manager seeks your directive as the Principal AML/KYC Examiner. Which of the following actions constitutes the legally compliant procedure under Indian AML statutes and relevant international BCBS/FATF standards?
option_a: Immediately freeze all outward remittances, but allow the term deposit to mature and payout the principal to the registered beneficial owner to avoid breach of contract.
option_b: Instantly freeze the current account, the term deposit (including principal and accrued interest), and seal the safe deposit locker without prior notice or intimation to the customer, followed by immediate reporting to UAPA nodal authorities and FIU-IND.
option_c: Issue a show-cause notice to the customer demanding an explanation of funds before enforcing the freezing order, ensuring adherence to principles of natural justice.
option_d: Freeze only the liquid accounts and permit the operation of the safe deposit locker under dual-key branch supervision to retrieve non-financial personal assets.
explanation: Under Section 51A of the UAPA, 1967, and RBI guidelines issued thereunder, banks must freeze funds, financial assets, or economic resources without delay and without prior notice to the designated individuals/entities. This covers current accounts, term deposits with interest, and safe deposit lockers. Notification or tipping-off must be strictly avoided.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT10-Q094] An authorized branch of a scheduled commercial bank in India identifies a complex corporate structure involving a foreign non-resident company holding a 14% controlling ownership interest, alongside three domestic entities holding 12%, 15%, and 9% respectively, none of whom are registered as companies limited by shares. Simultaneously, the branch receives an urgent freezing order under Section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967, concerning an individual who is a beneficial owner of the 12% domestic entity. Concurrently, the transaction monitoring system flags unusual, fragmented cash deposits aggregating just below the ₹10 lakh threshold across multiple linked accounts within a 3-day window, followed immediate outward wire transfers to a high-risk jurisdiction. Evaluating the bank's statutory obligations under the PML Rules, 2005, and RBI Master Directions on KYC, which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT?
audio_script: AMLKYC-CBT10-Q094. An authorized branch of a scheduled commercial bank in India identifies a complex corporate structure involving a foreign non-resident company holding a 14% controlling ownership interest, alongside three domestic entities holding 12%, 15%, and 9% respectively, none of whom are registered as companies limited by shares. Simultaneously, the branch receives an urgent freezing order under Section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967, concerning an individual who is a beneficial owner of the 12% domestic entity. Concurrently, the transaction monitoring system flags unusual, fragmented cash deposits aggregating just below the ₹10 lakh threshold across multiple linked accounts within a 3-day window, followed immediate outward wire transfers to a high-risk jurisdiction. Evaluating the bank's statutory obligations under the PML Rules, 2005, and RBI Master Directions on KYC, which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT?
option_a: The threshold for determining the Beneficial Owner for the foreign non-resident company structured as a company is an ownership/entitlement of more than 10%, making it a beneficial owner, whereas for the domestic entities not being companies, the threshold remains more than 15%.
option_b: Upon receipt of the UAPA Section 51A freezing order, the bank must immediately freeze funds and financial resources of the designated individual without prior notice, and simultaneously report the attempted or executed transactions to the FIU-IND through an STR within 7 working days, while preserving records for a minimum of 5 years from the date of cessation of the business relationship.
option_c: The fragmented cash deposits aggregating just below the CTR threshold across multiple linked accounts constitute structured transactions ('smurfing'), mandating the filing of a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) within 7 days of arriving at a conclusion that the transactions are suspicious, regardless of whether they crossed the Cash Transaction Report (CTR) limit.
option_d: Under the PML Rules, the statutory timeline for maintaining all necessary records of transactions—both domestic and international—as well as customer identification data and KYC records, is a minimum of five years from the date of cessation of the transaction or the termination of the business relationship, whichever is later.
explanation: Statement A is INCORRECT because per Rule 9(3) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and RBI Master Directions on KYC, the threshold for determining beneficial ownership for companies is a controlling ownership interest of more than 10% (making the 14% foreign company a BO), but for juridical persons other than companies or trusts (such as association of persons or partnerships), the threshold is ownership/entitlement of more than 15% (making the 12%, 15%, and 9% entities subject to the specific percentage criteria: entities with 12% and 9% do not meet the >15% threshold, while the 15% entity does not exceed 15%). Statement A incorrectly states the non-company threshold application across multiple entities. Statements B, C, and D accurately reflect statutory timelines, STR filing mandates under PMLA, and UAPA Section 51A freezing obligations.

audio_script: AMLKYC-CBT10-Q067. An authorized branch of a scheduled commercial bank discovers that a previously submitted Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) requires urgent supplementary information regarding a complex layering transaction. According to the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, what is the exact statutory timeline mandated for reporting suspicious transactions to the FIU-IND from the date of initial conclusion of transaction-level suspicion, and does this supplemental filing alter the original reporting obligation?
option_a: Within 7 working days of establishing suspicion; supplemental information must be provided promptly upon request by FIU-IND without resetting the original 7-day compliance window.
option_b: Within 7 days of establishing suspicion; supplementary details must be furnished within 3 working days.
option_c: Within 15 days of the close of the month in which suspicion arose; supplementary data has no statutory timeline.
option_d: Within 3 working days of establishing suspicion; supplemental disclosures must follow within 7 days.
explanation: According to the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules and RBI Master Direction on KYC, reporting entities must furnish Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) to the FIU-IND not later than 7 working days from the date of arriving at a conclusion that the transaction is suspicious. Subsequent or supplementary information must be furnished promptly upon request or as soon as detected, without violating the primary 7-day reporting mandate.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT10-Q047] During an ongoing trial under the PMLA, 2002, an accused individual argues that the funds found in their possession are legitimate business earnings and not proceeds of crime derived from a scheduled offense. The prosecution invokes Section 24 of the PMLA pertaining to the 'Burden of Proof'. Which of the following accurately describes how the burden of proof is statutorily distributed under Section 24 of the PMLA?
audio_script: Question 47. During an ongoing trial under the PMLA, 2002, an accused individual argues that the funds found in their possession are legitimate business earnings and not proceeds of crime derived from a scheduled offense. The prosecution invokes Section 24 of the PMLA pertaining to the 'Burden of Proof'. Which of the following accurately describes how the burden of proof is statutorily distributed under Section 24 of the PMLA?
option_a: The burden lies entirely on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the property constitutes proceeds of crime in all instances.
option_b: In the case of any person charged with the offense of money laundering under Section 3, the authority or court shall presume that such property is proceeds of crime, and the burden of proving that it is not proceeds of crime shall be on the accused.
option_c: The burden shifts to the accused only after the FIU-IND establishes a prima facie nexus through an independent forensic audit report submitted to the Special Court.
option_d: The burden is shared equally (50-50 evidentiary threshold) between the Enforcement Directorate and the defendant throughout the trial proceedings.
explanation: Section 24 of the PMLA, 2002 explicitly lays down the rule relating to burden of proof. Under Section 24(a), in any proceeding relating to proceeds of crime under this Act, in the case of a person charged with the offense of money laundering under Section 3, the court or Adjudicating Authority shall, unless the contrary is proved, presume that such property is proceeds of crime, thereby placing the onus squarely on the accused to prove otherwise.

audio_script: Question 48. An audit team visiting a regional branch of a foreign bank in India discovers that records pertaining to closed accounts, identity verification documents, and domestic wire transfer logs for the financial year 2014-2015 were systematically purged in December 2020. The Branch Manager defends this action by stating that the bank's internal data retention policy mandates a 5-year retention period which was duly fulfilled. option_a: The branch complied with the law, as the statutory retention period is exactly 5 years from the date of account closure or transaction completion.
option_b: The branch violated statutory requirements because the PMLA and RBI guidelines mandate that records relating to identification of customers and records of all transactions must be maintained for at least five years from the date of cessation of the transaction or termination of the business relationship, whichever is later, but some transactions required reference checks beyond standard closures.
option_c: The branch violated statutory requirements because the PMLA mandates record retention for a minimum of ten years from the date of account opening.
option_d: The branch complied with the law, provided that prior approval was obtained from the Principal Officer of the reporting entity before data purging.
explanation: According to Rule 3 of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and RBI Master Direction on KYC, reporting entities must maintain records of all transactions (both domestic and international) and customer identification documents for a period of five years from the date of transaction or cessation of the business relationship (account closure), whichever is later. Purging records without accounting for the 'cessation of business relationship' or pending investigations constitutes a statutory violation.

audio_script:
Question 24. A compliance audit of a major bank's branches reveals the following transactional anomalies:
- Branch A processed 14 cash deposits of INR 95,000 each across five separate accounts held by members of the same family within a span of three days.
- Branch B failed to maintain records of customer identification data and transaction logs for accounts closed four years ago.
- Branch C submitted Cash Transaction Reports (CTRs) for all cash transactions above INR 10 lakh, but excluded cross-border wire transfers of equivalent value from the Cross-Border Wire Transfer Report (CBWTR).
Evaluate the statutory violations under the PMLA and PML Rules and select the most accurate assessment:
option_a: Branch A committed structuring/smurfing, Branch B violated the 5-year statutory record retention rule post-account closure, and Branch C violated CBWTR reporting obligations.
option_b: Branch A is compliant as each deposit is below the INR 1 lakh CTR threshold, Branch B complied with the 3-year record retention rule, and Branch C has no obligation to report wire transfers.
option_c: Branch A violated the STR obligation by not aggregating, Branch B violated anti-money laundering laws by failing to retain records for 10 years, and Branch C's omission is permitted under RBI operational guidelines.
option_d: Branch A, B, and C have fully complied with all regulatory thresholds stipulated under the PML Rules.
explanation: Branch A's actions indicate 'structuring' or 'smurfing' to evade CTR limits, which must trigger an STR regardless of the individual amount. Branch B violated Rule 3 and Rule 10 of PML Rules, which mandate that records of customer identification and transactions must be maintained for at least 5 years after the business relationship has ended or account has been closed. Branch C violated the statutory requirement to report all cross-border wire transfers exceeding INR 5 lakh or equivalent through the CBWTR.

audio_script:
Question 74. An audit team reviewing the CKYCR database compliance of a bank discovers the following instances:
1. Uploading CKYC data of walk-in customers undertaking occasional transactions below INR 50,000 where no account-based relationship is established.
2. Failing to update existing customer KYC records in CKYCR when a customer submits updated officially valid documents during periodic updation.
3. Reusing an existing 14-digit CKYC identifier retrieved from the CKYCR search facility to onboard a customer without repeating full physical documentation.
Which of the above practices complies with regulatory instructions?
option_a: 1 and 2 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_c: 3 only
explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect because CKYCR upload is mandatory for 'account-based relationships', not for occasional customers below INR 50,000 unless specified by rules. Statement 2 is incorrect because reporting entities are statutorily required to upload/update updated KYC records to CKYCR when changes occur during periodic updation. Statement 3 is correct: banks can fetch and use the 14-digit CKYC identifier to pull records from the registry instead of fresh collection of documents, fulfilling CDD requirements efficiently.

audio_script: Question 72. Consider a complex corporate structure where a foreign holding company holds 24% in an Indian operating client, an offshore private equity fund holds 16%, and an Indian resident individual holds 15%, with various other fragmented holdings. The compliance officer is evaluating the Beneficial Ownership (BO) threshold under Rule 9 of the PML Rules, 2005 for a company. Which of the following statements regarding the determination of Beneficial Ownership for a company is correct?
option_a: The threshold for determining the beneficial owner in a company is holding of legally controlled ownership interest of more than 10%, whereas for a partnership firm or trust it is more than 15%.
option_b: The threshold for determining the beneficial owner in a company is holding of legally owned shares, capital, or profits of more than 25%, while for a partnership firm or unincorporated association it is more than 15%, and for a trust it is the author, trustee, or beneficiary holding 15% or more.
option_c: Beneficial ownership rules apply only to companies listed on recognized stock exchanges, setting a strict threshold of 5% voting rights.
option_d: The reporting entity is exempted from determining beneficial ownership if the corporate entity is incorporated outside FATF-compliant jurisdictions.
explanation: Rule 9(3) of the PML Rules, 2005 prescribes the thresholds for identifying beneficial owners: (a) For a company, the beneficial owner is the natural person(s), who, whether acting alone or together, or through one or more juridical person, has a controlling ownership interest or ownership of entitlements of more than 25% of the company; (b) For a partnership firm, it is more than 15% of capital or profits; (c) For an unincorporated association or body of individuals, it is more than 15% of the property/capital/profits; (d) For a trust, identification includes the author, trustees, beneficiaries, etc., holding 15% or more interest.

audio_script: Question 23. An Egmont Group member Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) issues an international secure information request regarding a trade-based money laundering (TBML) scheme involving systematic over-invoicing of capital machinery imports between an Indian shell company and an offshore counterparty in a secrecy jurisdiction. As the Principal AML Examiner evaluating your bank's exposure, which combination of red flags and compliance obligations must be prioritized under PMLA and FATF/Egmont guidelines?
option_a: Disclose the unredacted STR details directly to the offshore counterparty's commercial bank to expedite asset tracing.
option_b: File a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) with FIU-IND within the statutory timeline, ensure strict confidentiality to prevent 'tipping off', and review all related trade finance transactions (Letters of Credit, Bill of Lading discrepancies) for systemic vulnerabilities.
option_c: Immediately close the account and return all funds to the originating offshore entity via telegraphic transfer to mitigate direct liability.
option_d: Treat the FIU request as a formal freezing order under PMLA Section 12 and confiscate the bank guarantee margins.
explanation: Under PMLA, STRs must be filed with FIU-IND maintaining absolute confidentiality (prohibition of tipping-off). Egmont Group information sharing principles emphasize secure, channel-specific intelligence sharing and domestic statutory compliance. Closing accounts prematurely without FIU/Law Enforcement guidance can compromise investigations.

audio_script:
Question 97. Consider the following statements regarding Nested Correspondent Banking relationships and evaluate which of them are TRUE according to regulatory frameworks:
I. Nested correspondent banking refers to the use of a correspondent bank's products and services by a respondent bank's own customers.
II. Nested relationships pose high AML/KYC risks because the home correspondent bank has no direct relationship with, nor visibility over, the respondent's downstream client base utilizing the account (payable-through accounts).
III. Banks must explicitly prohibit respondent banks from allowing shell banks or unregulated entities to utilize nested accounts.
Which of the above statements are correct?

option_b: II and III only
option_c: I and III only
option_d: I, II, and III
explanation: Statement I is incorrect because nested correspondent banking refers to the use of a correspondent's account by other financial institutions (downstream respondent banks), not the respondent bank's retail/corporate customers directly. Statements II and III accurately capture the structural risks and mandatory controls regarding nested accounts and shell bank prohibitions.

II. Control through means other than voting rights, such as shareholder agreements or voting trusts, mandates the identification of the natural person exercising control, regardless of the percentage of shares held.

audio_script:
Question 20. An IIBF-certified compliance officer is evaluating a complex corporate structure for a Tier-1 private banking client under the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) guidelines on Sound Management of Risks Related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism, alongside the RBI Master Direction on KYC. The entity, registered in a high-risk jurisdiction, has a multi-layered shareholding pattern where an intermediate holding company holds 24% of voting rights, another trust holds 15%, and an individual holds 11% while exercising ultimate effective control through a shareholders' agreement. Which of the following statements regarding the identification of Beneficial Ownership (BO) and CDD application is/are TRUE?

I. The 25% ownership threshold for companies under the PML Rules, 2005 must be strictly adhered to, meaning the intermediate holding company (24%) does not trigger BO identification based on shareholding alone.
II. Control through means other than voting rights, such as shareholder agreements or voting trusts, mandates the identification of the natural person exercising control, regardless of the percentage of shares held.
III. Under BCBS guidelines, private banking relationships require a lower level of scrutiny for legal persons compared to standard retail accounts due to pre-existing wealth verification.
IV. The bank must establish the source of wealth and source of funds for the ultimate beneficial owner given the involvement of a high-risk jurisdiction corporate layer.
option_a: I, II and IV only
option_b: II and IV only
option_c: I and III only
option_d: All of the above
explanation: Under the PML Rules, 2005 and RBI Master Directions, the threshold for a company is indeed 25% ownership for natural persons. However, control can be exercised through other means (like agreements), making statement II true. Statement III is false because BCBS guidelines mandate enhanced due diligence (EDD) and higher scrutiny for private banking clients, not lower. Statement IV is true as high-risk jurisdictions necessitate establishing the source of wealth and funds for beneficial owners.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q050] Which of the following statements regarding the powers of authorities and legal immunities under the PMLA, 2002 is legally INACCURATE?
audio_script: Question 50. Which of the following statements regarding the powers of authorities and legal immunities under the PMLA, 2002 is legally INACCURATE?
option_a: Authorities under the PMLA (such as the Director, Additional Director, Joint Director, etc.) are vested with specific powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including discovery and inspection, enforcing attendance of persons, and compelling production of records.
option_b: Under Section 13 read with Section 45, officers of the Enforcement Directorate possess the power to arrest any person without a warrant based on material in their possession, and offenses under PMLA are cognizable and non-bailable.
option_c: Suits, prosecutions, or other legal proceedings can be easily instituted against the Director or any other officer of the FIU-IND or Enforcement Directorate for any action taken or intended to be done in good faith under the provisions of the PMLA without requiring prior sanction.
option_d: The Director, FIU-IND or officers of the Enforcement Directorate have the power to conduct searches and seizures of records and property pursuant to Sections 17 and 18 of the PMLA, provided there is reason to believe that any person has secreted documents or proceeds of crime.
explanation: Statement C is legally inaccurate and therefore the correct answer to the 'INACCURATE' question. Section 71 / statutory indemnity provisions of the PMLA (and similar statutes) protect officers from suits or prosecutions for actions taken or intended to be done in *good faith*. However, statement C claims proceedings can be instituted *without* prior sanction and implies lack of protection, whereas statutory provisions specifically bar suits and prosecutions against government officers for acts done in good faith in discharge of their duties (barring malicious prosecution rules, and suits are typically restricted or subject to protective immunities). Let's review standard immunity clauses: Section 41 of PMLA provides protection of action taken in good faith, stating no suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against the Central Government or any officer for anything which is done in good faith. Hence, saying they *can* be instituted easily without safeguards/good faith consideration is false.

audio_script: Question 45. An authorized branch of a scheduled commercial bank in Mumbai fails to maintain records of transactions and to furnish information to the Director, FIU-IND, as required under Section 12 of the PMLA, 2002. Consequently, the Director, FIU-IND, initiates proceedings under Section 13 of the Act. Which of the following punitive powers can the Director legally exercise against the banking company or its designated Principal Officer upon establishing the default?
option_a: Impose a monetary penalty ranging from Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 1 Lakh for each failure directly on the reporting entity, but the Director has no authority to penalize the Principal Officer individually.
option_b: Impose a monetary penalty on the reporting entity, its designated director, or employee ranging from Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 1 Lakh for each failure, alongside issuing a warning, directing compliance training, or ordering regular reporting.
option_c: Order immediate suspension of the banking license for up to 6 months and direct the attachment of the bank's operational vault assets under Section 5 of the Act.
option_d: Imprison the Principal Officer for a term extending up to 3 years and levy an administrative fine not exceeding 10% of the total suspicious transaction value.
explanation: Under Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, the Director FIU-IND may, if he considers that a reporting entity or its designated director on the Board or any of its employees has failed to comply with any of the terms of maintenance of records and reporting under Section 12, inflict any of the following penalties: (a) issue a warning; (b) direct compliance training; (c) order the reporting entity to make a specific report at specific intervals; or (d) impose a monetary penalty not less than Rs. 10,000 and which may extend to Rs. 1 Lakh for each failure.

option_d: They offer guaranteed high returns on illicit investments.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q066] When conducting Customer Due Diligence (CDD) for a legal person, under what circumstance is the identification of a Beneficial Owner not required?

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q028] As per the PMLA Rules and FIU-IND guidelines, what is the statutory timeline within which a banking company must furnish a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) to the Financial Intelligence Unit - India (FIU-IND) from the date of the conclusion of its evaluation?

module: Module B: Legal & Regulatory Framework in India
question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q030] Under the regulatory framework of PMLA and RBI guidelines, what is the prescribed frequency for conducting periodic KYC updates for 'High-Risk' customers?

option_a: Every 2 years
option_b: Every 5 years
option_c: Every 8 years
option_d: Every 10 years
explanation: As per the RBI Master Direction on KYC, periodic updation of KYC shall be carried out at least once in every 2 years for high-risk customers, at least once in every 8 years for medium-risk customers, and at least once in every 10 years for low-risk customers.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q075] An auditing team is reviewing the branch compliance logs regarding CKYCR data uploads and PEP management. They identify an instance where a branch executed an account opening for a foreign PEP without obtaining formal senior management approval, relying instead on the branch manager's discretionary power. According to the RBI Master Direction on KYC and the PML Rules, what is the precise regulatory implication of this procedural lapse?
audio_script: Question 75. An auditing team is reviewing the branch compliance logs regarding CKYCR data uploads and PEP management. They identify an instance where a branch executed an account opening for a foreign PEP without obtaining formal senior management approval, relying instead on the branch manager's discretionary power. According to the RBI Master Direction on KYC and the PML Rules, what is the precise regulatory implication of this procedural lapse?
option_a: It is a minor operational irregularity that can be rectified within 90 days without attracting regulatory penalties.
option_b: It constitutes a direct violation of PML Rules (Rule 9) and RBI Master Directions on KYC regarding PEP protocols, exposing the institution to regulatory enforcement actions and severe compliance penalties.
option_c: It is permissible if the account has a low transactional turnover and maintains a balance below INR 1 Lakh.
option_d: Branch managers are legally empowered to grant PEP approvals under delegated authority without involving senior management.
explanation: Rule 9(1A) of the PML Rules and RBI Master Directions explicitly mandate that senior management approval (such as from the Principal Officer or designated senior committee) must be obtained for establishing or continuing relationships with PEPs. Delegating this to a branch manager constitutes a severe regulatory violation.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q009] Which of the following actions represents an attempt to disrupt the 'Layering' process by a compliance officer or investigator?

option_a: Identifying the original source of the cash deposit during initial customer onboarding.
option_b: Tracking complex, rapid, and economically unjustified transfers of funds across multiple international shell companies.
option_c: Verifying the identity of the beneficial owner of a company opening a basic savings account.
option_d: Filing a Cash Transaction Report (CTR) for transactions exceeding ₹10 lakhs.
explanation: Layering involves complex movements to hide the audit trail; therefore, investigating and untangling rapid, unjustified multi-layer transfers across shell entities directly addresses the layering stage.

audio_script: Question 86. Under Section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967, and relevant orders of the Central Government, what is the mandatory immediate action required by a Scheduled Commercial Bank upon receiving the consolidated list of individuals and entities associated with UN Security Council Resolution 1267?
option_a: Report the names to FIU-IND within 7 working days via STR without restricting account operations.
option_b: Immediately freeze, without prior notice, all funds, financial assets, or economic resources held by such designated entities or individuals.
option_c: Issue a show-cause notice to the customer within 24 hours before freezing any movable assets.
option_d: Submit a suspicious transaction report to RBI and wait for specific instructions prior to asset freezing.
explanation: Section 51A of the UAPA, 1967 empowers the Central Government to freeze funds, financial assets, or economic resources of individuals/entities linked to UNSCR 1267. Banks must immediately freeze such assets without prior notice as per statutory requirements.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q022] The Egmont Group of Financial Intelligence Units establishes standards for international cooperation and secure information exchange between FIUs. In a complex cross-border trade-based money laundering (TBML) investigation involving an Indian bank branch, the FIU-IND receives a spontaneous information request from an Egmont Secure Web (ESW) member FIU. Which of the following conditions govern the use, dissemination, and handling of this information under Egmont principles and domestic PMLA frameworks?
audio_script: Question 22. The Egmont Group of Financial Intelligence Units establishes standards for international cooperation and secure information exchange between FIUs. In a complex cross-border trade-based money laundering (TBML) investigation involving an Indian bank branch, the FIU-IND receives a spontaneous information request from an Egmont Secure Web (ESW) member FIU. Which of the following conditions govern the use, dissemination, and handling of this information under Egmont principles and domestic PMLA frameworks?
option_a: The information received via the ESW can be directly used for public criminal prosecution without the prior consent of the disclosing FIU.
option_b: The recipient FIU must maintain the same level of confidentiality as requested by the disclosing FIU, and any dissemination of the information to law enforcement agencies or judicial authorities requires the prior consent of the disclosing FIU.
option_c: Egmont information is non-actionable intelligence and cannot be used by domestic banks to file Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) or freeze accounts.
option_d: The Indian bank branch must directly contact the foreign bank via SWIFT to verify the Egmont intelligence before submitting an STR to FIU-IND.
explanation: The Egmont Group principles strictly require that information exchanged between FIUs must be used only for the purpose for which it was sought and cannot be disseminated to third parties (such as law enforcement or tax authorities) without the prior express consent of the disclosing FIU.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q021] The Wolfsberg Group Anti-Money Laundering Principles for Private Banking emphasize rigorous controls regarding Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs). audio_script: Question 21. The Wolfsberg Group Anti-Money Laundering Principles for Private Banking emphasize rigorous controls regarding Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs). Consider the following branch situational dilemma: A domestic Politically Exposed Person (PEP), who is a senior minister, wishes to open a private banking account in the name of a private discretionary trust where his adult children are primary beneficiaries and an offshore corporate entity acts as the settlor. According to Wolfsberg Principles and RBI KYC guidelines, what is the mandatory sequence of approvals and control procedures that the bank must execute prior to account activation?
option_a: Approval from the branch manager suffices if the initial deposit is below INR 10 Crore, followed by regular periodic monitoring.
option_b: Senior Management approval is mandatory prior to opening the account, the bank must establish the source of wealth and source of funds of both the PEP and beneficial owners, and the account must be subjected to enhanced ongoing monitoring.
option_c: Approval can be delegated to the Relationship Manager provided an indemnity bond is signed by the PEP, as domestic PEPs carry lower risk than foreign PEPs under international standards.
option_d: The account must be rejected outright because Wolfsberg Principles prohibit private banking relationships with trusts settled by domestic PEPs.
explanation: Wolfsberg Principles and RBI Master Directions dictate that for all PEP accounts (whether foreign or domestic, noting that RBI harmonized domestic and foreign PEP definitions), establishing a relationship requires Senior Management approval prior to account opening, comprehensive verification of the source of wealth and source of funds, and enhanced ongoing monitoring.

question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q025] Under the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) Paper on 'Customer Due Diligence for Banks' and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) provisions in India, what are the strict statutory record-retention obligations regarding customer identification data, account files, and business correspondence following the termination of the business relationship or closure of the account?
audio_script: Question 25. Under the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) Paper on 'Customer Due Diligence for Banks' and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) provisions in India, what are the strict statutory record-retention obligations regarding customer identification data, account files, and business correspondence following the termination of the business relationship or closure of the account?
option_a: Records must be retained for a minimum of 3 years from the date of account closure.
option_b: Records must be retained for a minimum of 5 years from the date of cessation of the business relationship or account closure.
option_c: Records must be retained for a minimum of 10 years after the business relationship ends, along with all transaction records.
option_d: Records must be retained permanently in digital archives until ordered destroyed by the High Court.
explanation: As per the PMLA, 2002 (specifically Section 12 read with PML Rules), records pertaining to the identification of customers, address proofs, and all transaction records (both domestic and international) must be maintained and preserved for a period of at least five (amended to ten years under recent PMLA amendments) years from the date of cessation of the transaction / business relationship between the client and the reporting entity. (Note: PMLA rules mandate maintaining records for 5 years post-relationship, but specific RBI/PMLA harmonized instructions and amendments require maintaining records for up to 10 years).

option_a: Merely holding funds in a foreign bank account without notifying tax authorities

option_c: Failing to maintain books of accounts for cash transactions exceeding ten lakh rupees
option_d: Willful default of bank loans obtained from scheduled commercial banks
explanation: Section 3 of the PMLA, 2002 defines the offence of money laundering as whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge or knowingly assists or is a party or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projecting it as untainted property.

When conducting OFAC (Office of Foreign Assets Control) sanction screening for international wire transfers, an Indian bank identifies a transaction involving a designated entity incorporated in a jurisdiction outside the US, but the transaction is denominated in USD and clears through a correspondent bank in New York. module: Module A: Anti-Money Laundering Overview
question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q001] In the context of the three classic stages of money laundering, which of the following activities best exemplifies the 'Layering' stage?
audio_script: Question 1. In the context of the three classic stages of money laundering, which of the following activities best exemplifies the 'Layering' stage?
option_a: Depositing large amounts of physical cash into multiple bank accounts using different fictitious names.
option_b: Purchasing high-value real estate properties directly using proceeds from illicit drug trafficking.
option_c: Executing multiple complex wire transfers across offshore shell companies to obscure the audit trail.
option_d: Blending illegal cash proceeds into the daily legitimate revenue of a cash-intensive retail business.
explanation: Layering involves moving funds around through various financial transactions (such as complex wire transfers through shell companies) to distance them from their illicit source and make the audit trail difficult to follow.

module: Module A: Anti-Money Laundering Overview
question_text: [AMLKYC-CBT11-Q010] Which statement accurately differentiates between 'Placement' and 'Layering' in the money laundering lifecycle?
audio_script: Question 10. Which statement accurately differentiates between 'Placement' and 'Layering' in the money laundering lifecycle?
option_a: Placement involves integrating funds into the economy, while layering involves moving funds offshore.
option_b: Placement is the introduction of dirty cash into the financial system, whereas layering involves distancing the funds from their source through complex transactions.
option_c: Placement is illegal, while layering is a legitimate tax-avoidance mechanism.
option_d: Placement utilizes shell corporations, whereas layering utilizes physical cash couriers.
explanation: Placement focuses on getting illicit cash into the financial system, while layering focuses on executing subsequent transactions to obscure the audit trail and distance the funds from the original crime.

audio_script: Question 3. Which of the following describes the fundamental operational mechanism of the Hawala or Informal Value Transfer System (IVTS) in money laundering?

option_b: Transfer of value without actual physical movement of currency, relying on a network of brokers (hawaladars) and trust.
option_c: Execution of high-frequency trades on recognized stock exchanges using encrypted algorithmic bots.
option_d: Use of decentralized cryptocurrency tumblers to obfuscate transaction histories on public blockchains.
explanation: Hawala is an informal value transfer system based on trust, where money is transferred without any actual physical movement of currency, typically settled through a network of brokers known as hawaladars.

[AMLKYC-CBT11-Q024] A meticulous AML investigation uncovers a sophisticated structuring scheme (smurfing) executed across five different branches of an Indian bank in a metropolitan area over a rolling 7-day period. According to the PML Rules and RBI Master Direction on KYC, evaluate the following statements and identify the correct combination:

I. Separate cash transactions below INR 10 Lakhs in multiple branches do not require aggregation unless they occur in a single branch on the same operational day.
II. The bank is obligated to file a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) with FIU-IND regardless of the threshold amount if transactions indicate structuring or suspected proceeds of crime.
III. The statutory timeline for filing an STR with FIU-IND is within 7 working days from the date of establishing the suspicion.
IV. Cash Transaction Reports (CTRs) must be submitted to FIU-IND by the 15th day of the succeeding month for individual cash transactions exceeding INR 10 Lakhs.
audio_script:
Question 24. A meticulous AML investigation uncovers a sophisticated structuring scheme (smurfing) executed across five different branches of an Indian bank in a metropolitan area over a rolling 7-day period. Multiple individuals deposit cash amounts just below the statutory reporting threshold of INR 10 Lakhs into a single current account belonging to a shell entity. According to the PML Rules and RBI Master Direction on KYC, evaluate the following statements and identify the correct combination:

I. Separate cash transactions below INR 10 Lakhs in multiple branches do not require aggregation unless they occur in a single branch on the same operational day.
II. The bank is obligated to file a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) with FIU-IND regardless of the threshold amount if transactions indicate structuring or suspected proceeds of crime.
III. The statutory timeline for filing an STR with FIU-IND is within 7 working days from the date of establishing the suspicion.
IV. Cash Transaction Reports (CTRs) must be submitted to FIU-IND by the 15th day of the succeeding month for individual cash transactions exceeding INR 10 Lakhs.
option_a: I, II and IV only
option_b: II, III and IV only
option_c: I and III only
option_d: All of the above
explanation: Statement I is false because interconnected accounts and patterns of structuring across multiple branches must be aggregated and monitored; the rule against 'smurfing' specifically targets splitting transactions across branches/accounts to evade thresholds. Statement II is true (STRs have no monetary threshold and must be filed for suspicious behavior). Statement III is true (STR must be filed within 7 working days of establishing suspicion). Statement IV is true (CTRs are submitted monthly by the 15th of the succeeding month).

question_text:
[AMLKYC-CBT11-Q047] Under the statutory record-retention mandates prescribed by the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and RBI Master Directions on KYC, analyze the following statements regarding timelines and document types:

1. All records pertaining to customer identification (KYC) and address must be maintained along with transaction records for at least five years from the date of cessation of the business relationship or closure of the account.
2. In cases where records relate to ongoing investigations or matters currently under litigation before any court or regulatory authority, the 5-year retention countdown pauses, and records must be retained until the final conclusion of the legal proceedings, overriding the standard 5-year destruction rule.
3. Transaction records must be maintained in a manner that enables reconstitution of individual transactions, and such records must be preserved for a period of five years from the date of the respective transaction, irrespective of whether the account is active or closed.

Which of the above statements are legally correct?
audio_script:
Question 47. Under the statutory record-retention mandates prescribed by the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and RBI Master Directions on KYC, analyze the following statements regarding timelines and document types:

1. All records pertaining to customer identification (KYC) and address must be maintained along with transaction records for at least five years from the date of cessation of the business relationship or closure of the account.
2. In cases where records relate to ongoing investigations or matters currently under litigation before any court or regulatory authority, the 5-year retention countdown pauses, and records must be retained until the final conclusion of the legal proceedings, overriding the standard 5-year destruction rule.
3. Transaction records must be maintained in a manner that enables reconstitution of individual transactions, and such records must be preserved for a period of five years from the date of the respective transaction, irrespective of whether the account is active or closed.

Which of the above statements are legally correct?
option_a: 1 and 3 only
option_b: 2 and 3 only
option_d: 1 only
explanation: All three statements are correct. Per PML Rules and RBI guidelines, reporting entities must maintain records of all transactions (both domestic and international) for at least 5 years from the date of transaction (Statement 3). Additionally, records of customer identification and related documents must be maintained for at least 5 years after the business relationship has ended or account closed (Statement 1). Furthermore, if any litigation, audit, or investigation is pending, records must be retained beyond the statutory minimum until the matter is finally resolved (Statement 2).

question_text:
[AMLKYC-CBT11-Q072] Consider a complex compliance scenario in a large commercial bank involving a newly identified PEP account. Evaluate the following statements regarding the regulatory obligations under the RBI Master Direction on KYC and the PML Rules:
I. Senior management approval is required only when establishing a business relationship with a PEP, and subsequent elevation of an existing customer to PEP status does not trigger this requirement.
II. The requirement to establish the 'source of wealth' is distinct from establishing the 'source of funds' in PEP due diligence.
III. Enhanced ongoing monitoring must be applied to all PEP relationships regardless of whether they are domestic or foreign PEPs.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
audio_script:
Question 72. Consider a complex compliance scenario in a large commercial bank involving a newly identified PEP account. Evaluate the following statements regarding the regulatory obligations under the RBI Master Direction on KYC and the PML Rules:
I. Senior management approval is required only when establishing a business relationship with a PEP, and subsequent elevation of an existing customer to PEP status does not trigger this requirement.
II. The requirement to establish the 'source of wealth' is distinct from establishing the 'source of funds' in PEP due diligence.
III. Enhanced ongoing monitoring must be applied to all PEP relationships regardless of whether they are domestic or foreign PEPs.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
option_a: I and II only
option_b: II and III only
option_c: I and III only
option_d: All I, II, and III
explanation: Statement I is incorrect because senior management approval is required both at the commencement of the relationship and when an existing customer/beneficial owner is subsequently identified as a PEP. Statement II is correct (source of wealth refers to the origin of the PEP's entire net worth, while source of funds refers to the origin of the particular funds in the specific transaction/account). Statement III is correct as RBI guidelines apply EDD universally to both foreign and domestic PEPs (though domestic PEPs may be evaluated on a risk-categorized basis, the core PEP protocols demand rigorous scrutiny).
